title: Forecasting the Leading Indicator of a Recession: The 10-Year minus 3-Month Treasury Yield Spread
text: This paper investigates the predictive efficacy of the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield spread as a leading indicator for United States recessions. While the spread between the 10-year and 2-year Treasury notes is a widely cited predictor, the 10-year minus 3-month spread has demonstrated superior historical performance, often providing earlier and more reliable signals. This study aims to rigorously evaluate this indicator's forecasting power using a comprehensive dataset spanning from 1982 to the present. We employ a probit model framework to estimate the probability of a recession occurring within a specified forecast horizon, conditional on the observed yield spread. Our analysis controls for potential structural breaks and incorporates robustness checks against other established leading indicators, such as unemployment claims and manufacturing activity indices. The empirical results confirm that an inversion of the 10-year minus 3-month spread is a statistically significant and economically meaningful predictor of impending economic downturns. The model exhibits a high degree of in-sample fit and demonstrates substantial out-of-sample predictive accuracy, particularly over horizons of six to eighteen months. Furthermore, we find that the predictive power of the spread is not uniform; it is more pronounced in periods following sustained economic expansions. We also analyze the dynamic relationship between the spread and recession probabilities using a time-varying parameter model, revealing that the sensitivity of the indicator has evolved over time. The findings underscore the critical importance of the 10-year minus 3-month spread for policymakers, investors, and economic analysts. We conclude that while no single indicator is infallible, this specific yield curve measure remains an indispensable tool in the macroeconomic forecaster's toolkit, offering a valuable, forward-looking metric for anticipating economic contractions.

title: Detection and Annotation of Plant Organs from Digitized Herbarium Scans using Deep Learning
text:
Digitized herbarium specimens constitute a vast and growing resource for biodiversity research, documenting plant diversity, phenology, and distribution across centuries. However, extracting meaningful biological information from these scans remains challenging due to the complexity and variability of specimen layouts, which typically include pressed shoots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and labels arranged in unpredictable configurations. Manual annotation of such structures is labor-intensive and does not scale to the millions of specimens now available in digital repositories.

Recent advances in deep learning, particularly in object detection and semantic segmentation, offer promising tools for automating the analysis of herbarium scans. Yet, applying these methods to botanical specimens is complicated by the scarcity of annotated training data, the wide morphological diversity across plant families, and the visual clutter inherent in scanned sheets. Consequently, robust methods for detecting and annotating plant organs are needed to unlock the full scientific value of herbaria.

In this paper, we present a deep learning approach for the detection and annotation of plant organs from digitized herbarium scans. We describe our dataset, model architecture, and evaluation strategy, and demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately localize and classify key organs such as leaves, flowers, and fruits. Our results highlight both the potential and the current limitations of automated organ annotation, providing a foundation for future work in large-scale herbarium digitization and biodiversity informatics.

title: Prediction of Chronic Kidney Disease Using Deep Neural Network
text: The proposed Deep Neural Network (DNN) model was evaluated against Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) on a dataset of 1,200 patient records with 24 clinical attributes. Using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, the DNN achieved the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.8%, precision of 96.9%, recall of 98.2%, and an F1-score of 97.5%. In comparison, LR reached 91.2% accuracy, RF 94.6%, and SVM 93.1%. The DNN also yielded the lowest false-negative rate (1.8%), which is critical in clinical screening where missed CKD cases carry severe consequences. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for the DNN was 0.991, versus 0.943 for RF and 0.928 for SVM. Ablation analysis showed that removing serum creatinine and glomerular filtration rate reduced accuracy by 6.4 and 5.1 percentage points, respectively, confirming their diagnostic importance. Training converged in 120 epochs with a batch size of 32 and a dropout rate of 0.3, which mitigated overfitting; the gap between training and validation accuracy remained below 1.5%. These results demonstrate that the DNN outperforms conventional classifiers and offers a reliable, non-invasive tool for early CKD prediction.

title: Exact Combinatorial Optimization with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
In this paper, we introduced a graph convolutional neural network approach for learning to solve mixed-integer linear programs exactly. Our method leverages the bipartite graph representation of MILPs to learn branching policies that generalize across problems of varying sizes and structures, eliminating the need for handcrafted heuristics or per-instance tuning. Through extensive experiments on four NP-hard problem classes—set covering, combinatorial auctions, capacitated facility location, and maximum independent set—we demonstrated that our learned branching rule, when integrated into a state-of-the-art branch-and-bound solver, consistently reduces the number of branch-and-bound nodes explored and often improves solving time compared to classical branching strategies such as strong branching, pseudocost branching, and reliability branching.

A key finding is that the learned policy transfers effectively across problem scales: models trained on small instances retain strong performance on substantially larger instances, without retraining. This suggests that the network captures structural signals that are intrinsic to the problem family rather than memorizing instance-specific patterns. Furthermore, our approach remains competitive on instances whose structure differs from the training distribution, underscoring its robustness as a general-purpose branching heuristic.

Despite these encouraging results, several directions remain open. The current framework assumes access to the full MILP formulation at solving time and does not exploit primal information or cutting-plane dynamics, both of which could further inform branching decisions. Extending the model to incorporate such signals, as well as to other combinatorial structures and solver components beyond branching, is a promising avenue for future work. More broadly, our results support the view that graph learning is a natural and effective tool for combinatorial optimization, bridging the gap between data-driven methods and the exactness guarantees of classical solvers. We hope this work stimulates further research at the intersection of machine learning and discrete optimization.

title: Wheel-Rail Interface Condition Estimation (W-RICE)
text: This paper presents Wheel-Rail Interface Condition Estimation (W-RICE), a novel framework for estimating the contact condition at the wheel-rail interface, a critical determinant of traction, braking, and safety in railway operations. Existing approaches rely on direct measurement or indirect inference from vehicle dynamics, yet they often struggle with varying environmental conditions and limited sensor observability. W-RICE addresses these challenges by fusing multi-source signals, including axle-box acceleration, bogie vibration, and wheel-rail contact forces, within a probabilistic estimation architecture. The framework extracts condition-sensitive features in both time and frequency domains and employs a physics-informed learning model to map these features to a continuous friction coefficient estimate. A key contribution is the incorporation of a degradation-aware prior that adapts to evolving surface states such as contamination, wear, and moisture. The proposed method is validated using field data collected from a full-scale roller rig and revenue service trains under diverse operating scenarios. Results demonstrate that W-RICE achieves a mean absolute error below 0.04 in friction estimation and maintains robustness against sensor noise and wheel irregularities. Compared with conventional estimators, the framework improves accuracy by up to 32% and reduces false alarms in low-adhesion detection. These findings suggest that W-RICE offers a practical and scalable solution for real-time wheel-rail interface monitoring, with potential applications in condition-based maintenance and adhesion control systems.

title: Generalised linear models for prognosis and intervention: Theory, practice, and implications for machine learning
text: The growing availability of longitudinal and high-dimensional data has renewed interest in statistical models that can support both prognosis and intervention. Generalised linear models (GLMs) remain a cornerstone of applied regression, offering interpretable effect estimates, well-established inferential theory, and computational tractability. Yet their use in prognosis and intervention research is often framed narrowly, as a baseline prediction tool rather than as a coherent framework linking estimation, causal reasoning, and decision-making. This paper examines GLMs through that broader lens. We first review the theoretical foundations of GLMs, including link functions, variance structures, and the conditions under which coefficients admit meaningful prognostic and interventional interpretations. We then discuss practical issues that arise in applied work, such as model specification, confounding, effect modification, penalisation, and validation, with emphasis on how these choices shape downstream conclusions. We further consider the relationship between GLMs and machine learning methods, arguing that the two are not competing paradigms but complementary components of a modelling workflow. In particular, GLMs provide a transparent reference against which flexible learners can be benchmarked, calibrated, and interpreted, while machine learning can extend GLMs through nonlinearity, regularisation, and high-dimensional feature selection. By clarifying what GLMs can and cannot deliver for prognosis and intervention, we aim to provide methodological guidance for researchers and to identify implications for the design of interpretable, causally informed machine learning systems in health and social research.

title: Tracking the Progression of Reading Through Eye-gaze Measurements
text: Reading is a complex cognitive process that unfolds over time, and understanding its temporal dynamics is essential for both theoretical models of comprehension and practical applications such as adaptive learning systems and reading assessment. This paper presents a framework for tracking the progression of reading through eye-gaze measurements, leveraging the tight coupling between ocular movements and underlying linguistic and cognitive processing. We collected high-resolution eye-tracking data from participants reading texts of varying difficulty while their fixation durations, saccade amplitudes, regression patterns, and pupil responses were recorded. A set of gaze-derived metrics—including first-pass fixation time, gaze duration, total reading time, and regression rate—was computed at the word, sentence, and passage levels. These metrics were then used to construct temporal profiles of reading progression, capturing how attentional allocation shifts as readers move from early lexical access to higher-level integrative comprehension. To model progression quantitatively, we employed sequential and probabilistic approaches, including hidden Markov models and recurrent neural networks, to infer latent reading states and predict comprehension outcomes. Results show that gaze-based indicators reliably distinguish between fluent and effortful reading, and that the evolution of fixation patterns predicts comprehension accuracy with high precision. Furthermore, our analysis reveals characteristic signatures of processing difficulty, such as increased regressions and prolonged fixations, that emerge before explicit comprehension failures become apparent. The proposed approach offers a non-invasive, continuous, and fine-grained means of monitoring reading in real time, with implications for personalized instruction, early detection of reading difficulties, and human–computer interaction systems that adapt to the reader’s cognitive state.

title: Genetic optimization algorithms applied toward mission computability models
text:
The increasing complexity of modern computational missions demands models that can evaluate not only raw performance but also the feasibility of deploying algorithms under real-world resource constraints. Mission computability models formalize this evaluation by characterizing whether a given computational task can be completed within specified bounds on time, energy, memory, and hardware availability. As mission requirements grow more stringent, identifying configurations that satisfy these constraints becomes a combinatorial optimization problem of considerable difficulty.

Genetic optimization algorithms offer a compelling approach to this challenge. By mimicking the mechanisms of natural selection—selection, crossover, and mutation—these algorithms explore large, non-convex search spaces without requiring gradient information, making them well suited to the discrete and multi-objective nature of mission computability. Prior work has applied evolutionary methods to scheduling, resource allocation, and task mapping, yet their systematic integration with formal computability models remains underexplored.

This paper investigates the application of genetic optimization algorithms to mission computability models. We formulate the mapping of computational tasks to heterogeneous resources as an optimization problem constrained by mission-specific feasibility criteria, and we evaluate the ability of genetic algorithms to discover configurations that maximize mission success under varying resource budgets. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of this approach and highlight directions for future refinement.

title: Endogenous Representation of Asset Returns
text: We estimate the endogenous representation model on monthly returns of 500 U.S. equities (2000–2020). The first latent factor explains 42.3% of cross-sectional variance, versus 35.1% for the leading PCA component, and the second adds 18.7% (cumulative 61.0%). Out-of-sample, the model attains an average cross-sectional R² of 0.287, compared with 0.194 for PCA and 0.221 for a five-factor Fama–French specification. Pricing errors shrink accordingly: mean absolute alpha falls from 0.41% to 0.19% per month, and the GRS statistic drops from 3.87 (p = 0.002) to 1.42 (p = 0.118). The estimated factor risk premia are 0.63% (t = 3.11) and 0.34% (t = 2.07) per month. Endogenous loadings exhibit a half-life of 7.4 months, implying slow information diffusion. During the 2008 crisis, factor volatility rose 2.8-fold while loadings remained stable, suggesting the representation captures persistent rather than transient comovement.

title: Addressing the Privacy Implications of Mixed Reality: A Regulatory Approach
text: In conclusion, the rapid advancement of mixed reality technologies presents unprecedented challenges to individual privacy, as these systems continuously collect, process, and infer sensitive data from users and their surroundings. This paper has argued that existing legal frameworks are insufficient to address the unique risks posed by MR, including pervasive biometric tracking, spatial mapping, and behavioral inference. A proactive, multi-layered regulatory approach is therefore essential—one that combines updated data protection statutes, transparency obligations, and technical privacy-by-design standards. Such regulation must balance innovation with fundamental rights, ensuring that users retain meaningful control over their data. Without decisive regulatory intervention, the immersive nature of mixed reality threatens to normalize surveillance in ways that current consent models cannot adequately mitigate.

title: The effect of intermittent upwelling events on plankton blooms
text: Intermittent upwelling events are a common feature of coastal and eastern boundary current systems, yet their role in regulating plankton bloom dynamics remains poorly constrained relative to steady or seasonal upwelling. Here we investigate how repeated, time-limited upwelling pulses influence the timing, magnitude, and taxonomic composition of phytoplankton and zooplankton blooms using a combination of idealized nutrient–phytoplankton–zooplankton (NPZ) modeling, a one-dimensional vertical water-column model forced with realistic wind stress, and analysis of satellite chlorophyll and sea surface temperature records from a representative upwelling region. The results show that intermittency exerts a strong nonlinear control on bloom development. Short pulses separated by relaxation periods allow surface nutrient concentrations to be replenished while retaining phytoplankton biomass within the euphotic zone, producing blooms that can exceed those generated by continuous upwelling of equivalent cumulative nutrient flux. However, when the interval between upwelling events exceeds a critical threshold, advective loss and zooplankton grazing suppress accumulation, and bloom magnitude declines sharply. The model also reveals a phase-dependent response: upwelling events that coincide with an established phytoplankton population trigger rapid, transient blooms, whereas events that initiate a population from low biomass produce weaker and more delayed responses. Zooplankton grazing introduces a lagged negative feedback that amplifies sensitivity to event spacing, favoring blooms under intermediate intermittency. Satellite analyses are consistent with these model results, showing that bloom intensity in intermittent upwelling regions correlates more strongly with the duration of relaxation periods than with total upwelling-favorable wind forcing. These findings demonstrate that the temporal structure of upwelling, not merely its total intensity, is a first-order determinant of plankton bloom dynamics, with implications for predicting ecosystem productivity and biogeochemical fluxes under changing wind regimes.

title: Internet of Things for Elderly and Fragile People
text: The rapid aging of the global population has intensified the demand for innovative solutions that support elderly and fragile individuals in maintaining independence, safety, and quality of life. The Internet of Things (IoT) offers transformative potential in this context by enabling continuous monitoring, ambient assisted living, and timely intervention through interconnected smart devices and sensors. Despite growing research interest, significant challenges remain regarding usability, privacy, interoperability, and ethical deployment. This paper examines the role of IoT in addressing the multifaceted needs of elderly and fragile populations. It reviews current technological developments, identifies key barriers to adoption, and proposes a human-centered framework for designing inclusive IoT systems. The aim is to inform researchers, practitioners, and policymakers about how IoT can be responsibly leveraged to enhance care and autonomy for vulnerable groups.

title: DQI: A Guide to Benchmark Evaluation
text: Benchmarks are widely used to compare and rank the performance of AI systems, yet their results are often reported without sufficient attention to the quality of the evaluation itself. Flawed benchmark items, ambiguous annotations, contaminated test sets, and inconsistent scoring protocols can all distort conclusions and mislead both researchers and practitioners. This paper introduces DQI (Data Quality Index), a practical guide for benchmark evaluation that shifts attention from leaderboard outcomes to the integrity of the evaluation process. DQI organizes assessment around four dimensions: data quality, task validity, scoring reliability, and interpretive transparency. For each dimension, we define concrete indicators, describe common failure modes, and provide actionable procedures for auditing existing benchmarks and designing new ones. We further present a lightweight scoring rubric that aggregates these indicators into a single interpretable index, enabling comparison across benchmarks while preserving diagnostic detail. We demonstrate the utility of DQI through case studies of widely used benchmarks in natural language processing and machine learning, showing how the framework surfaces issues that conventional reporting obscures. Our analysis reveals that many reported performance differences shrink or disappear once evaluation quality is taken into account. We argue that benchmark evaluation should be treated as a first-class research activity rather than an afterthought, and that claims of progress should be accompanied by evidence of evaluation quality. DQI offers a shared vocabulary and a reproducible protocol for that purpose, supporting more trustworthy comparisons and more informed decisions about which benchmarks to use, extend, or retire.

title: Bridging the Gap between Optimal Trajectory Planning and Safety-Critical Control with Applications to Autonomous Vehicles
text:
Autonomous vehicles must generate agile maneuvers while guaranteeing safety under tight state and input constraints, yet trajectory planning and safety-critical control are typically developed in isolation. Planning computes dynamically feasible, often time-optimal trajectories offline or over a receding horizon, whereas safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) enforce set invariance in real time. This separation yields conservative behavior, since the safety layer treats the nominal plan as an exogenous reference, and may even render the planned trajectory infeasible.

This paper bridges that gap by embedding a time-optimal trajectory parameterization directly into a CBF-based quadratic program. The resulting controller tracks the optimal path while a higher-order CBF enforces input and state constraints, and a line-search on the path parameter preserves feasibility without sacrificing optimality. We prove recursive feasibility for the resulting optimization problem and characterize the conditions under which the safety filter leaves the optimal solution unmodified.

Simulations and experiments on an autonomous racing platform show that the proposed approach recovers near-optimal lap times while guaranteeing constraint satisfaction, outperforming standard safety filters that slow the vehicle unnecessarily.

title: Analysis of Safe Ultrawideband Human-Robot Communication in Automated Collaborative Warehouse
text:
The measurement campaign yielded 1,248 received pulse waveforms across four operational zones of the automated warehouse. After bandpass filtering (3.1–10.6 GHz) and 20 dB amplification, the mean received signal amplitude at 1 m separation was −41.3 dBm (σ = 2.7 dB), decreasing to −68.9 dBm at 8 m, consistent with a path loss exponent of 1.87 in the line-of-sight (LOS) aisle and 2.94 in obstructed shelving areas.

Safety performance was evaluated using the specific absorption rate (SAR) and the peak spatial-average power density. At the maximum transmit power of 0.5 mW, the measured maximum 1 g-averaged SAR at 10 cm from the human torso was 0.42 W/kg, remaining below the 1.6 W/kg FCC limit with a margin of 74%. The power density at 20 cm was 8.7 µW/cm², i.e., 0.9% of the ICNIRP reference level (1 mW/cm²). No thermal effect exceeding 0.1 °C was recorded during 30-minute continuous exposure.

Communication reliability was assessed via packet error rate (PER) and latency. In LOS conditions, PER remained below 0.8% for robot speeds up to 2.0 m/s, with a mean end-to-end latency of 4.3 ms (99th percentile: 11.7 ms). Under non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions caused by metal racking, PER increased to 3.9% at 6 m, requiring one retransmission in 2.1% of frames; latency rose to 9.8 ms mean. Interference from 12 co-located IEEE 802.11ac access points raised the noise floor by 6.2 dB but degraded PER by only 1.4 percentage points owing to the UWB duty cycle of 0.6%.

Emergency stop commands were transmitted with 100% success across 500 trials at all tested distances (1–10 m) and robot speeds (0.5–2.5 m/s), with worst-case latency of 13.2 ms, well within the 50 ms safety threshold. These results confirm that ultrawideband links satisfy both electromagnetic safety and real-time control requirements in collaborative warehouse environments.

title: Please, do not decentralize the Internet with (permissionless) blockchains!
text:
The push to decentralize the Internet with permissionless blockchains rests on a compelling narrative: return power to users, eliminate trusted intermediaries, and make infrastructure censorship-resistant. Our analysis suggests that this narrative does not survive contact with technical and economic reality. Permissionless blockchains achieve decentralization by paying an enormous price in throughput, latency, storage, and energy, and they do so by re-introducing, rather than removing, concentrated power: mining pools, stake whales, core developers, and infrastructure providers already dominate these supposedly leaderless systems. Rebuilding DNS, identity, storage, or content delivery on such foundations would trade functioning, if imperfect, institutions for slower, costlier, and less accountable alternatives.

We therefore argue for a clear separation of concerns. Blockchains are a poor substitute for Internet infrastructure, but they remain a legitimate tool for applications whose value depends on credible neutrality and verifiable state, such as payments, asset issuance, and coordination among mutually distrusting parties. The appropriate response to the genuine problems of the Internet—platform concentration, surveillance, opaque moderation—is not wholesale replacement with permissionless chains, but targeted institutional, regulatory, and protocol-level reforms, combined with permissioned or federated systems where decentralization is actually required.

Decentralization should be treated as a means, not an end. Advocating it indiscriminately undermines both the Internet and the credibility of the very technologies invoked to save it. Researchers and policymakers should evaluate each proposal on its demonstrated merits, not on the ideological appeal of the label it carries.

title: Noise induces continuous and noncontinuous transitions in neuronal interspike intervals range
text: Noise is ubiquitous in neural systems and plays a constructive role in shaping the statistical structure of spike trains. In this paper, we investigate how noise intensity and correlation properties govern transitions in the range of neuronal interspike intervals (ISIs) within a stochastic Hodgkin–Huxley-type framework. By systematically varying the noise amplitude and its temporal correlation, we characterize the distribution of ISI ranges and identify two distinct transition scenarios: continuous and noncontinuous. For weak noise, the ISI range varies smoothly with noise intensity, reflecting a gradual broadening of the firing regularity. Beyond a critical noise level, however, the ISI range exhibits an abrupt jump, indicating a noncontinuous transition accompanied by a sharp reorganization of the underlying firing dynamics. We further show that the nature of these transitions depends nonmonotonically on the noise correlation time, with an optimal correlation window that separates the continuous and noncontinuous regimes. A bifurcation analysis of the corresponding deterministic skeleton, combined with the effective Fokker–Planck description, reveals that the noncontinuous transition originates from noise-induced switching between coexisting attractors, whereas the continuous transition arises from a smooth noise-dependent drift of the spiking threshold. These results demonstrate that noise is not merely a disruptive factor but a key control parameter that can switch the qualitative behavior of neuronal ISI statistics, with potential implications for neural coding and information transmission in noisy environments.

title: Distributed Consensus of Nonlinear Multi-Agent Systems With Mismatched Uncertainties and Unknown High-Frequency Gains (Extended Version)
text:
1. Introduction

Distributed consensus of multi-agent systems (MASs) has attracted considerable attention over the past two decades due to its broad applications in formation control, sensor networks, power grids, and unmanned swarms. The core objective is to design local interaction protocols such that all agents reach a common state or output using only neighboring information. For linear MASs, consensus conditions are now well understood under fixed or switching topologies, with or without communication delays.

However, practical agents are inherently nonlinear, and their dynamics often involve uncertainties that do not satisfy the matching condition, i.e., mismatched uncertainties that enter through channels different from the control input. Such uncertainties may arise from unmodeled dynamics, parameter perturbations, or external disturbances, and they can severely degrade consensus performance or even destroy stability. Meanwhile, in many physical systems—such as robotic manipulators, aircraft, and chemical processes—the control input is scaled by unknown high-frequency gains (also termed unknown control directions or unknown input coefficients). These gains are typically state-dependent, time-varying, and not accessible for measurement, which invalidates standard adaptive or robust consensus designs that presume known input effectiveness.

Existing results on MASs with uncertainties mainly address matched uncertainties or known input gains. Adaptive consensus schemes with Nussbaum-type functions can handle unknown control directions, but they usually require symmetric or identical gain signs and are restricted to matched channels. Robust consensus based on sliding modes or disturbance observers can attenuate mismatched uncertainties, yet they assume known input gains and bounded disturbances with known bounds. To date, the problem of distributed consensus for nonlinear MASs subject to *both* mismatched uncertainties and unknown high-frequency gains remains largely open, especially when the communication topology is directed and the nonlinearities are not globally Lipschitz.

This paper aims to fill this gap. We consider a class of nonlinear MASs where each agent suffers from mismatched uncertainties and unknown, possibly state-dependent, high-frequency gains. By integrating a distributed adaptive law with a dynamic gain technique and a novel Nussbaum-type function that accommodates asymmetric and time-varying gain signs, we propose a fully distributed consensus protocol requiring neither global topology information nor a priori bounds on the uncertainties. Sufficient conditions are established to guarantee asymptotic consensus under a directed spanning tree. The effectiveness of the proposed scheme is illustrated by a numerical example.

title: IAN: Combining Generative Adversarial Networks for Imaginative Face Generation
text: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated remarkable success in synthesizing realistic facial images, yet generating faces that are simultaneously novel and semantically coherent remains a challenge. Existing approaches often compromise between photorealism and imaginative diversity, producing either conventional portraits or distorted artifacts. This paper introduces IAN, a novel framework that combines multiple GAN architectures to generate imaginative faces with high visual fidelity. IAN integrates an adversarial generator with a learned latent-space mapping network, enabling the synthesis of faces that transcend conventional facial distributions while preserving structural plausibility. A multi-discriminator strategy is employed to jointly enforce photorealism, identity consistency, and creative variation, while a diversity regularization term prevents mode collapse and encourages exploration of the latent manifold. We evaluate IAN on benchmark face datasets, comparing it against state-of-the-art generative models using both quantitative metrics—Frechet Inception Distance and diversity scores—and human perceptual studies. Experimental results demonstrate that IAN produces faces that are rated as more imaginative and visually appealing, without sacrificing realism or coherence. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for creative applications in art, design, and entertainment, where novel yet believable facial identities are desired.

title: New Insights on Learning Rules for Hopfield Networks: Memory and Objective Function Minimisation
text:
Hopfield networks have long served as a foundational model for associative memory, yet the learning rules that shape their energy landscapes remain an active subject of investigation. Classical formulations, such as the Hebbian and Storkey rules, were derived primarily to guarantee memory retrieval, often treating the minimisation of an explicit objective function as a secondary or implicit concern. This separation has left open the question of how learning rules relate to the geometry of the energy surface they induce.

In this paper, we revisit the learning problem for Hopfield networks and derive new learning rules that explicitly connect memory storage with the minimisation of an objective function. Rather than imposing storage constraints and then inspecting the resulting dynamics, we formulate learning as a direct optimisation over the network's energy landscape, allowing the rule to emerge from the objective itself. This perspective reveals previously unobserved relationships between established rules and clarifies the conditions under which they succeed or fail.

We analyse the resulting rules in terms of storage capacity, convergence, and robustness, and compare them against classical approaches on standard benchmarks. Our results offer new insights into the design of learning rules for recurrent associative networks and suggest that objective-driven formulations provide a more principled route to understanding memory in Hopfield networks.

title: Simulation of cloud drop collisions in ABC flow
text:
We simulated 10,000 cloud droplet pairs with radii ranging from 5 to 25 μm in a steady Arnold–Beltrami–Childress (ABC) flow at Taylor–Reynolds number Re_λ = 72. The collision kernel Γ was computed for three Stokes numbers (St = 0.05, 0.1, and 0.2) and compared with the Saffman–Turner and Hall kernels.

For St = 0.1, the simulated geometric collision rate was 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ cm³ s⁻¹, approximately 2.3 times higher than the Saffman–Turner prediction (7.8 × 10⁻⁹ cm³ s⁻¹) and 1.6 times the Hall kernel (1.1 × 10⁻⁸ cm³ s⁻¹). The enhancement peaked at 3.1× for droplet pairs with radius ratio r₂/r₁ ≈ 0.7, where preferential concentration and caustic formation were strongest. At St = 0.05, enhancement dropped to 1.4×, while St = 0.2 yielded 2.6× but with increased collision-angle dispersion.

The radial distribution function g(r) at contact reached 4.2 for St = 0.1, confirming significant clustering. Relative velocity variance increased from 0.8 cm² s⁻² (Saffman–Turner) to 2.1 cm² s⁻² in our simulations, driven by both sling and caustic effects. Energy dissipation rate was fixed at ε = 100 cm² s⁻³, and the Kolmogorov scale η = 0.3 mm. Our results indicate that ABC flow, despite its idealized topology, reproduces turbulent collision statistics within 15% of direct numerical simulations for St ≤ 0.1, validating its use for cloud microphysics parameterizations.

title: Neuronal mechanisms for sequential activation of memory items: dynamics and reliability
text: We investigated the neuronal mechanisms underlying the sequential activation of memory items, focusing on the dynamics and reliability of transitions between stored representations. Using a network model of coupled excitatory and inhibitory populations, we showed that sequences can be generated intrinsically through competitive dynamics, without requiring external timing signals. The reliability of sequence order depends critically on the balance between excitation and inhibition, the strength of item-specific adaptation, and noise amplitude. Moderately strong adaptation ensures unambiguous transitions, whereas excessive noise or weak inhibition leads to skipped or repeated items. We further demonstrated that the same network can store and replay multiple sequences by switching the effective connectivity pattern, suggesting a flexible substrate for episodic recall. Our results link dynamical principles to behavioral constraints such as speed–accuracy trade-offs and provide testable predictions for sequential activity observed in prefrontal and hippocampal circuits.

title: Vertical Coherence of Turbulence in the Atmospheric Surface Layer: Connecting the Hypotheses of Townsend and Davenport
text: The vertical coherence of turbulence in the atmospheric surface layer is examined by connecting two classical hypotheses: Townsend’s attached-eddy hypothesis and Davenport’s gust factor hypothesis. While both frameworks describe the structure of turbulent fluctuations, their relationship in terms of vertical coherence remains underexplored. This study analyzes coherence spectra from field measurements to quantify how turbulent eddies retain vertical organization across heights. Results show that vertical coherence follows a scaling behavior consistent with Townsend’s attached eddies, but with a damping that depends on Davenport’s aerodynamic admittance. A unified model is proposed, linking the coherence decay rate to the normalized frequency and surface-layer stability. The findings reconcile the two hypotheses and provide a practical parameterization for wind engineering applications, improving predictions of wind loading on tall structures.

title: Ensemble model for pre-discharge icd10 coding prediction
text:
International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) coding is essential for hospital reimbursement, clinical research, quality reporting, and public health surveillance. In practice, coders assign these codes retrospectively after reviewing the full inpatient record, which is time-consuming, costly, and prone to inconsistency. As electronic health records become increasingly available, automated ICD-10 prediction has attracted considerable attention. Accurate prediction before discharge is particularly valuable: it can support prospective coding, reduce claim denials, shorten the billing cycle, and allow clinicians and coders to verify codes while the patient is still hospitalized.

However, pre-discharge ICD-10 prediction remains challenging. First, the label space is extremely large and highly imbalanced, with thousands of fine-grained codes and a long-tailed distribution. Second, clinical narratives, laboratory results, and administrative data are heterogeneous and noisy, and their predictive value varies across code categories. Third, because only information available before discharge can be used, the observation window is incomplete and evolving, which weakens models trained on fully documented records. Single-model approaches often capture only part of this complex signal and tend to overfit frequent codes while performing poorly on rare but clinically important ones.

Ensemble learning offers a principled way to address these difficulties by combining complementary learners to improve robustness, calibration, and generalization. Nevertheless, simply averaging heterogeneous models may be suboptimal when base learners differ in feature views, code granularity, and error patterns. Effective ensembles therefore require careful design of diversity, weighting, and decision fusion, as well as validation under realistic pre-discharge conditions.

In this study, we propose an ensemble model for pre-discharge ICD-10 coding prediction using routinely collected electronic health record data. The model integrates multiple base learners trained on structured and unstructured features and combines their outputs through a learned fusion strategy. We evaluate the proposed approach on a large real-world inpatient cohort and compare it with strong single-model and ensemble baselines. The results demonstrate improved predictive performance, especially for infrequent codes, suggesting that ensemble modeling is a practical pathway toward reliable prospective ICD-10 coding.

title: Adaptive time series analysis of Mauna Loa CO2 data: tvf-EMD based detrend and extraction of seasonal variability
text: Atmospheric CO₂ concentrations recorded at the Mauna Loa Observatory constitute the longest continuous direct measurement of background CO₂ and a benchmark for detecting anthropogenic climate forcing. However, the iconic Keeling Curve is shaped by multiple superimposed processes—long-term anthropogenic increase, seasonal biospheric exchange, and episodic volcanic and ENSO-related perturbations—whose nonstationary amplitudes and phases complicate conventional decomposition. This study applies time-varying filtering-based empirical mode decomposition (tvf-EMD), an adaptive, fully data-driven technique designed for nonstationary and nonlinear signals, to the deseasonalized and seasonally adjusted Mauna Loa records spanning 1958–2024. The decomposition separates a monotonic growth component, quasi-periodic seasonal oscillations, and residual modes associated with volcanic eruptions and ENSO events. Reconstructed seasonal cycles reveal increasing amplitude over recent decades, with peak CO₂ uptake and release dates exhibiting measurable temporal shifts, while the secular trend shows accelerating growth with superimposed multi-year fluctuations. The extracted modes are validated against independent records and cross-checked with alternative decomposition methods, including EMD and ensemble EMD. Results demonstrate that tvf-EMD provides improved mode separation, reduced mode mixing, and physically interpretable components, offering a robust framework for characterizing nonstationary variability in long-term atmospheric CO₂ observations.

title: Towards sample-efficient episodic control with DAC-ML
text:
Reinforcement learning agents classically require large amounts of interaction to learn effective policies, a limitation that is particularly acute in environments where data collection is costly or dangerous. Episodic control offers a promising alternative by rapidly storing and reusing past experiences, enabling fast learning in sparse-reward settings. However, existing episodic control methods still struggle with sample efficiency, as they often rely on exhaustive memory lookups or hand-crafted similarity metrics that scale poorly with state dimensionality.

Recent advances in deep learning have produced architectures capable of learning compact, task-relevant representations directly from high-dimensional inputs, yet their integration with episodic memory remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce DAC-ML, a framework that combines differentiable attention mechanisms with contrastive learning to construct a learned episodic memory that generalizes across similar states. By jointly optimizing representation and retrieval, DAC-ML reduces the number of episodes required to achieve competitive performance.

We evaluate DAC-ML on a suite of benchmark tasks, including procedurally generated environments and continuous control problems. Our results show that DAC-ML achieves comparable or superior returns to established episodic control baselines while using significantly fewer samples, and that its learned memory transfers effectively to novel task variations. These findings suggest that combining attention-based retrieval with representation learning is a viable path toward more sample-efficient episodic control.

title: A Novel Ramp Metering Approach Based on Machine Learning and Historical Data
text: The proposed machine learning-based ramp metering approach was evaluated against fixed-time and ALINEA controllers in a calibrated simulation of a 12-km freeway corridor. Over a 6-hour peak period, the proposed method reduced average mainline travel time by 21.4% (from 14.2 to 11.2 min) and increased average mainline speed by 17.8% (from 62.3 to 73.4 km/h) compared with fixed-time control. Compared with ALINEA, it achieved a further 9.6% reduction in travel time and a 12.1% decrease in ramp queue length (from 38 to 33 vehicles). Total vehicle throughput improved by 8.7%, while total delay fell by 24.3%. These gains were consistent across three demand scenarios, with the largest improvements (up to 27.5% delay reduction) under oversaturated conditions, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating historical data with machine learning for adaptive ramp metering.

title: Contact Tracing: Beyond the Apps
text: Contact tracing is a cornerstone of epidemic control, yet its effectiveness cannot be reduced to the adoption of digital tools. This paper has shown that app-based solutions, while promising in speed and scalability, remain constrained by low uptake, privacy concerns, and inequitable access, and that they function best as one component within a broader, hybrid system. Manual interviewing, community-based outreach, and trusted local networks continue to reach populations that apps miss, particularly in low-resource and marginalized settings. The evidence reviewed here indicates that success depends less on technological sophistication than on integration: combining digital efficiency with human judgment, clear governance, and sustained public trust. Future research should move beyond measuring downloads and notifications toward evaluating health outcomes, equity, and the social acceptability of combined approaches. Contact tracing, in short, must be understood as a socio-technical practice. Apps are instruments, not answers; their value is realized only when embedded in inclusive, well-resourced public health infrastructures.

title: Masks and COVID-19: a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted widespread use of masks as a public-health intervention, yet estimating their causal effect remains challenging due to confounding, behavioural responses, and varying implementation contexts. This paper develops a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions, with masks as a motivating case. We formalise the problem of attributing changes in transmission outcomes to mask adoption when randomisation is infeasible and observational data are shaped by endogenous policy decisions. The framework combines potential-outcomes reasoning with structural assumptions about exposure, adherence, and interference, and clarifies the conditions under which effect estimates can be interpreted causally. We show how value can be imputed under alternative counterfactual scenarios and how sensitivity to unmeasured confounding can be assessed. The approach is illustrated using COVID-19 data and provides a general template for evaluating non-pharmaceutical interventions where causal inference must inform policy under uncertainty.

title: Teaching Economics with Interactive Browser-Based Models
text: The teaching of economics increasingly demands tools that make abstract theoretical constructs tangible for digitally native students. While traditional instruction relies heavily on static graphs and algebraic derivations, these methods often fail to convey the dynamic, interdependent nature of economic systems. Interactive browser-based models offer a promising pedagogical alternative: they require no specialized software, run on any device with a web browser, and allow students to manipulate parameters in real time and observe immediate graphical and numerical feedback. Despite growing interest in simulation-based learning, the literature lacks a consolidated account of how such lightweight, accessible tools can be effectively designed and integrated into undergraduate economics curricula. This paper addresses that gap by presenting a framework for developing interactive browser-based models and evaluating their impact on student engagement and conceptual understanding. Drawing on case studies from microeconomics, macroeconomics, and game theory, we demonstrate how these models bridge the gap between formal theory and intuitive reasoning. We argue that the low barrier to entry and high degree of interactivity make browser-based models a scalable, inclusive, and pedagogically powerful addition to the economics classroom. The paper concludes with design principles and practical recommendations for instructors.

title: UAV Target Tracking in Urban Environments Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
text: Target tracking in urban environments presents significant challenges for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) due to occlusions, cluttered backgrounds, dynamic obstacles, and complex three-dimensional structures that degrade conventional tracking methods. This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for autonomous UAV target tracking in dense urban settings. The problem is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process, where the UAV learns continuous control policies for navigation and target following directly from high-dimensional visual observations. A dueling double deep Q-network architecture with prioritized experience replay is employed to improve sample efficiency and training stability, while a curriculum learning strategy gradually increases environmental complexity. The proposed method is evaluated in a photorealistic urban simulation across scenarios involving varying target motion patterns, building densities, and occlusion frequencies. Experimental results demonstrate that the DRL-based tracker achieves a 23% improvement in tracking success rate and a 31% reduction in average tracking error compared with state-of-the-art baselines, including Kalman filter-based and imitation learning approaches. The learned policy exhibits robust generalization to unseen environments without retraining. These findings indicate that deep reinforcement learning offers a promising pathway toward reliable autonomous aerial tracking in challenging urban airspace.

title: Daily Middle-Term Probabilistic Forecasting of Power Consumption in North-East England
text:
Accurate short-term electricity demand forecasting is essential for grid stability, economic dispatch, and the integration of variable renewable generation. While day-ahead point forecasts are well established, medium-term probabilistic forecasts spanning several days to two weeks remain comparatively underdeveloped, despite their growing importance for unit commitment, fuel procurement, and maintenance scheduling. This gap is particularly relevant for regions with distinct seasonal and weather-driven consumption patterns, where uncertainty compounds rapidly beyond the day-ahead horizon.

North-East England offers a compelling case study. The region exhibits pronounced heating-related winter peaks, a significant industrial load component, and increasing penetration of distributed renewable generation, all of which complicate demand dynamics. Reliable probabilistic forecasts at daily resolution over a middle-term horizon could support both network operators and market participants in managing these challenges. However, few studies have addressed this region or horizon specifically, and existing approaches often rely on deterministic methods that fail to quantify predictive uncertainty.

This paper develops and evaluates a daily middle-term probabilistic forecasting framework for power consumption in North-East England. Using historical load, meteorological, and calendar data, we compare several statistical and machine learning models, including quantile regression and gradient boosting, over forecast horizons of up to fourteen days. Forecast skill is assessed using pinball loss, calibration diagnostics, and sharpness measures. The results aim to establish practical benchmarks for medium-term probabilistic demand forecasting in the region and to identify the model classes best suited to this task.

title: Using detrended deconvolution foreign exchange network to identify currency status
text: Applying the detrended deconvolution foreign exchange network (DDFXN) to daily exchange rates of 42 currencies from 2015 to 2023, we constructed directed networks using a 60-day rolling window. The average degree centrality of the USD remained the highest across all windows (mean = 0.87, SD = 0.05), confirming its dominant status. The EUR followed with a mean centrality of 0.71 (SD = 0.07), while the CNY rose from 0.38 in 2015 to 0.64 in 2023, indicating its growing regional influence. Deconvolution filtering reduced noise: the signal-to-noise ratio improved by 34.2% compared to standard correlation networks. Community detection revealed three stable clusters: a dollar bloc (USD, CAD, MXN; modularity Q = 0.61), a European cluster (EUR, CHF, SEK; Q = 0.58), and an Asian cluster (CNY, JPY, KRW; Q = 0.53). Notably, the GBP exhibited fluctuating status, with centrality dropping from 0.69 (2016) to 0.52 (2020) before recovering to 0.60 (2023). Granger causality tests showed that USD returns led 28 of 41 other currencies at the 5% significance level, while CNY led 9 currencies, primarily in Asia. These results demonstrate that DDFXN effectively distinguishes core and peripheral currencies and captures dynamic status shifts, offering a robust tool for exchange rate network analysis.

title: Multiple Sclerosis disease: a computational approach for investigating its drug interactions
text: This study presented a computational framework for investigating drug interactions in Multiple Sclerosis, integrating systems biology, network pharmacology, and molecular modeling approaches. By reconstructing the molecular landscape of MS and mapping approved and investigational compounds onto disease-associated targets, we identified key interaction hubs and potential synergistic or antagonistic drug combinations. Our results highlight the centrality of immunomodulatory pathways, particularly those involving TNF-α, IL-17, and JAK/STAT signaling, and reveal that certain combination therapies may produce non-additive effects that warrant further experimental validation. The computational pipeline developed here offers a scalable and cost-effective strategy for prioritizing drug repurposing candidates and predicting polypharmacological outcomes, thereby reducing the reliance on exhaustive in vitro screening. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. The predictions are inherently dependent on the completeness and accuracy of the underlying interaction databases, and the absence of dynamic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters may oversimplify real-world drug behavior. Additionally, inter-individual variability in MS patients, including genetic and environmental factors, was not fully captured in our models. Despite these caveats, the study demonstrates the utility of computational approaches in narrowing the therapeutic search space and generating testable hypotheses. Future work should focus on integrating patient-specific omics data, longitudinal clinical outcomes, and advanced machine learning algorithms to refine interaction predictions. Ultimately, this work contributes to the growing field of computational drug interaction analysis and supports the rational design of combination therapies for Multiple Sclerosis, aiming to improve efficacy while minimizing adverse effects.

title: A Topological Approach to Inferring the Intrinsic Dimension of Convex Sensing Data
text: We study the problem of inferring the intrinsic dimension of data generated by a convex sensing model, where a high-dimensional signal is observed through a set of random linear measurements followed by a convex transformation. Traditional dimension estimation methods often rely on local geometric or statistical assumptions that may fail under such nonlinear, high-dimensional observations. We propose a topological approach based on persistent homology to recover the intrinsic dimension from the observed data. Our key insight is that the intrinsic dimension of the signal space is encoded in the asymptotic behavior of the persistent homology of the sensing data, specifically through the growth rate of Betti numbers as a function of the filtration parameter. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that, under suitable conditions on the measurement matrix and the convex function, the persistent homology of the data converges to that of a determinantal point process whose dimension equals the intrinsic dimension. This leads to a consistent estimator of the intrinsic dimension. We further develop a practical algorithm that computes the persistent homology of a filtered simplicial complex built from the data and estimates the dimension via a slope-based method. Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications, including phase retrieval and one-bit compressed sensing, demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach compared to existing methods. Our results highlight the potential of topological tools for dimension inference in nonlinear sensing problems and open new directions for integrating persistent homology with convex geometry and high-dimensional statistics.

title: Knowledge Discovery in Cryptocurrency Transactions: A Survey
text: Cryptocurrencies have evolved from niche digital assets into a global financial infrastructure processing millions of transactions daily. These transactions are recorded on public ledgers, forming massive, heterogeneous, and ever-growing datasets that encode rich information about monetary flows, market behaviour, and illicit activities. Extracting actionable knowledge from such data has become a vibrant research area at the intersection of data mining, blockchain analytics, and financial forensics. Unlike conventional payment systems, cryptocurrency networks offer unprecedented transparency while preserving pseudonymity, creating both opportunities and challenges for knowledge discovery. Researchers have applied clustering, network embedding, graph mining, and machine learning to link addresses, detect anomalies, trace illicit flows, and infer market sentiment. However, the field remains fragmented: studies differ in data sources, feature engineering, evaluation metrics, and ethical constraints, making systematic comparison difficult. This survey provides a comprehensive review of knowledge discovery techniques in cryptocurrency transactions. We organise existing work along the analytical pipeline—data acquisition, address profiling, transaction graph construction, pattern mining, and downstream applications such as anti-money laundering and market prediction. We also discuss open challenges, including scalability, cross-chain analysis, privacy preservation, and reproducibility. By consolidating methods and identifying gaps, this survey aims to guide future research and support the development of robust, interpretable, and ethically sound analytical tools for cryptocurrency transaction data.

title: Influence of Absolute Humidity, Temperature and Population Density on COVID-19 Spread and Decay Durations: Multi-prefecture Study in Japan
text: This study analyzed the relationship between COVID-19 spread and decay durations and environmental factors. Environmental factors such as absolute humidity (AH), temperature, and population density have been reported to affect the spread of COVID-19. The spread and decay durations over the period between January and May 2020 in Japan were investigated. The infection spread and decay durations in 47 prefectures were calculated using a non-linear regression model. The results indicated that a higher population density accelerated the spread of COVID-19. The influence of AH and temperature on the spread and decay durations was also analyzed. A higher AH was associated with a shorter spread duration and a longer decay duration. A higher temperature was associated with a shorter spread duration and a shorter decay duration. The results of this study suggest that the spread and decay of COVID-19 are influenced by environmental factors such as AH, temperature, and population density, and that these factors should be considered in future pandemic response strategies.

title: Dynamics of fintech terms in news and blogs and specialization of companies of the fintech industry
text:
The rapid proliferation of financial technologies has generated a dynamic and evolving vocabulary that both reflects and shapes the fintech industry. Terms such as "blockchain," "neobank," "robo-advisor," and "open banking" emerge, diffuse, and sometimes fade across public discourse, yet little is known about how their usage patterns differ across communication channels or how they relate to the strategic positioning of fintech companies. News media and blogs represent two distinct arenas of fintech discourse: the former typically follows editorial gatekeeping and broader audience orientation, while the latter often serves as a space for practitioner commentary, technical elaboration, and niche community engagement. Understanding how fintech terminology evolves in these two arenas can illuminate the mechanisms by which industry language stabilizes, diversifies, or becomes obsolete, and can reveal whether public discourse anticipates, mirrors, or lags behind corporate activity.

This study addresses these questions by analyzing the dynamics of fintech terms in a large corpus of news articles and blog posts, tracking their frequency, dispersion, and co-occurrence over time. We then relate these linguistic dynamics to the specialization of companies operating in the fintech industry, using company descriptions and classification data to identify which subdomains—such as payments, lending, insurance, or wealth management—each firm occupies. By linking term trajectories to corporate specialization, we examine whether the vocabulary prominence of specific fintech concepts aligns with the concentration of companies in corresponding market segments, and whether news and blogs differ in their sensitivity to such industrial shifts.

The contribution of this work is twofold. First, it offers a longitudinal, comparative account of fintech terminology across two distinct media, extending prior research on technology discourse and lexical change. Second, it connects discursive patterns to the structural composition of the fintech industry, providing empirical evidence on the relationship between language and market specialization. The findings are expected to inform researchers, practitioners, and policymakers about how fintech narratives form and evolve, and about the extent to which public communication channels reflect the underlying segmentation of the industry.

title: Normalized Connectomes Show Increased Synchronizability with Age Through Their Second Largest Eigenvalue
text:
We analyzed structural connectomes from 88 healthy participants aged 6–85 years, reconstructed from diffusion MRI and normalized by dividing each row by its sum (row-stochastic normalization) to remove node-strength heterogeneity. Synchronizability was quantified as the inverse of the second largest eigenvalue of the normalized Laplacian, λ₂⁻¹, where smaller λ₂ indicates stronger synchronization capacity. Consistent with our hypothesis, λ₂ decreased monotonically with age (Spearman ρ = −0.61, p < 0.001), corresponding to an increase in synchronizability from 4.82 ± 0.71 (mean ± SD) in the youngest quartile (6–18 years) to 7.36 ± 0.94 in the oldest quartile (66–85 years), a 52.7% increase. A linear mixed-effects model controlling for sex and head motion confirmed a significant age effect (β = 0.041 per year, 95% CI [0.028, 0.054], p < 0.001), explaining 34% of the variance in λ₂⁻¹.

To test whether this effect depended on normalization, we repeated the analysis on unnormalized connectomes. Here, λ₂⁻¹ showed no significant age trend (ρ = −0.09, p = 0.40), and λ₂ values were dominated by a few high-degree hubs. Normalization thus unmasked the age-related shift in synchronizability.

We next examined the eigenvector associated with λ₂. Its participation coefficient increased with age (ρ = 0.48, p < 0.001), indicating that the mode governing synchronization became more spatially distributed. Modularity of the normalized connectome declined modestly with age (ρ = −0.27, p = 0.012), suggesting that increased synchronizability arises partly from reduced community isolation. Finally, λ₂⁻¹ correlated positively with a composite cognitive score (r = 0.44, p < 0.001), linking the spectral signature to behavior. Together, these results show that normalized connectomes become more synchronizable with age, and that λ₂ captures this effect where raw connectivity does not.

title: Image-Based Benchmarking and Visualization for Large-Scale Global Optimization
text: This paper introduced a framework for image-based benchmarking and visualization of large-scale global optimization algorithms. By mapping high-dimensional search spaces onto two-dimensional representations, the proposed approach enables intuitive inspection of algorithm behavior, convergence patterns, and landscape interactions that are otherwise obscured in numerical tables or low-dimensional projections. We demonstrated the utility of this framework across a diverse set of benchmark functions and state-of-the-art optimizers, showing that visual signatures can reveal stagnation, premature convergence, and exploration–exploitation imbalances that traditional performance metrics may miss. Furthermore, the image-based benchmarking protocol facilitates qualitative comparison across algorithms and problem instances, complementing quantitative measures such as solution quality and convergence speed. Our experiments indicate that visual analytics can serve as a practical diagnostic tool for both algorithm designers and practitioners, particularly when dealing with the thousands of dimensions typical in modern large-scale optimization tasks. Several limitations remain. The projection from high-dimensional spaces to images inevitably loses information, and the interpretability of visual patterns depends on the chosen mapping and color scheme. Future work should investigate adaptive projection methods, interactive visual querying, and integration with automated hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, extending the framework to constrained, multi-objective, and dynamic optimization problems would broaden its applicability. Overall, image-based benchmarking offers a promising direction for making large-scale optimization more transparent, reproducible, and accessible, and we hope it encourages further research at the intersection of visual computing and evolutionary computation.

title: Implementing Stepped Pooled Testing for Rapid COVID-19 Detection
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has created an unprecedented demand for large-scale diagnostic testing, yet resource constraints often limit the capacity of laboratories to process individual samples in a timely manner. This paper presents a stepped pooled testing strategy designed to accelerate COVID-19 detection while conserving testing reagents and personnel. Unlike conventional pooled testing, which relies on a fixed pool size, the proposed approach employs a sequential, multi-stage algorithm that adaptively adjusts pool sizes based on the estimated prevalence and the results of earlier testing rounds. We formulate the expected number of tests per individual as a function of prevalence and pool size, and derive optimal pool configurations that minimize total testing burden under sensitivity and specificity constraints. Simulation experiments using prevalence rates ranging from 0.1% to 5% demonstrate that the stepped strategy reduces the average number of tests by 40–70% compared with individual testing, and outperforms single-stage pooling by 15–30% under low-prevalence conditions. We further validate the method on a real-world dataset of 10,000 nasopharyngeal swabs, showing that it maintains a false negative rate below 2% while increasing throughput by more than twofold. The results indicate that stepped pooled testing offers a practical, scalable, and cost-effective solution for rapid COVID-19 detection in resource-limited settings, and can be readily adapted to other infectious diseases with similar testing bottlenecks.

title: Variable Neighborhood Search for the Bin Packing Problem with Compatible Categories
text:
1. Introduction

The bin packing problem (BPP) is a classical NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem that arises in numerous logistics and resource allocation settings. Given a set of items with known sizes and a set of identical bins with fixed capacity, the BPP seeks to pack all items into the minimum number of bins without exceeding capacity. In practice, however, items are rarely interchangeable. In many real-world applications—such as warehousing, container loading, and cloud resource allocation—items belong to different categories, and only items from compatible categories may be placed together in the same bin. This practical constraint gives rise to the bin packing problem with compatible categories (BPPCC), in which a compatibility relation specifies which category pairs can share a bin. The BPPCC generalizes the classical BPP and is therefore at least as difficult, while its additional structure renders standard BPP heuristics ineffective.

The BPPCC has received limited attention compared with its practical importance. Existing studies have mainly focused on integer programming formulations and simple constructive heuristics, which struggle to produce high-quality solutions for large instances within reasonable time. Metaheuristics, and in particular variable neighborhood search (VNS), have proven highly effective for a wide range of packing and assignment problems, yet their potential for the BPPCC remains largely unexplored. VNS is attractive because it systematically explores neighborhoods of increasing size around a incumbent solution, balancing intensification and diversification without requiring extensive parameter tuning. These properties make it well suited to the BPPCC, where the interaction between category compatibility and capacity utilization creates a complex search landscape.

This paper addresses this gap by developing a variable neighborhood search algorithm for the BPPCC. The proposed method combines a dedicated construction heuristic, a set of neighborhood operators tailored to category compatibility, and an efficient local search procedure. We evaluate the algorithm on a broad set of benchmark instances and compare it with existing approaches. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formulates the problem. Section 4 presents the proposed VNS. Section 5 reports computational results, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

title: Using Multiple Imputation to Classify Potential Outcomes Subgroups
text: The classification of individuals into latent subgroups based on potential outcomes is central to many causal inference problems, including the identification of responder and non-responder types. However, these subgroups are inherently unobserved, as each individual is observed under only one treatment condition, and missing outcomes hinder direct classification. We propose a framework that treats unobserved potential outcomes as missing data and uses multiple imputation to account for the uncertainty in subgroup classification. By imputing the missing potential outcomes repeatedly, the method yields probabilistic subgroup memberships that propagate imputation uncertainty into subsequent analyses. We evaluate the approach through simulation studies and an empirical application, comparing it with complete-case and single-imputation alternatives. Results show that multiple imputation reduces misclassification, improves subgroup recovery, and provides valid confidence intervals for subgroup-specific effects. The framework is broadly applicable to settings where latent subgroup membership is of substantive interest.

title: Causal inference methods for small non-randomized studies: Methods and an application in COVID-19
text:
Randomized controlled trials are the gold standard for estimating causal effects, but they are often infeasible for small populations, rare exposures, or urgent public health crises. In such settings, researchers frequently rely on non-randomized observational data, where confounding and limited sample size complicate valid causal inference. The COVID-19 pandemic exemplifies this challenge: early in the crisis, decisions about treatments and interventions had to be made using small, non-randomized cohorts, often with few events and substantial baseline imbalance. Standard regression adjustment can perform poorly in these settings, and many propensity score methods require larger samples to achieve adequate balance and stable estimation.

This paper reviews and compares causal inference methods suitable for small non-randomized studies, focusing on approaches that remain robust when sample sizes are limited and overlap is imperfect. We consider propensity score matching and weighting, including their small-sample refinements, as well as doubly robust estimators, entropy balancing, and targeted maximum likelihood estimation. We evaluate these methods through a simulation study designed to mimic realistic small-study conditions, varying sample size, confounding strength, and outcome prevalence. Particular attention is given to bias, variance, and confidence interval coverage, since valid uncertainty quantification is essential for decision-making.

We then apply these methods to a COVID-19 observational dataset to estimate the effect of a treatment on clinical outcomes. By illustrating both the performance and practical constraints of each approach, we provide guidance for analysts conducting causal inference in small non-randomized settings, where methodological choices can materially affect conclusions.

title: Application of a system of indicatirs for assessing the socio-economic situation of a subject based on digital shadows
text: The proposed system of indicators was tested on the socio-economic data of the Kondratiev Oblast for the period 2021–2023. The integral index of socio-economic development, calculated on the basis of digital shadows, increased from 0.61 in 2021 to 0.74 in 2023, indicating a positive trend. The most significant growth was recorded in the "investment attractiveness" block, where the normalized indicator rose from 0.42 to 0.68, driven by a 17.3% increase in fixed capital investment. At the same time, the "demographic stability" block demonstrated a decline from 0.55 to 0.49, reflecting a 2.1% annual population decrease and a migration outflow of 8,400 people. Correlation analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between the digital shadow index and gross regional product per capita (r = 0.83, p < 0.01). The obtained results confirm that the proposed indicator system provides a more accurate and prompt assessment of territorial development compared to traditional statistical methods, reducing the lag in data acquisition from 6 months to 11 days.

title: A generalized linear threshold model for an improved description of the spreading dynamics
text: In this paper, we proposed a generalized linear threshold model to improve the description of spreading dynamics. By introducing a heterogeneous threshold distribution and incorporating the influence of cumulative exposure, our model captures the complex contagion process more accurately than the classical linear threshold model. Extensive simulations on synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate that the proposed model reproduces empirical spreading patterns, including the emergence of non-monotonic effects and the dependence of outbreak size on network structure. Our results reveal that the interplay between threshold heterogeneity and social reinforcement significantly alters the spreading threshold and final epidemic size. These findings provide a more nuanced understanding of information and behavior diffusion, and offer a versatile framework for future studies on complex contagion.

title: A nucleation and growth model for COVID-19 epidemic in Japan
text: The COVID-19 epidemic in Japan has exhibited multiple waves of infection, each characterized by distinct timing, regional heterogeneity, and varying effectiveness of public health interventions. Understanding the underlying transmission dynamics is essential for retrospective evaluation and future preparedness. This study proposes a nucleation and growth model to describe and analyze the epidemic trajectory of COVID-19 in Japan. The model conceptualizes the spread of infection as a two-stage process: initial localized nucleation events, where clusters emerge and seed transmission, followed by a growth phase driven by spatial diffusion and population-level mixing. We incorporate time-dependent reporting data from Japan, including confirmed cases and regional outbreaks, to calibrate the model parameters. The nucleation phase is modeled using a stochastic birth-death process, while the growth phase is captured by a deterministic logistic-type function with a time-varying growth rate that reflects changes in contact patterns and intervention intensity. Our results show that the proposed model reproduces the observed multi-wave pattern and provides quantitative estimates for key epidemiological quantities, such as the effective reproduction number and the per-capita growth rate during each wave. The model further reveals that the transition from nucleation to growth is sensitive to the size and frequency of initial clusters, as well as to the delay in implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions. We discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the role of cluster-based transmission and for designing targeted containment strategies. The nucleation and growth framework offers a flexible and interpretable tool for analyzing COVID-19 dynamics in Japan and can be adapted to other regions with similar epidemic characteristics.

title: Characterizing the COVID-19 Transmission in South Korea Using the KCDC Patient Data
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has posed unprecedented challenges to public health systems worldwide, with countries adopting diverse strategies to mitigate transmission. South Korea was among the first countries outside China to experience a significant outbreak, yet it rapidly gained international attention for its aggressive testing, contact tracing, and digital surveillance measures.
