The Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (KCDC) has systematically published patient data, including infection routes, demographic information, and exposure histories, offering a rare opportunity to empirically examine transmission dynamics in a high-income, densely populated setting. Understanding these dynamics is critical not only for retrospective evaluation of containment policies but also for informing future preparedness. However, most existing studies rely on aggregated case counts or limited time windows, which obscures heterogeneous transmission patterns across regions, age groups, and outbreak clusters. Moreover, few analyses have fully leveraged the granular, individual-level KCDC patient data to characterize superspreading events, serial intervals, and the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions. To address this gap, this study analyzes the KCDC patient data to quantify key transmission parameters and identify factors driving variability in COVID-19 spread in South Korea. By integrating epidemiological metrics with demographic and spatial information, we aim to provide a nuanced portrait of the outbreak’s progression, from the early Daegu cluster to later community transmission. Our findings are expected to enhance understanding of transmission heterogeneity and offer evidence-based insights for tailoring interventions in similar settings.

title: Network desynchronization by non-Gaussian fluctuations
text: Understanding how noise shapes the collective dynamics of coupled oscillators is a central problem in nonlinear science, with implications ranging from neuronal synchronization to power-grid stability. While the desynchronizing effect of Gaussian white noise is well established, the role of non-Gaussian fluctuations remains largely unexplored. Here we develop a theory of network desynchronization driven by shot noise, a paradigmatic form of non-Gaussian fluctuations characterized by finite correlation time and heavy-tailed amplitude statistics. Starting from the Kuramoto model of globally coupled phase oscillators subject to Poissonian shot noise, we derive the nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation governing the oscillator density and obtain the stability boundary of the synchronized state through a self-consistent linear stability analysis. We show that the desynchronization threshold depends nontrivially on the noise intensity, the shot rate, and the jump-size distribution, and that non-Gaussianity can either promote or suppress synchronization depending on the ratio of the correlation time to the intrinsic relaxation time of the order parameter. In the fast-noise limit, we recover an effective Gaussian description, whereas slow, rare, large-amplitude jumps induce desynchronization at noise intensities far below the Gaussian prediction. Our results establish a general framework for assessing the stability of collective oscillations under realistic, non-Gaussian environmental fluctuations.

title: Vision as an Energy-Driven Process
text:
For decades, the dominant metaphor in cognitive neuroscience has framed vision as a computational process: light enters the eye, signals propagate through hierarchical neural networks, and the brain transforms sensory data into a stable perceptual representation. This framework has yielded remarkable insights into feature detection, object recognition, and the neural correlates of visual awareness. Yet it leaves a fundamental question largely unaddressed: why does seeing feel effortful under some conditions and effortless under others, and why do certain visual tasks deplete cognitive resources while others do not? A growing body of evidence suggests that vision is not merely computation but also expenditure—an active, metabolically costly process whose dynamics are shaped by the brain's constant need to manage limited energy resources.

This paper develops the thesis that vision is fundamentally an energy-driven process. We argue that the brain's visual system operates under tight metabolic constraints, and that many of its characteristic properties—selective attention, predictive coding, perceptual bistability, and even visual fatigue—are best understood as adaptations to these constraints rather than as purely informational strategies. Drawing on findings from neuroenergetics, psychophysics, and computational modeling, we propose a framework in which perceptual decisions are governed by a trade-off between the expected informational gain of a visual act and its anticipated metabolic cost. Under this view, phenomena such as inattentional blindness, the attentional blink, and the preference for gist over detail are not bugs in the visual system but rational responses to energy scarcity.

We begin by reviewing evidence that visual processing consumes a substantial and variable fraction of the brain's energy budget. We then formalize an energy-driven model of visual selection and test its predictions against established findings. Finally, we consider implications for theories of perception, attention, and consciousness, arguing that energy constraints are not peripheral to vision but constitutive of it.

title: City size and the spreading of COVID-19 in Brazil
text: We analyzed the evolution of COVID-19 across 5,570 Brazilian municipalities. Larger cities were hit earlier and harder: the first 100 confirmed cases appeared in state capitals, and by epidemiological week 20, municipalities with over 500,000 inhabitants (n = 49) accounted for 62.3% of all cases despite representing only 29.1% of the population. The cumulative incidence per 100,000 residents reached 487.2 in large cities (>500,000), compared to 132.5 in medium cities (100,000–500,000) and 41.8 in small municipalities (<20,000). A similar gradient was observed for mortality: 32.1 deaths per 100,000 in large cities versus 3.4 in small ones. We fitted a linear mixed model regressing the cumulative number of cases on log-population size, controlling for distance to the state capital and time since first case. City size was positively associated with case counts (β = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.76–0.90, p < 0.001), with an R² of 0.71. The mean doubling time during the first 30 days was shorter in larger cities (5.8 days) than in smaller ones (9.4 days). Our findings indicate that the epidemic spread followed a hierarchical, size-dependent diffusion pattern, with larger urban centers acting as initial superspreading hubs before the virus reached smaller municipalities, where health system capacity is more limited.

title: Seamless multi-model postprocessing for air temperature forecasts in complex topography
text: This study introduced a seamless multi-model postprocessing framework for air temperature forecasts in complex topography, addressing the challenge of discontinuities that arise when separate statistical models are applied to different forecast horizons or model sources. By integrating multiple numerical weather prediction systems within a unified postprocessing architecture, the proposed approach mitigates the abrupt transitions and skill degradation typically observed at model and lead-time boundaries. Evaluation across a topographically heterogeneous region demonstrates that the seamless method consistently outperforms both raw ensemble output and conventional horizon-specific postprocessing, with the most pronounced gains in mountainous terrain where elevation-dependent biases are large and forecast uncertainty is high. The framework also proves robust to the varying availability and changing composition of input models, a practical requirement for operational forecasting. These results indicate that seamless multi-model postprocessing offers a computationally feasible and operationally viable pathway to more reliable temperature forecasts in complex terrain. Future work should extend the approach to probabilistic calibration, other meteorological variables, and finer spatial resolutions, and should assess its transferability to regions with different climatic and orographic characteristics.

title: On forward invariance in Lyapunov stability theorem for local stability
text: This paper addresses a subtle yet critical issue in Lyapunov stability theory concerning the local stability of nonlinear dynamical systems. The classical Lyapunov theorem guarantees stability when a positive definite Lyapunov function has a negative semi-definite derivative along system trajectories. However, for local stability analysis, the theorem implicitly requires that the sublevel sets of the Lyapunov function be forward invariant, a condition that is not always automatically satisfied when the domain of the Lyapunov function is a proper subset of the state space. We demonstrate that the conventional statement of the theorem may fail if the intersection of the sublevel set with the domain of the vector field is not positively invariant, leading to trajectories that leave the domain within finite time. To resolve this issue, we propose a refined formulation that explicitly incorporates a forward invariance condition on a suitable sublevel set. We show that under this modified condition, the standard conclusions of Lyapunov stability hold without additional regularity assumptions. Furthermore, we provide counterexamples illustrating the necessity of the invariance condition and discuss its connections to barrier certificates and set invariance theory. Our results clarify the foundational assumptions of Lyapunov’s direct method and offer practical guidelines for verifying local stability in constrained or non-globally defined systems.

title: Informed Bayesian Inference for the A/B Test
text: The A/B test is a cornerstone of online experimentation, widely used to compare two variants and guide product decisions. Conventional analyses rely on null-hypothesis significance testing, which answers whether an effect exists but not how large it is, and is frequently misinterpreted as evidence for the null or the alternative. Bayesian methods address these limitations by quantifying evidence directly and permitting optional stopping, yet their results depend strongly on prior specification, and default priors are often chosen arbitrarily. This paper develops an informed Bayesian framework for the A/B test in which prior distributions are elicited from historical experiments through a meta-analytic power prior, so that past evidence is incorporated in a principled and transparent manner. We derive closed-form posteriors for the difference in conversion rates under Beta priors, provide decision-theoretic rules based on the region of practical equivalence, and examine frequentist operating characteristics via simulation. We further propose a sensitivity diagnostic that reports how conclusions change across a plausible range of prior weights. Empirical evaluations on both simulated and real industrial datasets show that informed priors improve calibration and reduce the sample size required for conclusive decisions relative to weakly informative alternatives, while the diagnostic safeguards against prior-data conflict. The framework thus offers a practical and defensible route to Bayesian A/B testing.

title: Bessel-like birth-death process
text: We introduce and study a one-dimensional birth-death process whose transition rates are governed by a Bessel-like recurrence structure, obtained as a discrete analogue of the radial diffusion associated with the Bessel process. The generator of the chain is characterized by state-dependent birth and death rates that interpolate between classical birth-death dynamics and the continuum Bessel operator, with the index parameter controlling the behaviour at the boundary and the strength of the drift toward or away from the origin. We first establish existence, uniqueness, and regularity properties of the process, including a complete classification of the boundary as absorbing, reflecting, or accessible, in terms of the index and the scaling parameters. We then derive explicit expressions for the transition probabilities and the Green function, exploiting a spectral representation in terms of discrete Bessel functions and analysing the associated orthogonal polynomial system. Several quantities of probabilistic interest are computed exactly: hitting times and their distributions, the absorption probability at the origin, and the invariant measure when it exists. A key feature is the appearance of a phase transition in the long-time behaviour, where the process either converges to a non-degenerate stationary distribution, escapes to infinity, or is absorbed at the boundary, depending on a critical value of the index. We further discuss connections with continuous Bessel processes, Karlin-McGregor theory, and models in population genetics and queuing, and we illustrate the results with numerical examples.

title: Effect of COVID-19 Pandemic on Oceans
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, emerged as a global health crisis in early 2020, triggering unprecedented disruptions to human society. Lockdowns, travel restrictions, and the abrupt contraction of industrial and maritime activities led to a temporary but dramatic reduction in anthropogenic pressures on the environment, including a marked decline in greenhouse gas emissions, shipping traffic, coastal tourism, and industrial fishing. These sudden changes created a unique, unintended natural experiment that offered a rare window into how marine ecosystems respond when human activity is sharply curtailed.

This paper examines the multifaceted effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the world's oceans, synthesizing evidence across physical, chemical, and biological dimensions. On one hand, reduced vessel traffic lowered underwater noise pollution, decreased oil discharges, and alleviated pressure on commercially exploited fish stocks, while improved water quality was observed in some coastal and tourist-heavy regions. On the other hand, the pandemic exacerbated other stressors: the surge in single-use plastics, including disposable masks and gloves, added substantial plastic pollution to marine environments, and economic hardship in many coastal communities intensified illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

Importantly, these impacts were largely transient, revealing both the resilience and the fragility of marine systems. The pandemic demonstrated that meaningful reductions in ocean stressors are possible through systemic change, yet also underscored that short-term behavioral shifts cannot substitute for sustained, coordinated ocean governance. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing post-pandemic recovery strategies that align with long-term ocean sustainability and climate goals.

title: Bayesian Topological Learning for Classifying the Structure of Biological Networks
text: We evaluated our Bayesian topological learning (BTL) framework on three biological network datasets: protein–protein interaction (PPI), gene regulatory, and neuronal connectivity networks. Using a 10-fold cross-validation protocol, BTL achieved a classification accuracy of 94.3% ± 1.2% on the PPI dataset, outperforming persistence landscapes (89.7% ± 1.8%) and graph kernel SVM (87.4% ± 2.1%). On gene regulatory networks, BTL reached 91.8% ± 1.5% accuracy versus 86.2% ± 2.0% for the strongest baseline. Neuronal networks proved most challenging, yet BTL still attained 88.6% ± 2.3%, compared with 82.9% ± 2.7% for persistence landscapes. Ablation analysis showed that removing the Bayesian posterior over persistence diagrams reduced accuracy by 5.1–7.4 percentage points, confirming the contribution of topological uncertainty quantification. Runtime scaled near-linearly with network size, processing 500-node networks in 42.7 ± 3.4 seconds. These results demonstrate that BTL robustly captures discriminative topological structure across diverse biological networks.

title: Detecting bearish and bullish markets in financial time series using hierarchical hidden Markov models
text: This paper introduced hierarchical hidden hidden Markov models (HHMMs) for detecting bullish and bearish market regimes in financial time series. Unlike conventional HMMs, which assume a single latent state sequence, HHMMs decompose the regime structure into multiple layers, allowing coarse-grained bull and bear phases to be modelled alongside finer-grained sub-regimes that capture within-phase dynamics such as corrections, rallies, and consolidation periods. Using daily returns from major equity indices, we showed that the proposed framework identifies persistent market phases more accurately than single-layer benchmarks, delivers superior out-of-sample regime classification, and improves the risk-adjusted performance of simple regime-based trading strategies. The hierarchical structure also provides a natural interpretation of nested market dynamics, with bull and bear states emerging as aggregates of more transient sub-states rather than as monolithic regimes. Several limitations remain. The model relies on a fixed number of hidden states, which must be selected via information criteria or cross-validation, and computational cost grows with the depth of the hierarchy. Furthermore, the analysis is confined to univariate return series; extending the framework to multivariate settings, alternative data sources, and regime-dependent volatility dynamics is a promising direction for future research. Overall, the results suggest that hierarchical hidden Markov models offer a flexible and interpretable tool for regime detection, bridging the gap between parsimonious statistical models and the multi-scale nature of real financial markets.

title: Structural Balance and Interpersonal Appraisals Dynamics: Beyond All-to-All and Two-Faction Networks
text: Structural balance theory has long provided a foundational framework for understanding how affective ties evolve in social networks, with the classic assumption that triads tend toward balance by resolving inconsistent configurations. However, most existing models and empirical analyses restrict their attention to either all-to-all interaction structures or simplified two-faction topologies, thereby overlooking the heterogeneous and often sparse architectures of real interpersonal networks. This paper develops a generalized dynamical framework that embeds structural balance processes within arbitrary signed network topologies, explicitly accounting for the interplay between interpersonal appraisals and the underlying connectivity patterns. We introduce a family of continuous-time models in which individuals update their sentiments toward one another based on both direct interactions and indirect social influence, while the network structure itself may be static or coevolving. Through a combination of analytical results and numerical simulations, we characterize the conditions under which balanced configurations emerge, the role of network sparsity and clustering in modulating convergence, and the emergence of multi-faction or fragmented steady states that lie beyond the classical two-faction paradigm. Our findings reveal that the path to balance is highly sensitive to local structural features, such as the presence of bridging ties and degree heterogeneity, and that stable configurations may retain a mixture of positive and negative relations that cannot be reduced to a simple bipolar division. We further show that appraisal dynamics on realistic networks can exhibit long transients, metastable states, and sensitivity to initial conditions, challenging the view that balance is an inevitable attractor. These results extend structural balance theory beyond its traditional confines and offer new insights into the coevolution of interpersonal evaluations and social structure in complex organizations and online communities.

title: Low-Cost Maximum Entropy Covariance Matrix Reconstruction Algorithm for Robust Adaptive Beamforming
text: Adaptive beamforming is highly sensitive to covariance matrix estimation errors, especially when the available snapshot number is small or the desired signal is present in the training data. Although maximum entropy covariance matrix reconstruction has shown promising robustness, existing methods often rely on expensive optimization or high-complexity eigenvalue decomposition, which limits their practical deployment in low-cost hardware. This paper proposes a low-cost maximum entropy covariance matrix reconstruction algorithm for robust adaptive beamforming. The key idea is to reconstruct the interference-plus-noise covariance matrix by exploiting the maximum entropy principle under properly designed linear constraints, while avoiding iterative optimization and large-scale matrix inversion. The resulting beamformer is computationally efficient and easy to implement. Simulations under various array imperfections and snapshot regimes demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with significantly reduced complexity compared with several representative robust beamformers.

title: An AI-powered blood test to detect cancer using nanoDSF
text: Early cancer detection is critical for improving patient survival, yet current diagnostic methods are often invasive, costly, or insufficiently sensitive. Here, we present an AI-powered blood test for cancer detection based on nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF), a label-free technique that monitors thermal unfolding of plasma proteins. We profiled the thermal stability of blood plasma samples from cancer patients and healthy controls, generating high-dimensional thermostability fingerprints. A machine learning pipeline was trained to discriminate between the two groups, leveraging subtle disease-associated alterations in the plasma proteome. The model achieved high diagnostic accuracy across multiple cancer types and stages, demonstrating sensitivity to early-stage disease. Our results establish nanoDSF combined with artificial intelligence as a rapid, minimally invasive, and scalable platform for pan-cancer screening. This approach holds promise for integration into routine clinical workflows, enabling earlier intervention and improved patient outcomes.

title: Smartphone Security Behavioral Scale: A New Psychometric Measurement for Smartphone Security
text:
Smartphones have become central to modern life, storing sensitive personal, financial, and professional information. Despite growing awareness of security threats such as malware, phishing, and unauthorized access, users frequently fail to adopt recommended protective behaviors. Understanding why individuals engage in or neglect smartphone security practices requires reliable and valid measurement tools that capture the behavioral dimensions of smartphone security.

Existing instruments for assessing security-related behavior have primarily targeted general cybersecurity or computer use, and they often emphasize knowledge, attitudes, or intentions rather than actual smartphone-specific practices. Consequently, researchers and practitioners lack a psychometrically sound scale tailored to the unique context of smartphone security, including behaviors such as lock-screen use, app permission management, software updates, and safe network selection.

This paper introduces the Smartphone Security Behavioral Scale (SSBS), a new psychometric instrument designed to measure smartphone security behavior across distinct domains. We describe the scale's development, factor structure, reliability, and validity evidence, and we examine its relationships with demographic and psychological variables. The SSBS offers a concise, empirically grounded tool for research and intervention design aimed at improving smartphone security behavior.

title: Roadmap to a Roadmap: How Could We Tell When AGI is a 'Manhattan Project' Away?
text: Our analysis of 1,247 expert forecasts reveals a 23% decline in median AGI timelines between 2022 and 2024, from 37 to 28.5 years, alongside rising variance (σ² = 142). Bibliometric mapping of 89,000 papers shows capability-relevant research doubling every 14 months, yet only 6.2% addresses milestone verification. Survey responses (n = 412) indicate 68% of researchers would support a dedicated coordination effort, but 74% could not specify quantitative trigger conditions. We identify three convergent indicators—compute scaling exceeding 10²⁶ FLOP, cross-domain transfer above 85%, and autonomous research output doubling in under 9 months—that, if simultaneously met, would justify Manhattan Project-scale mobilization. No current system satisfies more than one.

title: On critical dynamics and thermodynamic efficiency of urban transformations
text: This paper has investigated the critical dynamics and thermodynamic efficiency of urban transformations by coupling stochastic nonlinear dynamics with nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Using a theoretical framework that treats cities as dissipative structures maintained far from equilibrium, we showed that urban transitions exhibit hallmark signatures of criticality, including diverging correlation lengths, slowing down, and enhanced fluctuations near tipping points. These critical phenomena are not merely mathematical curiosities; they directly govern the rate at which energy and resources are dissipated during restructuring events. Our analysis further reveals a trade-off between thermodynamic efficiency and adaptive capacity: highly efficient urban configurations near criticality become fragile to perturbations, while inefficient, disordered states offer greater resilience but higher entropy production. We derived a general expression linking the Fisher information of urban observables to the excess entropy production, providing a quantitative indicator of proximity to critical transitions. Numerical simulations on synthetic and empirical city datasets confirm that periods of rapid urban transformation coincide with peaks in thermodynamic efficiency and critical slowing down. These findings suggest that sustainable urban planning should monitor early-warning signals of criticality and manage efficiency–resilience trade-offs rather than optimizing either alone. Future work should extend this framework to spatially explicit, multi-scale urban systems and incorporate socioeconomic constraints. Ultimately, bridging critical dynamics and thermodynamics offers a principled pathway for understanding and steering urban transformations in an era of rapid global change.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning Forecasts for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2019
text: This paper presents a hybrid machine learning approach to forecast match outcomes for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2019. The proposed framework combines a statistical model, based on team strength ratings derived from historical match results, with a machine learning classifier that incorporates additional features such as recent form, goal differentials, and tournament-specific covariates. A ensemble strategy is employed to integrate the outputs of both components, improving predictive accuracy over either method alone. The model is trained on international women's matches played between 2015 and 2019, and evaluated using cross-validation as well as out-of-sample predictions for the 2019 tournament. Results show that the hybrid approach outperforms conventional ranking-based and pure machine learning benchmarks in terms of log-loss and Brier score. The findings highlight the value of combining domain-informed statistical priors with data-driven learning for sports forecasting, and provide a reproducible baseline for future Women's World Cup prediction tasks.

title: Considerations for developing predictive models of crime and new methods for measuring their accuracy
text: The rapid growth of computational criminology has produced a wide array of predictive models of crime, ranging from spatio-temporal hotspot forecasting to individual-level risk assessment. Yet the development of these models is often driven by methodological convenience rather than by the substantive nature of crime data, which is characterised by rarity, spatial and temporal dependence, reporting bias, and class imbalance. As a result, many published models report performance metrics that appear impressive but offer limited practical value for policing, resource allocation, or prevention. This paper addresses two interrelated gaps. First, it examines the key considerations that should guide the construction of crime prediction models, including the choice of spatial and temporal units, the treatment of zero-inflated and imbalanced outcomes, the distinction between explanation and prediction, and the risk of data leakage arising from the reuse of police-recorded data. Second, it argues that conventional accuracy measures such as overall accuracy, AUC, and RMSE can be misleading in crime prediction contexts, because they obscure performance on rare events, ignore the spatial clustering of errors, and fail to reflect operational costs. We therefore propose a set of alternative evaluation methods, including precision-recall curves, lift and capture rates, spatially explicit error diagnostics, and cost-sensitive metrics that align model assessment with decision-making. By integrating modelling considerations with evaluation design, this paper aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a more rigorous framework for developing and validating crime prediction models, and to encourage greater transparency in reporting their real-world utility.

title: Estimation of number of runaway electrons per avalanche in Earth's atmosphere
text: The measurement of the number of runaway electrons per avalanche is essential for understanding the dynamics of high-energy atmospheric physics phenomena such as terrestrial gamma-ray flashes and gamma-ray glows. In this study, we present a systematic estimation of the electron multiplication factor, defined as the average number of runaway electrons produced per avalanche, under varying electric field strengths and atmospheric conditions representative of thundercloud environments. Using Monte Carlo simulations based on the relativistic Boltzmann equation, we model the propagation of seed electrons through air and track the development of runaway electron avalanches. The simulations incorporate the effects of elastic and inelastic scattering, bremsstrahlung emission, and pair production, allowing for a self-consistent treatment of avalanche growth and feedback mechanisms. Our results show that the number of runaway electrons per avalanche depends strongly on the reduced electric field and air density, with values ranging from a few to several hundred under typical thunderstorm conditions. We derive an empirical parameterization of the multiplication factor as a function of the electric field and altitude, which can be directly implemented in macroscopic models of terrestrial gamma-ray flash production. The findings highlight the importance of accurate avalanche multiplication estimates for predicting the intensity and spatial extent of high-energy emissions from thunderstorms, and provide a benchmark for future experimental validation.

title: Enterprise Systems Lifecycle-wide Innovation Readiness
text:
Enterprise systems (ES) such as ERP, CRM, and SCM have become foundational to organizational operations, yet many implementations fail to deliver expected innovation outcomes. A key reason is that innovation readiness is typically assessed only at the pre-implementation stage, neglecting how readiness evolves across the ES lifecycle. This narrow view limits organizations' ability to anticipate and respond to innovation opportunities and disruptions during operation, upgrade, and extension phases.

This paper addresses that gap by developing the concept of lifecycle-wide innovation readiness for enterprise systems. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and absorptive capacity, we conceptualize readiness as a dynamic, multi-dimensional capability that spans initiation, adoption, adaptation, acceptance, routinization, and infusion. We argue that readiness must be continuously cultivated rather than treated as a one-time gate.

Through a synthesis of prior literature and empirical insights, this paper proposes a framework that identifies the resources, capabilities, and contextual factors enabling innovation readiness at each lifecycle stage. The framework offers researchers a holistic lens and practitioners actionable guidance for sustaining innovation across the full ES lifecycle.

title: Artificial neural networks for disease trajectory prediction in the context of sepsis
text: We evaluated the predictive performance of four artificial neural network architectures for sepsis trajectory prediction on a retrospective cohort of 12,480 ICU admissions, of which 3,214 (25.8%) met Sepsis-3 criteria. The dataset was split temporally into training (n = 8,736), validation (n = 1,872), and test (n = 1,872) sets. The best-performing model, a bidirectional gated recurrent unit (Bi-GRU) with attention, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.871 (95% CI: 0.856–0.886) for 48-hour mortality prediction, outperforming the multilayer perceptron (AUROC 0.812, 95% CI: 0.795–0.829), standard LSTM (AUROC 0.843, 95% CI: 0.827–0.859), and the sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) baseline (AUROC 0.734, 95% CI: 0.716–0.752). The Bi-GRU also attained an AUPRC of 0.648 and a Brier score of 0.112, indicating good calibration. For the secondary task of predicting vasopressor initiation within 24 hours, the Bi-GRU reached an AUROC of 0.839 (95% CI: 0.823–0.855), a 9.3% relative improvement over the SOFA baseline. Feature importance analysis using integrated gradients revealed that lactate (mean absolute attribution 0.184), heart rate variability (0.152), and creatinine (0.131) were the strongest predictors, consistent with established pathophysiology. Performance degraded modestly when the prediction horizon was extended to 72 hours (AUROC 0.842) and 7 days (AUROC 0.798). Subgroup analysis showed no significant disparity across sex (ΔAUROC = 0.009, p = 0.41), though performance was slightly lower for patients over 75 years (AUROC 0.851 vs. 0.879, p = 0.03). These results suggest that attention-augmented recurrent networks capture temporal dependencies in sepsis progression more effectively than static severity scores.

title: Hierarchical communities in the walnut structure of the Japanese production network
text:
This study investigated the hierarchical community structure of the Japanese production network, revealing a distinctive walnut-like architecture in which densely connected communities are nested within broader, sparsely connected modules. By applying hierarchical community detection methods to firm-level transaction data, we demonstrated that the network exhibits multiple levels of organization, with small, tightly knit communities of firms at the finest scale and larger, loosely integrated groups at coarser scales. This nested structure resembles the layered shells of a walnut, where each successive layer encompasses the previous one while maintaining relatively weak inter-layer connectivity.

Our analysis further showed that the hierarchical organization is closely tied to firm attributes such as industry sector, geographic location, and firm size. Communities at lower levels tend to consist of firms within the same industry and region, reflecting localized supply chains and close business relationships, whereas higher-level communities span multiple sectors and regions, indicating broader economic integration. The persistence of this hierarchical pattern across different resolution parameters suggests that it is a robust feature of the Japanese production network rather than an artifact of a particular detection algorithm.

These findings contribute to the growing literature on the mesoscale structure of economic networks and offer practical implications for understanding how shocks propagate through the economy. The walnut structure implies that disruptions may be contained within local communities but can also cascade across layers under certain conditions, depending on the strength of inter-community linkages. Future research should examine the temporal evolution of this hierarchical structure and compare it with production networks in other countries to assess the generality of the walnut architecture. Overall, our results highlight the importance of considering multiple levels of community organization when analyzing the resilience and vulnerability of interfirm networks.

title: The Snowball Earth transition in a climate model with drifting parameters
text: The Snowball Earth transition represents one of the most dramatic climate bifurcations in Earth's history, yet its dynamics remain incompletely understood. Here we investigate this transition using a global climate model in which key parameters—solar luminosity, greenhouse gas forcing, and surface albedo—are allowed to drift slowly over time. Unlike conventional hysteresis experiments with instantaneous parameter changes, our drifting-parameter framework reveals how the rate of forcing influences the critical thresholds and the stability of intermediate climate states. We find that slow drift substantially alters the bifurcation structure, delaying the onset of global glaciation and producing transient states with partial ice coverage that are absent in quasi-static simulations. The transition exhibits rate-dependent hysteresis, with the width of the bistable region depending sensitively on the drift timescale. Our results suggest that the Snowball Earth onset may have been governed not only by the magnitude of forcing but also by its temporal evolution, offering a new perspective on Neoproterozoic climate dynamics.

title: Summer vacation and COVID-19: effects of metropolitan people going to summer provinces
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has revealed complex interactions between human mobility and infectious disease transmission. In China, the summer vacation period typically triggers massive population flows from metropolitan areas to popular summer destinations, particularly provinces with cooler climates such as Guizhou, Yunnan, and Qinghai. While previous studies have examined travel restrictions and lockdown measures, the specific impact of seasonal vacation migration on epidemic dynamics remains underexplored. This study investigates how the influx of metropolitan residents into summer provinces during the 2020–2022 summer vacations influenced local COVID-19 transmission patterns. Using provincial-level epidemiological data and mobile phone signaling records, we analyze the temporal and spatial correlations between population inflow and case incidence. Our findings suggest that summer vacation migration created distinct transmission risks, with effects varying by destination province characteristics and local vaccination coverage. These results highlight the need for targeted public health strategies during seasonal population movements, even in periods of relatively low national transmission. The study contributes to understanding the role of domestic tourism in shaping regional epidemic trajectories and offers implications for future pandemic preparedness.

title: A rank-3 network representation for single-affiliation systems
text: Single-affiliation systems—where each node belongs to exactly one group and groups do not overlap—are widely used to model collaboration, affiliation, and membership structures, yet they are typically represented as bipartite graphs whose analysis obscures higher-order organization. We introduce a rank-3 tensor representation for single-affiliation systems that encodes group–member–attribute relations in a unified algebraic form. The representation admits a canonical decomposition into three modes corresponding to groups, members, and attributes, and we show that several standard bipartite and hypergraph quantities, including degree sequences, co-membership counts, and modularity, can be recovered as contractions of the tensor. We develop spectral methods for the rank-3 representation, establish bounds relating its singular values to those of the associated incidence matrices, and demonstrate that community detection in the tensor framework identifies group structure more reliably than bipartite projection when groups vary in size. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and empirical collaboration networks confirm that the proposed representation preserves information lost under one-mode projection and scales to systems with millions of affiliations. The framework extends naturally to weighted and temporal single-affiliation systems, providing a principled foundation for analyzing higher-order relational data.

title: A novel hand-held interface supporting the self-management of Type 1 diabetes
text:
Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong intensive insulin therapy, and achieving glycaemic targets depends heavily on daily self-management decisions. Although continuous glucose monitoring and insulin pumps have improved outcomes, users still must interpret trends and calculate doses, often under time pressure and with limited support.

Existing hand-held tools typically address isolated tasks, such as logging glucose or computing boluses, and rarely integrate contextual factors like physical activity, meals, and stress. This fragmentation increases cognitive load and reduces adherence, particularly for adolescents and newly diagnosed adults.

This paper presents a novel hand-held interface that unifies glucose sensing, dose advice, and behavioural feedback within a single device. We describe the design rationale, interaction model, and a preliminary usability study with 12 adults with Type 1 diabetes. Results suggest improved confidence and faster decision-making, supporting further clinical evaluation.

title: Peut-on former les enseignant$\cdot$e$\cdot$s en un rien de temps ?
text: Nos résultats montrent qu'une formation courte de 6 heures permet d'améliorer significativement les connaissances déclaratives des enseignant·e·s, mais reste insuffisante pour transformer durablement les pratiques de classe. Le groupe expérimental (n = 48) obtient un score moyen de 14,2/20 au post-test de connaissances, contre 9,8/20 pour le groupe contrôle (n = 45), soit un écart significatif (t(91) = 5,34, p < .001, d = 0,87). Toutefois, l'observation en classe réalisée six semaines plus tard révèle un effet beaucoup plus modeste : seuls 27 % des enseignant·e·s formé·e·s mobilisent au moins deux stratégies enseignées, contre 11 % dans le groupe contrôle (χ²(1) = 4,12, p = .042). Le temps de mise en œuvre effective de ces stratégies demeure faible, avec une moyenne de 8,3 minutes par séance de 55 minutes, sans différence significative entre les groupes (p = .31). Par ailleurs, la satisfaction déclarée est élevée (M = 4,3/5), mais ne prédit pas l'usage réel des acquis (r = .14, p = .34). Ces résultats suggèrent qu'une formation brève produit un gain cognitif réel mais superficiel, qui ne se traduit que marginalement dans les gestes professionnels. Ils invitent à repenser l'ingénierie de formation en intégrant un accompagnement longitudinal et des dispositifs de suivi en situation de travail.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Lookahead Factor Models for Quantitative Investing
text: We presented uncertainty-aware lookahead factor models, a framework for quantitative investing that integrates predictive uncertainty directly into portfolio construction. By combining a lookahead factor model with principled uncertainty estimation, our approach distinguishes between regions of the feature space where return predictions are reliable and those where they are not, allowing the portfolio optimizer to discount or avoid positions whose expected returns rest on fragile forecasts. Across extensive backtests spanning multiple equity universes and market regimes, the proposed method improved risk-adjusted performance relative to standard factor models, with the largest gains observed during periods of elevated market volatility and structural change—precisely the conditions under which conventional models tend to fail. Ablation studies confirmed that both the lookahead mechanism and the uncertainty quantification contribute meaningfully to these results, and that the framework remains robust to reasonable choices of uncertainty calibration and transaction cost assumptions. Our findings suggest that treating uncertainty as a first-class input to portfolio optimization, rather than a post hoc diagnostic, offers a practical path toward more resilient quantitative strategies. Several directions remain open. Extending the framework to alternative asset classes, incorporating richer distributional forecasts beyond variance, and endogenizing the interaction between uncertainty estimates and turnover control are promising avenues. More broadly, as machine learning models grow increasingly expressive, the ability to know when they do not know will remain essential for any decision-making system operating in adversarial and non-stationary financial markets. We hope this work encourages further research at the intersection of uncertainty quantification, sequential decision-making, and quantitative finance, and provides a useful benchmark for evaluating future uncertainty-aware investment systems.

title: The impact of small changes in thoroughfare connectivity on the potential for student walking
text: Small changes in thoroughfare connectivity can play a meaningful role in shaping students’ potential for walking to school. This study examines how minor alterations to street network connectivity—such as adding pedestrian links, removing barriers, or modifying intersection configurations—affect the likelihood that students will walk along school routes. Using network-based walkability measures and student travel data, we model the sensitivity of walking potential to incremental changes in connectivity around schools. The results indicate that even modest improvements can substantially increase modeled walking potential, particularly where disconnected cul-de-sacs and long block perimeters currently limit direct routes. However, the magnitude of these effects varies by neighborhood context, school location, and the spatial distribution of student residences. The findings suggest that planners and school authorities should consider small-scale connectivity interventions as cost-effective strategies for promoting active school travel, while recognizing that such changes alone may not overcome broader social and perceptual barriers to walking.

title: Hybrid Voltage Stability and Security Assessment using Synchrophasors with Consideration of Generator Q-limits
text: The increasing penetration of renewable generation and the growing complexity of interconnected power systems have intensified voltage stability and security concerns. Accurate and timely assessment of voltage stability margins is essential for preventing voltage collapse and maintaining secure operation. With the widespread deployment of phasor measurement units (PMUs), synchrophasor data provide real-time, time-synchronized information that enables more responsive assessment than conventional SCADA-based methods. However, most existing synchrophasor-based approaches focus primarily on load-side Thevenin equivalent estimation and often neglect generator reactive power limits, which can significantly affect the accuracy of stability margins and may lead to overly optimistic security assessments. When generators reach their reactive power limits, their terminal voltage regulation capability is lost, and the system's voltage stability characteristics change abruptly. Consequently, incorporating generator Q-limits into synchrophasor-based assessment is necessary for practical and reliable evaluation. This paper proposes a hybrid voltage stability and security assessment method that integrates synchrophasor measurements with generator reactive power limit considerations. The proposed approach combines measurement-based Thevenin equivalent tracking with limit-induced contingency identification to provide a more realistic stability margin. A hybrid framework is developed to coordinate continuous synchrophasor monitoring and discrete Q-limit events, enabling adaptive assessment under both normal and stressed conditions. The method is validated through simulations on standard test systems and compared with existing approaches. Results demonstrate that ignoring generator Q-limits can overestimate voltage stability margins, while the proposed hybrid method offers improved accuracy and security awareness for online applications.

title: People infer recursive visual concepts from just a few examples
text: How do people learn to recognize novel visual concepts from just a few examples? Prior work has largely focused on learning simple, single-level categories, yet many real-world concepts are defined recursively—their parts are themselves instances of the same concept. We propose that human concept learning is sensitive to this recursive structure, allowing people to infer rich, hierarchical representations from sparse data. Across a series of behavioral experiments, we show that participants can learn recursively defined visual concepts, such as nested spirals and fractal-like shapes, from as few as two or three positive examples, and can generalize these concepts to novel instances in a manner consistent with a recursive generative model. We formalize this capacity in a computational framework based on probabilistic program induction, in which concepts are represented as recursive programs that generate images through repeated self-similar transformations. The model captures human judgments across our experiments, including patterns of generalization and the perceived complexity of learned concepts, and outperforms non-recursive alternatives. These findings suggest that recursion is a core principle of human visual concept learning, enabling people to acquire productive, open-ended concepts from remarkably limited evidence.

title: Transfer Learning Based Automatic Model Creation Tool For Resource Constraint Devices
text:
The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and edge computing platforms has created a growing demand for deploying machine learning models directly on resource-constrained hardware such as microcontrollers, embedded systems, and mobile devices. On-device inference offers significant advantages, including reduced latency, improved privacy, lower bandwidth consumption, and operational independence from cloud infrastructure. However, building effective models for such devices remains a challenging task, as developers must balance predictive performance against strict limitations on memory, processing power, and energy availability.

Traditional model development workflows rely heavily on domain expertise and extensive experimentation with neural architecture design, hyperparameter tuning, and compression techniques. These processes are time-consuming and often inaccessible to non-expert developers who lack deep knowledge of machine learning. Furthermore, collecting and labeling sufficient training data for every new task is frequently impractical in embedded application scenarios, where datasets tend to be small and task-specific. Transfer learning has emerged as a promising solution to this problem, enabling models pretrained on large-scale datasets to be adapted to new tasks with limited data and computational effort.

Despite the availability of transfer learning techniques and model optimization tools, there is a lack of integrated solutions that automatically generate deployable models tailored to the constraints of specific target devices. This paper presents a transfer learning based automatic model creation tool that enables users to produce resource-efficient models for constrained devices with minimal machine learning expertise. The proposed tool automates key stages of the development pipeline, including backbone selection, transfer learning strategy configuration, and device-aware optimization. By lowering the technical barrier to entry and reducing manual effort, the tool aims to accelerate the deployment of intelligent applications on edge and embedded platforms.

title: Complexity in economic and social systems: cryptocurrency market at around COVID-19
text: The COVID-19 outbreak induced a measurable shift in the cryptocurrency market's complexity. Before the pandemic (Jan–Feb 2020), the Hurst exponent of Bitcoin returns averaged 0.54, while Ethereum and Litecoin showed 0.51 and 0.49, respectively, indicating near-random dynamics. During the crash phase (March 2020), all exponents dropped below 0.45 (BTC: 0.42, ETH: 0.41, LTC: 0.43), signaling strong anti-persistent behavior and panic-driven mean reversion. Multifractal spectra widened: the width Δh increased from 0.38 to 0.61 for BTC, and from 0.35 to 0.57 for ETH. Cross-correlation coefficients rose from 0.62 (pre-crisis) to 0.87 (crisis), revealing contagion effects. By June 2020, exponents recovered to 0.50–0.53, yet Δh remained elevated (0.49 for BTC). These results suggest that COVID-19 amplified short-term inefficiency and synchronized crypto markets, with persistent complexity long after the initial shock.

title: Gamification of Enterprise Systems: A Synthesis of Mechanics, Dynamics, and Risks
text: This paper synthesized current knowledge on gamification of enterprise systems through the mechanics–dynamics–risks lens. The evidence indicates that gamification can enhance employee engagement, motivation, and participation in routine enterprise tasks when mechanics such as points, badges, leaderboards, progress bars, and challenges are aligned with meaningful dynamics—competence, autonomy, relatedness, and goal reinforcement. However, benefits are contingent rather than automatic. Misfit between game elements and organizational context, overemphasis on extrinsic rewards, and poor design can produce unintended dynamics including competition-driven dysfunction, gaming the metrics, and diminished intrinsic motivation. Our synthesis further identifies risks that are often underrepresented in optimistic accounts: privacy and surveillance concerns arising from granular behavioral tracking, ethical tensions around manipulation and consent, inequitable outcomes for diverse user groups, and the potential for short-lived novelty effects that erode engagement over time. These risks amplify when gamification is implemented in enterprise systems characterized by mandatory use, hierarchical control, and performance evaluation. We therefore argue that successful gamification requires a sociotechnical, participatory design approach that treats mechanics as hypotheses, monitors dynamics continuously, and governs risks transparently. Future research should move beyond short-term experiments toward longitudinal, cross-context studies that examine sustained effects, unintended consequences, and boundary conditions. Practitioners should prioritize user autonomy, meaningful feedback, and integration with existing work practices, ensuring that gamification augments rather than subverts enterprise goals. Ultimately, gamification is neither a panacea nor a passing fad, but a design strategy whose value depends on careful alignment of mechanics, emergent dynamics, and explicit risk management.

title: Image to Bengali Caption Generation Using Deep CNN and Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit
text: Generating meaningful and contextually relevant captions for images in Bengali remains a challenging task due to the limited availability of large-scale annotated datasets and the complex linguistic structure of the Bengali language. This paper presents a deep learning-based framework for automatic image caption generation in Bengali, combining a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for visual feature extraction with a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) for sequential caption decoding. The proposed architecture employs a pre-trained CNN, such as VGG16 or ResNet-50, to encode input images into high-level feature representations, which are then passed to a BiGRU-based language model capable of capturing bidirectional temporal dependencies in the target text. To address the scarcity of Bengali image-caption corpora, we construct and preprocess a Bengali caption dataset by translating and adapting existing benchmark datasets, followed by tokenization and vocabulary construction tailored to Bengali morphology. The model is trained end-to-end using a cross-entropy loss with teacher forcing, and beam search is applied during inference to generate fluent and diverse captions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CNN-BiGRU architecture outperforms several baseline models, including CNN-LSTM and unidirectional GRU variants, across standard evaluation metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and ROUGE-L. The bidirectional design proves particularly effective in preserving syntactic and semantic coherence in Bengali captions. This study contributes to low-resource multilingual image captioning and provides a reproducible baseline for future research on Bengali vision-language tasks.

title: Body sway responses to pseudorandom support surface translations of vestibular loss subjects resemble those of vestibular able subjects
text:
Balance control during standing depends on the integration of visual, proprioceptive, and vestibular information. When the support surface moves unexpectedly, the central nervous system must rapidly reweight these sensory inputs to produce appropriate postural responses. Because vestibular signals are critical for detecting self-motion when proprioceptive cues are altered, individuals with bilateral vestibular loss (BVL) are often assumed to show fundamentally abnormal body sway responses to support surface translations. However, accumulating evidence suggests that the postural behaviour of BVL subjects may not differ qualitatively from that of vestibular-able subjects, particularly when the perturbation is unpredictable and proprioceptive feedback remains available.

Previous studies have typically employed sinusoidal or step translations, which allow anticipatory and predictive mechanisms to influence the response. Such paradigms may overestimate the contribution of vestibular loss to postural instability. Pseudorandom support surface translations, by contrast, reduce predictability and thus provide a more rigorous test of sensory reweighting. Whether BVL subjects exhibit compensatory sway patterns that resemble those of healthy controls under such conditions remains unclear.

The present study addressed this question by comparing body sway responses to pseudorandom support surface translations between subjects with bilateral vestibular loss and vestibular-able controls. We hypothesised that, despite absent vestibular function, BVL subjects would produce sway responses that are qualitatively and quantitatively similar to those of controls, reflecting the dominance of proprioceptive and visual feedback in this task. Demonstrating such resemblance would challenge the view that vestibular loss inevitably produces distinctive postural signatures and would clarify the conditions under which sensory substitution is sufficient for stable balance control.

title: A HJB-POD approach for the control of nonlinear PDEs on a tree structure
text: We propose a novel approach for the optimal control of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) defined on a tree-structured domain. The method combines a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) formulation with a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduced-order model. The HJB equation is solved numerically on the tree, where the dynamics are governed by the PDE and the cost functional accounts for both state and control efforts. To mitigate the curse of dimensionality, we employ POD to construct a low-dimensional surrogate of the nonlinear PDE, enabling efficient approximation of the value function via a semi-Lagrangian scheme. The reduced-order model is adaptively updated along the tree to preserve accuracy. We validate the proposed HJB-POD approach on benchmark problems, demonstrating significant computational savings while maintaining near-optimal control performance.

title: Input-to-state stability and Lyapunov functions with explicit domains for SIR model of infectious diseases
text:
The study of infectious disease dynamics has long relied on compartmental models to capture the mechanisms of transmission, recovery, and population-level spread. Among these, the SIR model remains a foundational framework, dividing a population into susceptible, infectious, and recovered individuals. While classical analyses focus on equilibrium stability and basic reproduction numbers, the increasing need for robust control strategies—especially in the presence of uncertainties, interventions, and external perturbations—has motivated the application of input-to-state stability (ISS) theory. ISS provides a powerful system-theoretic framework for quantifying how external inputs, such as vaccination rates, treatment availability, or behavioral changes, affect the evolution of an epidemic. However, applying ISS to epidemiological models requires careful treatment of the nonlinearities and the constrained state space inherent to population dynamics.

A central challenge in this context is the construction of Lyapunov functions that not only certify ISS but also possess explicit domains of validity. Unlike global stability analyses that assume unbounded or idealized conditions, real-world epidemic models operate within bounded, positively invariant sets determined by the total population. Lyapunov functions with explicit domains allow for sharper stability estimates and enable the derivation of quantitative bounds on the asymptotic gain from inputs to states. For the SIR model, the nonlinear incidence term and the coupling between compartments complicate the search for such functions, particularly when the system is subject to time-varying inputs that may represent public health interventions or seasonality.

This paper addresses the gap by developing ISS-based Lyapunov functions with explicitly characterized domains for the SIR model of infectious diseases. We first formulate the SIR system with external inputs and identify a positively invariant region that reflects biological constraints. Then, we construct candidate Lyapunov functions whose domains are given in terms of the model parameters and the initial conditions, ensuring that the ISS property holds within these domains. Our results provide computable conditions for input-to-state stability and yield explicit bounds on the system's response to perturbations, thereby offering a rigorous foundation for analyzing the robustness of epidemic control strategies.

title: Getting to Know One Another: Calibrating Intent, Capabilities and Trust for Human-Robot Collaboration
text:
We conducted a within-subjects study (N = 48) in which participants collaborated with a robot arm on a joint construction task across three calibration conditions: fixed-intent, adaptive-intent, and adaptive intent-plus-capability. Trust was measured via the Trust in Automation Scale (TiA, 1–7); task efficiency via completion time and error rate; perceived capability via a 5-item Likert questionnaire.

Adaptive calibration outperformed fixed-intent. The adaptive intent-plus-capability condition yielded the highest trust (M = 5.82, SD = 0.71) versus adaptive-intent (M = 5.21, SD = 0.83) and fixed-intent (M = 4.36, SD = 0.94), F(2, 94) = 18.42, p < .001, η² = .28. Post-hoc comparisons were significant (both p < .01). Task completion time fell from 214.6 s (SD = 31.2) in fixed-intent to 176.3 s (SD = 27.8) in adaptive-intent and 168.9 s (SD = 24.5) in adaptive intent-plus-capability, F(2, 94) = 11.07, p < .001. Error rates followed the same pattern: 14.6% (SD = 4.1), 9.8% (SD = 3.3), and 8.2% (SD = 2.9), respectively.

Mediation analysis showed that perceived capability partially mediated the relationship between adaptive calibration and trust (indirect effect β = .19, 95% CI [.07, .34]), suggesting that trust grows when the robot both communicates intent and demonstrably adjusts to its own limits. Interestingly, trust gains plateaued when calibration addressed intent alone, indicating that capability transparency is the stronger driver. These results support our hypothesis that calibrated intent and capability signals jointly foster warranted trust and improve collaboration efficiency.

title: Identifying Usability Issues of Software Analytics Applications in Immersive Augmented Reality
text:
This paper investigated the usability of software analytics applications presented in immersive augmented reality. Through a user study with twelve participants performing analysis tasks on a 3D city metaphor displayed via a head-mounted display, we identified usability issues across navigation, selection, layout, and annotation. Our findings show that while immersive AR offers intuitive spatial interaction and strong engagement, current interaction paradigms introduce substantial friction: mid-air gestures caused fatigue, depth-based selection was error-prone, and labels frequently occluded the data they described. These issues mirror, but also amplify, known challenges in desktop analytics, suggesting that immersive AR does not simply inherit the usability of its 2D counterparts.

We contribute a categorized set of usability issues and derive design implications for AR analytics tools, including hybrid interaction combining handheld controllers with gestures, depth cues for precise selection, adaptive label placement, and view management strategies that preserve context. Our results highlight the need for usability evaluation to accompany the growing interest in immersive analytics, rather than following it. Future work should replicate our study with larger samples, varied tasks, and diverse AR hardware to test the generality of these findings. We hope this work supports researchers and practitioners in building immersive analytics applications that are not only visually compelling but also usable for real analytical work.

title: Personalized fall detection monitoring system based on learning from the user movements
text: Falls among the elderly and mobility-impaired individuals constitute a major public health concern, yet conventional fall detection systems often suffer from high false alarm rates because they rely on generic thresholds that ignore inter-individual variability. This paper presents a personalized fall detection monitoring system that learns from each user's own movement patterns. The proposed approach employs wearable inertial sensors to continuously collect tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity data, from which a set of time-domain and frequency-domain features is extracted. A lightweight one-class classifier is then trained incrementally on the user's normal activities of daily living, enabling the model to distinguish genuine falls from idiosyncratic but harmless movements such as sitting down quickly or kneeling. To balance on-device efficiency and accuracy, feature selection and model updating are performed locally, while fall alerts and confidence scores are transmitted to caregivers. Experimental results on both public datasets and real-world recordings show that the personalized model outperforms generic baselines, achieving high sensitivity and specificity with a low false alarm rate.

title: Population dynamics in stochastic environments
text:
Understanding how populations persist in fluctuating environments remains one of the central problems in theoretical ecology and evolutionary biology. Environmental stochasticity, driven by temporal variation in weather, resource availability, and disturbance regimes, can fundamentally alter population trajectories, extinction risk, and long-term coexistence. Unlike demographic stochasticity, which arises from random individual-level events and is most influential in small populations, environmental stochasticity affects all individuals simultaneously and can destabilize even large populations. Its consequences are therefore relevant not only to conservation biology but also to the management of harvested species, the spread of invasive organisms, and the response of communities to climate change.

Classical models of population dynamics often assume deterministic or purely demographic randomness, yet empirical studies increasingly show that environmental fluctuations can generate complex phenomena, including intermittent outbreaks, altered competitive hierarchies, and stochastic tipping points. A key challenge is to determine when environmental noise merely adds variance around a deterministic mean and when it qualitatively changes dynamical outcomes. Theoretical advances have addressed this through diffusion approximations, stochastic difference and differential equations, and stationary distribution analysis. However, many existing results rely on simplifying assumptions such as small noise, white-noise spectra, or single-species settings, which limit their applicability to realistic ecological communities.

In this paper, we develop a general framework for analyzing population dynamics in stochastic environments, with emphasis on how noise color, autocorrelation, and nonlinear density dependence interact to shape persistence and extinction. We first derive conditions for stochastic boundedness and long-term growth rates in single-species models subject to correlated environmental perturbations. We then extend the analysis to interacting species, examining how environmental stochasticity modifies coexistence criteria and the stability of community states. Using both analytical approximations and numerical simulations, we identify parameter regimes where environmental noise enhances or diminishes population persistence, and we show that the sign of these effects depends critically on the interplay between noise characteristics and life-history traits. Our results provide a unified perspective on stochastic population dynamics and offer practical criteria for assessing extinction risk in variable environments.

title: On scenario construction for stochastic shortest path problems in real road networks
text: Stochastic shortest path (SSP) problems arise in real road networks whenever travel times are uncertain, yet most solution methods are evaluated on synthetic or idealized instances that fail to reproduce empirical travel-time distributions. This paper addresses the gap between algorithmic research and practice by examining how scenarios for SSP problems should be constructed from real road network data. We analyze the statistical properties of travel times observed in urban networks—such as skewness, heteroscedasticity, spatial and temporal correlation, and non-stationarity—and show how common scenario-generation practices distort these features, biasing the assessment of solution quality, risk measures, and algorithm ranking. We propose a scenario-construction framework that preserves empirically relevant dependence structures while remaining computationally tractable for large-scale instances, and we provide guidelines for calibrating scenario sets from historical and real-time data. Computational experiments on real road networks demonstrate the impact of scenario design on solution robustness and reliability.

title: Modeling, Vibration Control, and Trajectory Tracking of a Kinematically Constrained Planar Hybrid Cable-Driven Parallel Robot
text:
Cable-driven parallel robots (CDPRs) offer significant advantages in terms of large workspace, high payload capacity, and modular architecture, making them attractive for applications ranging from material handling to rehabilitation. However, conventional fully-constrained CDPRs require a number of cables exceeding the degrees of freedom to maintain positive tension, which increases complexity and cost. Hybrid cable-driven parallel robots, which combine cables with rigid links or other actuation mechanisms, have emerged as a promising alternative to address these limitations while preserving the benefits of cable actuation. Among these, kinematically constrained planar hybrid CDPRs represent a class of systems where the end-effector motion is partially restricted by mechanical constraints, introducing unique modeling and control challenges.

Despite growing interest in hybrid CDPRs, the coupled effects of kinematic constraints, cable tension distribution, and dynamic vibration behavior remain insufficiently explored, particularly for planar configurations intended for high-precision trajectory tracking tasks. Existing studies often simplify the system dynamics or neglect the influence of structural flexibility, which can lead to degraded tracking performance and residual vibrations in practical implementations. Furthermore, effective vibration suppression and accurate trajectory tracking require an integrated modeling and control framework that accounts for the constrained motion and the hybrid actuation characteristics simultaneously.

This paper addresses these gaps by developing a comprehensive model for a kinematically constrained planar hybrid cable-driven parallel robot, followed by the design of a vibration control strategy and a trajectory tracking controller. The dynamic model incorporates the kinematic constraints and cable-driven actuation, while the proposed control scheme aims to suppress unwanted oscillations and achieve precise end-effector tracking. Simulation and experimental results are presented to validate the effectiveness of the proposed modeling and control approach.

title: Predicting United States policy outcomes with Random Forests
text: We trained Random Forests on 7,412 congressional bills (1990–2018), using 214 features spanning sponsor ideology, cosponsor networks, committee composition, and macroeconomic indicators. Under five-fold cross-validation, the model achieved 84.3% accuracy (AUC = 0.91) in predicting enactment, outperforming logistic regression (76.1%) and gradient boosting (82.7%). Variable importance analysis identified committee chair alignment (0.18), bipartisan cosponsor share (0.15), and district competitiveness (0.12) as the strongest predictors. Out-of-sample tests on the 2019–2020 sessions yielded 79.6% accuracy despite divided government. Partial dependence plots revealed a nonlinear threshold: bills with more than 37% opposition-party cosponsors passed at nearly triple the baseline rate. Prediction errors clustered among omnibus spending packages, suggesting the model underestimates strategic bundling.

title: Parallel Oculomotor Plant Mathematical Model for Large Scale Eye Movement Simulation
text: This paper presented a parallel implementation of the Oculomotor Plant Mathematical Model (OPMM) designed to enable large-scale eye movement simulation. By decomposing the model's numerical integration across parallel processing units, the proposed approach achieves substantial reductions in computation time while preserving the physiological fidelity of simulated eye movements. Experimental results demonstrate that the parallel OPMM scales efficiently with the number of simulated eyes and available processing cores, making it feasible to generate synthetic eye-tracking data for thousands of concurrent subjects. This capability supports applications in biometric security, human-computer interaction, and large-scale behavioral studies, where extensive, parameter-varied eye movement datasets are required. Future work will focus on GPU acceleration, integration with real-time gaze-contingent systems, and extension to more complex oculomotor phenomena such as vergence and vestibular interactions.

title: I like fish, especially dolphins: Addressing Contradictions in Dialogue Modeling
text: Recent dialogue systems struggle with contradictions, yet existing benchmarks rarely test whether models can detect and resolve them. We introduce the Contradiction in Dialogue (CiD) task and the DialoguE Contradiction Detection (DECODE) dataset, comprising 27,501 annotated dialogues in which a speaker expresses a preference that conflicts with an earlier statement. The dataset covers three contradiction types: self-contradiction, context-contradiction, and common-sense contradiction. We evaluate strong pretrained models, including GPT-2, BART, and RoBERTa, on contradiction detection and resolution. Results show that models perform well on explicit lexical contradictions but degrade sharply on implicit and commonsense cases, with the best model achieving only 62.3% accuracy. We further propose a Contradiction-Aware Dialogue Model (CADM) that jointly learns detection and response generation, improving both contradiction resolution and response quality. Our analysis reveals that models often rely on surface cues rather than genuine reasoning, highlighting the need for deeper semantic understanding in dialogue modeling.

title: Speak with signs: Active learning platform for Greek Sign Language, English Sign Language, and their translation
text: Sign languages are full-fledged natural languages with their own grammar and vocabulary, yet they remain underrepresented in mainstream language education and translation technology. This is particularly true for Greek Sign Language (GSL) and English Sign Language (ESL), for which few digital resources support learners, educators, and translators. Existing platforms tend to focus on a single sign language and rarely address bidirectional translation between two sign languages, limiting their practical value in inclusive and multilingual settings. To address this gap, this paper presents an active learning platform designed for GSL, ESL, and their translation. The platform combines interactive sign recognition, learner-driven practice, and translation support within a unified environment. By integrating active learning principles with computer vision and natural language processing, it aims to enhance learner engagement, support self-paced acquisition, and facilitate communication across sign language communities. This study describes the platform's design, core functions, and initial evaluation, contributing to more accessible and inclusive sign language education and translation.

title: On forward invariance in Lyapunov stability theorem for local stability
text: The Lyapunov stability theorem is a cornerstone of systems and control theory, providing sufficient conditions for the stability of equilibria without requiring explicit solutions of the system dynamics. Classical formulations guarantee that sublevel sets of a Lyapunov function are positively invariant, yet the exact role of forward invariance in establishing local stability is often treated implicitly or under assumptions that obscure its necessity. This paper presents a rigorous examination of forward invariance within the Lyapunov stability theorem, with particular emphasis on the local stability setting. We first clarify the logical relationships among Lyapunov decrease conditions, forward invariance of sublevel sets, and stability conclusions, showing that forward invariance cannot be dispensed with in general. Counterexamples are constructed to demonstrate that, in the absence of appropriate invariance properties, the standard decrease condition alone may fail to ensure local stability, especially when the vector field is not sufficiently regular or when the equilibrium is non-isolated.
