We then establish refined sufficient conditions under which forward invariance is automatically guaranteed, and we identify minimal hypotheses on the Lyapunov function and the flow that restore the classical stability implication. Our results are formulated for general dynamical systems on metric spaces, with corollaries for ordinary differential equations and switched systems. The analysis reveals that forward invariance serves as an indispensable bridge between pointwise decrease of the Lyapunov function and set-theoretic stability. These findings provide a clearer theoretical foundation for Lyapunov-based stability analysis and have direct implications for controller design and verification.

title: Sparse Network Optimization for Synchronization
text:
The synchronization of coupled dynamical systems underpins a wide range of natural and engineered phenomena, from neuronal firing and power-grid stability to consensus formation in distributed sensor networks. A central challenge in these settings is that synchronization performance depends not only on the dynamics of individual units but also on the topology and strength of the interactions among them. Dense coupling can guarantee coherence, yet it is often costly, fragile, or physically infeasible, motivating the design of sparse networks that achieve synchronization with as few links as possible.

Sparse network optimization for synchronization seeks to identify a minimal set of edges, or a minimal distribution of coupling weights, that renders a networked system synchronizable or that optimizes a specified synchrony measure. This problem is combinatorially hard in general, since the space of candidate topologies grows exponentially with network size, and the underlying synchronization condition typically depends on the spectrum of the network Laplacian in a nonlinear manner. Consequently, exact solutions are tractable only for small systems, and practical approaches rely on relaxation, greedy heuristics, or convex surrogates that trade optimality for scalability.

In this paper, we formulate sparse synchronization design as a constrained optimization problem over network structures and coupling strengths, and we develop a framework that balances sparsity against synchronizability. We characterize conditions under which sparse topologies can match the synchronization performance of dense counterparts, analyze the computational complexity of the resulting design problem, and propose efficient algorithms with provable approximation guarantees. Numerical experiments on representative oscillator and consensus models illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods and reveal fundamental trade-offs between the number of edges, coupling cost, and achievable synchrony.

title: Analyzing 50 years of major fog events across the central coastal plain of Israel
text:
Between 1973 and 2023, 214 major fog events were identified across the central coastal plain, averaging 4.3 events per year. Events were classified using visibility thresholds: 128 events (59.8%) with visibility below 500 m, 61 (28.5%) below 200 m, and 25 (11.7%) below 50 m. The annual frequency declined significantly over the study period (Mann–Kendall τ = −0.34, p < 0.01), from a decadal mean of 5.6 events in 1973–1982 to 3.1 events in 2013–2022, a 45% reduction.

Fog events peaked in autumn and winter, with November (38 events, 17.8%) and December (34 events, 15.9%) most affected; only nine events (4.2%) occurred between May and August. Mean event duration was 4.7 hours, with 22 long-duration events exceeding 10 hours, concentrated in December–January. Onset showed a pronounced nocturnal bias: 81% of events began between 22:00 and 04:00 local time, and 74% dissipated within three hours of sunrise.

Synoptic analysis revealed that 68% of events were associated with weak easterly to southeasterly flow on the eastern flank of a Siberian Ridge, promoting nocturnal radiative cooling. An additional 21% coincided with moist westerly maritime intrusions, while 11% were linked to post-frontal clearing. Sea surface temperatures above 21°C combined with land–sea thermal contrasts exceeding 4°C preceded 63% of events, suggesting a significant role for coastal boundary-layer processes.

Trends in visibility severity were mixed: the proportion of events below 200 m decreased from 34% (1973–1992) to 24% (2003–2022), while relative humidity during events declined by 3.2% per decade. These patterns are consistent with regional warming and reduced moisture availability. Overall, the results indicate a robust decline in major fog frequency, with autumn and winter radiative fog most strongly affected.

title: GARCH(1,1) model of the financial market with the Minkowski metric
text: This paper has developed a GARCH(1,1) model of the financial market embedded in a Minkowski metric, thereby extending the standard Euclidean framework to a relativistic setting. By introducing the Minkowski metric, we have shown that volatility clustering and heavy-tailed return distributions can be reinterpreted through the geometry of spacetime intervals, where time-like and space-like separations between price observations naturally account for asymmetric responses to past shocks. The model preserves the core dynamics of GARCH(1,1) while providing a novel geometric interpretation of persistence and mean reversion. Empirical calibration to major equity indices indicates that the Minkowski-based specification captures leverage effects more parsimoniously than conventional approaches. However, the analysis is limited to a single metric signature and does not incorporate regime switching or multivariate extensions. Future work should explore the stability of the proposed metric under different market conditions, derive option pricing formulas within this framework, and test the model against high-frequency data. Overall, the Minkowski metric offers a promising geometric foundation for volatility modeling, bridging econometrics and relativistic geometry.

title: Factor endowment--commodity output relationships in a three-factor two-good general equilibrium trade model: Further analysis
text: This paper revisits the factor endowment–commodity output relationships in a three-factor, two-good general equilibrium trade model. While the two-factor Heckscher–Ohlin–Vanek framework yields unambiguous Rybczynski predictions, the introduction of a third factor substantially complicates the mapping from endowment changes to output adjustments, because the number of factors exceeds the number of goods and the production structure is no longer square. Building on earlier analyses, we provide a systematic and more general treatment of these relationships by exploiting the dual structure of the equilibrium and the properties of the revenue and cost functions. We first derive the general comparative-static responses of outputs to changes in each factor endowment, expressed in terms of factor intensities, substitution elasticities, and the curvature of the production possibility frontier. We then identify necessary and sufficient conditions under which the standard Rybczynski sign pattern survives, and show how these conditions fail when the third factor is mobile across sectors and enters production in a sufficiently asymmetric manner. Special attention is paid to the role of factor complementarity and to the case in which one factor is sector-specific. Our analysis clarifies several seemingly conflicting results in the literature and demonstrates that the direction and magnitude of output responses depend crucially on the relative factor intensities of the two goods and on the degree of substitutability among the three factors. We also examine the implications for the magnification effect, showing that it generally does not extend to a three-factor setting without additional restrictions. Finally, we illustrate the results with numerical examples and discuss their implications for empirical work on endowment-driven structural change and for the interpretation of trade patterns in multi-factor economies.

title: Mastering Music Instruments through Technology in Solo Learning Sessions
text:
The acquisition of musical instrument proficiency has traditionally depended on sustained one-to-one instruction, yet an increasing number of learners now pursue solitary practice mediated by digital tools. This shift raises a fundamental question: can technology adequately substitute for, or at least substantially supplement, the pedagogical functions of a human teacher during individual learning sessions? While prior research has examined isolated applications such as metronomes, tuning software, and video tutorials, few studies have conceptualized how these discrete technologies coalesce into an integrated learning environment for solo practitioners.

This paper addresses that gap by investigating how learners master musical instruments through technology in solitary settings. We define "solo learning sessions" as self-directed practice periods in which the learner assumes primary responsibility for goal setting, feedback interpretation, and error correction, with technological artifacts serving as auxiliary agents. Such sessions are distinct from formal instruction and from collaborative music-making; they constitute a hybrid space where learner autonomy intersects with algorithmic guidance.

Drawing on a mixed-methods design that combines survey data from 214 amateur instrumentalists with in-depth case studies of twelve learners across piano, guitar, and violin, this study pursues three objectives. First, it maps the ecosystem of technologies employed in solo practice, ranging from mobile applications and digital audio workstations to motion-capture systems and AI-powered feedback platforms. Second, it analyzes how these tools mediate metacognitive processes—particularly self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and strategy adjustment. Third, it identifies the conditions under which technological mediation enhances rather than undermines musical development.

The significance of this inquiry is twofold. Theoretically, it extends sociomaterial perspectives on learning to the domain of music education, treating technology not as a neutral aid but as an active participant in the learning assemblage. Practically, it offers evidence-based recommendations for designers, educators, and learners seeking to optimize solitary practice. As the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of remote and self-directed learning worldwide, understanding how technology shapes instrumental mastery in solo contexts has become both timely and consequential. The remainder of this paper reviews relevant literature, describes the methodology, presents findings, and discusses implications for music pedagogy and educational technology design.

title: Hop-Hop Relation-aware Graph Neural Networks
text: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning from graph-structured data, with most existing approaches focusing on message passing along direct edges. However, real-world graphs often exhibit complex higher-order dependencies that cannot be adequately captured by one-hop neighborhoods alone. While multi-hop information can be implicitly propagated through stacked layers, this approach suffers from over-smoothing, limited receptive field control, and the inability to explicitly model the distinct semantics of different hop distances. In this paper, we propose Hop-Hop Relation-aware Graph Neural Networks (HHR-GNN), a novel framework that explicitly captures and leverages the relations between different hops for more expressive graph representation learning. Specifically, we introduce a hop-relation module that learns dedicated transformations for each hop distance, enabling the model to distinguish the unique structural and semantic contributions of one-hop, two-hop, and higher-order neighbors. Furthermore, we design a relation-aware aggregation mechanism that adaptively fuses information across multiple hops by modeling the pairwise interactions between hop-specific representations, rather than treating them independently. This design allows HHR-GNN to capture rich multi-scale dependencies while mitigating the over-smoothing issue inherent in deep GNN architectures. We provide theoretical analysis showing that our hop-relation formulation generalizes several popular GNN variants and enhances the expressive power beyond the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman test under certain conditions. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets for node classification, link prediction, and graph classification demonstrate that HHR-GNN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the effectiveness of explicitly modeling hop-hop relations in graph neural networks.

title: Predicting COVID-19 Pneumonia Severity on Chest X-ray with Deep Learning
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has placed unprecedented strain on healthcare systems worldwide, with pneumonia emerging as one of the most common and serious complications of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Chest radiography remains a widely available, low-cost, and rapid imaging modality for assessing pulmonary involvement, making it an essential tool for triage and clinical decision-making, particularly in resource-constrained settings. However, visual interpretation of chest X-rays is subject to inter-observer variability, and manually quantifying the extent of lung opacification is both time-consuming and challenging in high-volume scenarios.

Deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks, have demonstrated strong performance in medical image analysis tasks such as detection, classification, and segmentation. Nevertheless, most existing work on COVID-19 imaging has focused on binary diagnosis rather than severity assessment, and relatively few studies have leveraged the spatial information encoded in chest radiographs to predict disease progression or clinical outcomes. Accurate, automated severity prediction could support earlier intervention, improve resource allocation, and reduce radiologist workload.

In this work, we present a deep learning framework for predicting COVID-19 pneumonia severity from chest X-ray images. We train and evaluate models that estimate the extent and opacity of pulmonary involvement, and we assess their agreement with radiologist annotations and their association with clinical indicators of disease severity. Our results suggest that deep learning can provide a scalable and reproducible approach to severity assessment, potentially augmenting clinical workflows during future outbreaks.

title: Control design for partial stabilization of nonlinear mechanical systems with random disturbances
text: Simulations were conducted on a two-link pendulum with random torque disturbances (zero-mean Gaussian, σ = 0.5 N·m). Under the proposed partial stabilization controller, the actuated joint converged to the desired angle within 2.1 s with a steady-state error of 0.8°, compared to 5.4 s and 3.2° for the baseline PD controller. The unactuated joint exhibited bounded oscillations with amplitude below 4.5°, remaining within the prescribed safe region. When disturbance intensity was increased to σ = 1.0 N·m, the controlled coordinates still stabilized, with error growing only to 1.3°, while the uncontrolled subsystem stayed bounded—validating the theoretical robustness claim. Monte Carlo trials (N = 500) showed a 97.6% success rate versus 82.4% for the baseline. Control effort averaged 8.7 N·m, a 21% reduction relative to full-state stabilization, confirming that partial stabilization lowers actuation demand without sacrificing stability of the target coordinates.

title: Multimodal fusion for sea level anomaly forecasting
text: This study developed a multimodal fusion framework for sea level anomaly forecasting that integrates satellite altimetry, in situ tide gauge observations, and reanalysis-derived atmospheric variables within a unified deep learning architecture. By jointly learning cross-modal representations, the proposed model captures the complementary spatiotemporal dynamics that single-source approaches fail to resolve, including mesoscale eddy propagation and wind-driven coastal variability. Systematic evaluations across multiple ocean regions demonstrate that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal and late-fusion baselines, reducing root-mean-square error by a substantial margin and improving forecast skill at lead times of up to ten days. The results underscore the importance of adaptive modality weighting under heterogeneous data quality and spatiotemporal coverage. Beyond forecasting accuracy, the framework offers interpretability into which modalities dominate under different oceanic regimes. Future work will extend the approach to probabilistic forecasting and incorporate additional data streams such as sea surface temperature and salinity to further advance operational sea level prediction.

title: Embedded hyper-parameter tuning by Simulated Annealing
text: This paper introduces Embedded Hyper-Parameter Tuning by Simulated Annealing (EHTSA), a novel framework for optimizing the hyper-parameters of machine learning models during the training process rather than in a separate, computationally expensive outer loop. Conventional hyper-parameter optimization methods, such as grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization, treat model training and hyper-parameter selection as two disjoint phases. This separation often leads to substantial computational overhead and may overlook dynamic interactions between hyper-parameters and the evolving training state. EHTSA addresses these limitations by embedding a simulated annealing (SA) optimizer directly into the training loop. At each training epoch, the SA algorithm proposes perturbations to selected hyper-parameters, evaluates their impact on a validation-based objective, and accepts or rejects the changes according to a temperature schedule that balances exploration and exploitation. This embedded mechanism enables continuous, adaptive tuning without requiring multiple independent training runs. We formalize the EHTSA procedure, analyze its convergence properties under mild assumptions, and discuss practical implementation details including temperature decay, perturbation design, and early stopping criteria. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks—including image classification with convolutional neural networks and tabular regression with gradient boosting—demonstrate that EHTSA achieves competitive or superior predictive performance compared to state-of-the-art tuning methods, while reducing total tuning time by 30–60%. Furthermore, EHTSA exhibits robustness to initial hyper-parameter settings and scales gracefully to high-dimensional search spaces. Our results suggest that embedding simulated annealing into training offers a principled, efficient, and broadly applicable alternative to conventional hyper-parameter optimization.

title: Phishing and Spear Phishing: examples in Cyber Espionage and techniques to protect against them
text: Cyber espionage has become one of the most persistent threats to national security, corporate intellectual property, and critical infrastructure. Among the many attack vectors employed by state-sponsored and advanced persistent threat (APT) groups, phishing and spear phishing remain the most effective and widely used initial access techniques. While ordinary phishing campaigns rely on mass distribution and generic lures, spear phishing is carefully tailored to specific individuals or organizations, often leveraging open-source intelligence, social engineering, and contextual details to bypass user suspicion. This distinction is critical in the context of cyber espionage, where a single compromised credential can grant adversaries long-term access to sensitive networks. High-profile incidents, including the 2016 Democratic National Committee breach and numerous attacks attributed to APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group, demonstrate how spear phishing can serve as a gateway to strategic intelligence theft. Despite growing awareness, many organizations remain vulnerable due to insufficient technical controls and limited user training. This paper examines representative cases of phishing and spear phishing in cyber espionage, analyzes the psychological and technical mechanisms that make them effective, and evaluates current defensive techniques, including multi-factor authentication, email filtering, and security awareness programs. By synthesizing case evidence and protection strategies, this study aims to provide practical insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to strengthen organizational resilience against espionage-driven phishing attacks.

title: Analysing Meso and Macro conversation structures in an online suicide support forum
text: Online support forums provide vital spaces for individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts, yet little is known about how conversations unfold across different levels of interaction. This study analyses meso and macro conversation structures in an online suicide support forum, examining how threads develop and how participation is organised over time. Using a dataset of forum posts, we combine sequence analysis of interactional moves at the meso level with network-based methods at the macro level to identify recurring patterns of initiation, response, and closure. Our findings reveal distinct conversational trajectories, including supportive exchanges characterised by reciprocal disclosure and sustained engagement, alongside threads that terminate rapidly. Macro-level analysis shows that a small number of highly active users play a central role in maintaining conversational continuity, while newcomer-initiated threads attract fewer responses. These results highlight the structural mechanisms underpinning peer support and have implications for forum moderation, community design, and the training of peer responders.

title: Collaboration Analysis Using Deep Learning
text:
Collaboration is a fundamental driver of innovation and productivity across scientific, industrial, and social domains. Understanding how individuals and groups work together—who cooperates with whom, how frequently, and toward what ends—provides critical insight into the structure and dynamics of collective problem-solving. Traditionally, collaboration has been studied using network analysis, bibliometrics, and statistical models of co-authorship or team interaction. While these approaches have yielded valuable findings, they often rely on handcrafted features and struggle to capture the complex, non-linear, and temporal patterns inherent in real-world collaborative behavior. As collaboration data grows in scale and heterogeneity, spanning co-authorship records, communication logs, and project repositories, there is a pressing need for methods that can automatically learn rich representations from such data.

Deep learning offers a promising solution to this challenge. Its capacity to model high-dimensional, sequential, and relational data has transformed fields such as computer vision and natural language processing, and it is increasingly applied to social and organizational analysis. Recurrent and convolutional networks can capture the temporal evolution of teams, while graph neural networks can encode the relational structure of collaboration networks. Attention mechanisms further allow models to weigh the influence of different collaborators or time steps, revealing subtle patterns that conventional metrics overlook. Despite this potential, the application of deep learning to collaboration analysis remains fragmented, with studies differing in architecture, task definition, and evaluation criteria.

This paper presents a systematic investigation of deep learning for collaboration analysis. We review existing approaches, propose a unified framework for modeling collaborative interactions across multiple domains, and empirically compare representative architectures on tasks such as link prediction, team performance forecasting, and collaboration pattern discovery. Our goal is to clarify how deep learning can advance the understanding of collaboration and to identify open challenges for future research.

title: Corona-Warn-App: Tracing the Start of the Official COVID-19 Exposure Notification App for Germany
text:
The Corona-Warn-App was downloaded 6.3 million times within the first 72 hours after its release on June 16, 2020, reaching 11.8 million downloads by June 30 and 16.4 million by the end of July, corresponding to roughly 20% of the German population. Daily active use peaked at 9.7 million users in the first week and stabilized at approximately 7.2 million by mid-July. Between June 16 and July 31, the app generated 1,247,893 warning notifications, of which 412,655 (33.1%) were triggered by laboratory-confirmed positive test results uploaded via the QR-code verification procedure. The remaining notifications originated from telephonically transmitted test results during the initial rollout phase, when hotline capacity (averaging 4,800 calls per day) temporarily exceeded digital verification capacity.

Encounter matching proved effective but sensitive to configuration. With the default risk threshold of 15 minutes within 2 meters, the average confirmed-positive user triggered 3.4 warnings; lowering the duration criterion to 10 minutes increased this figure to 5.1, while raising it to 20 minutes reduced it to 2.2. Technical performance remained stable: the exposure notification framework consumed 1.8% of average daily battery capacity, and background synchronization succeeded in 97.4% of scheduled runs.

Adoption varied sharply by region. Saxony recorded the lowest per-capita installation rate (11.2%), while Hamburg recorded the highest (28.7%), a gap of 17.5 percentage points that correlated strongly with age structure and trust in public institutions (r = 0.71). Overall, the results indicate that the app achieved substantial but uneven early adoption, and that its epidemiological value depended less on download counts than on verification coverage and threshold calibration.

title: Phylogenetic Networks
text: Phylogenetic networks have become indispensable tools in evolutionary biology, offering a more realistic representation of evolutionary history than trees alone. By accommodating reticulate events such as hybridization, horizontal gene transfer, recombination, and polyploidization, networks capture the complex, non-treelike processes that shape the genomes of many organisms. This paper has surveyed the conceptual foundations, mathematical models, and algorithmic advances that underpin the field, ranging from split networks and explicit reticulation networks to galled trees and phylogenetic forests. We have also examined the principal methods for constructing and inferring networks from molecular data, along with the computational challenges these methods entail, many of which remain NP-hard. Despite substantial progress, open problems persist, including the development of scalable inference algorithms, robust statistical frameworks for model selection, and standardized measures of network complexity and support. Future work should also address the integration of networks with population-genetic and coalescent-based approaches, as well as the growing need for interpretable visualizations in the era of large-scale genomic data. As sequencing technologies continue to generate data from increasingly diverse taxa, phylogenetic networks will play a central role in reconstructing and understanding the full tapestry of life's evolutionary history, complementing and, in many cases, superseding the traditional tree of life paradigm.

title: Is Factor Momentum More than Stock Momentum?
text: This paper investigates whether factor momentum constitutes a distinct source of returns or merely reflects stock momentum. Using a comprehensive set of equity factors, we construct factor momentum strategies and decompose their profitability into components attributable to individual stock momentum and other effects. Our results show that factor momentum generates significant abnormal returns that cannot be fully explained by stock momentum, size, value, profitability, investment, or market factors. Time-series momentum in factors captures persistent autocorrelation in factor returns, and this predictability survives after controlling for the momentum of underlying stocks. Cross-sectional factor momentum further delivers substantial alphas, particularly among factors with low exposure to stock momentum. We find that factor momentum subsumes a large portion of stock momentum profits, whereas stock momentum explains only a modest fraction of factor momentum. The evidence indicates that factor momentum is not a repackaging of stock momentum but rather a separate and economically meaningful anomaly, likely driven by underreaction to common factor-level information. These findings have implications for asset pricing models and factor-based investing, suggesting that momentum operates at multiple levels of aggregation and that factor timing strategies may capture a distinct premium.

title: Virtual Telescope for X-Ray Observations
text: X-ray astronomy has revolutionized our understanding of the hot and energetic universe, yet its progress remains constrained by the limited number of large observatories and the impossibility of physically enlarging X-ray mirrors beyond current launch capacities. The Virtual Telescope for X-Ray Observations (VTXO) addresses this challenge by distributing optics and detector across multiple small spacecraft flying in precise formation, thereby synthesizing an aperture far larger than any single launch vehicle could accommodate. This approach exploits recent advances in CubeSat technology, autonomous formation flying, and X-ray focusing optics to achieve angular resolution and sensitivity previously attainable only with flagship missions. By enabling coordinated observations across separated platforms, VTXO also opens new pathways for time-domain and polarization studies. This paper presents the conceptual design, formation architecture, and expected performance of VTXO, demonstrating its potential to democratize high-resolution X-ray astronomy through distributed small-satellite systems.

title: An Initial Exploration of Bayesian Model Calibration for Estimating the Composition of Rocks and Soils on Mars
text: The composition of rocks and soils on Mars is typically inferred from remote sensing data using spectral unmixing or geochemical inversion, yet these methods often neglect uncertainties in model parameters and measurements. This paper presents an initial exploration of Bayesian model calibration as a framework for estimating mineral and elemental abundances from Martian surface observations. We formulate the inverse problem within a probabilistic framework, combining a forward model of spectral or geochemical response with prior information and a likelihood function that captures observational noise. Posterior distributions over composition are sampled using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Using synthetic and analogue datasets, we evaluate the sensitivity of inferred compositions to prior specification, model discrepancy, and data quality. Results suggest that Bayesian calibration can provide more robust uncertainty quantification than deterministic inversion, while highlighting challenges in computational cost and model misspecification. This work establishes a foundation for future applications to Mars rover and orbital datasets.

title: A general solution to the preferential selection model
text:
Preferential selection models describe how individuals choose among alternatives when options differ in attractiveness and availability, and they underpin applications ranging from mate choice and coalition formation to hiring and resource allocation. A central challenge in this literature is that outcomes depend on the joint distribution of preferences and on the decision rule used to resolve competition, so closed-form results have generally been restricted to special cases such as identical preferences, symmetric populations, or two-choice settings. These restrictions limit both the theoretical generality of the models and their usefulness for empirical work, where heterogeneous preferences and many alternatives are the norm.

We develop a general solution to the preferential selection model that holds for arbitrary numbers of choosers and options, arbitrary preference distributions, and a broad class of selection rules. Our approach reformulates the selection process as a fixed-point problem on the vector of acceptance probabilities, which admits a unique solution under mild regularity conditions. From this characterization we derive closed-form expressions for the distribution of matched pairs, the probability that a given option is selected, and aggregate measures such as the expected rank of chosen alternatives. The solution nests several classical results as special cases and clarifies when commonly invoked independence assumptions fail.

The framework yields several new insights. In particular, we show how the concentration of preferences governs the trade-off between choice quality and competition intensity, and we identify conditions under which increased preference heterogeneity raises or lowers aggregate match quality. We illustrate the results with applications to mate selection and hiring, and we discuss extensions to dynamic and strategic settings.

title: Interpretable modeling for short- and medium-term electricity load forecasting
text: We evaluated our interpretable model on the ISO-NE and PJM datasets over a two-year horizon. For short-term forecasting (1–24 h), the model achieved a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.87% on ISO-NE and 2.04% on PJM, outperforming SARIMA (3.12% and 3.45%) and matching a gradient-boosted baseline (1.91% and 2.08%) while remaining fully transparent. For medium-term forecasting (1–30 days), MAPE rose to 4.32% and 4.78%, respectively, compared with 6.15% and 6.89% for SARIMA and 4.51% and 4.93% for the black-box baseline. Ablation studies showed that removing temperature features increased short-term MAPE by 0.64 percentage points, whereas calendar features contributed 0.41 points. The learned model coefficients revealed intuitive effects: a 1°C rise above 24°C increased predicted load by 2.3% during summer afternoons, while weekend coefficients reduced morning load by 11.7%. Feature importance rankings remained stable across seasons (Spearman ρ = 0.89). Computational cost was modest: training required 42 seconds on a single CPU, and inference for a 24-hour forecast took 3 ms. These results demonstrate that interpretability need not sacrifice accuracy, and that the model’s transparent structure supports operator trust and diagnostic use in grid operations.

title: Atomic iron and titanium in the atmosphere of the exoplanet KELT-9b
text: We reported the detection of atomic iron and titanium in the atmosphere of the ultra-hot Jupiter KELT-9b, obtained from high-resolution spectroscopic observations with HARPS-N. Cross-correlation analysis of the transmission spectrum reveals both species at high significance, with iron detected at ~5σ and titanium at ~4σ. These detections represent the first unambiguous identification of neutral titanium in an exoplanet atmosphere and confirm that refractory elements can remain in the gas phase in the dayside hemisphere of an ultra-hot Jupiter, where temperatures exceed 4000 K. The results demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy is a powerful tool for characterizing the chemical composition of hot exoplanet atmospheres and provide new constraints for models of atmospheric chemistry, condensate formation, and vertical mixing in the most irradiated giant planets known to date.

title: Introduction of water-vapor broadening coefficients and their temperature dependence exponents into the HITRAN database, Part I: CO2, N2O, CO, CH4, O2, NH3, and H2S
text: We report the introduction of water-vapor broadening coefficients and their temperature dependence exponents into the HITRAN database for seven molecular species: CO2, N2O, CO, CH4, O2, NH3, and H2S. Although water vapor is the principal foreign broadening agent in the terrestrial atmosphere, the HITRAN database has historically provided air-broadening parameters, which are dominated by N2 and O2, while the explicit influence of H2O has been represented only through a single H2O-broadening coefficient for a limited set of transitions. In this work, we have compiled and evaluated H2O-broadening coefficients (γ_H2O) and their temperature dependence exponents (n_H2O) from available laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations, and have incorporated them into the HITRAN database in a consistent format. For each species, the adopted values are provided with estimated uncertainties and references to the original sources. Where experimental data are scarce, we employ scaling relationships and empirical estimates based on the corresponding air-broadening parameters, and we flag such cases accordingly. The new parameters enable more accurate modeling of absorption line shapes in environments where water vapor is abundant, such as the lower troposphere, combustion systems, and exoplanetary atmospheres. This paper, the first part of a two-part series, describes the data sources, the evaluation methodology, and the structure of the updated database entries, and it illustrates the impact of the new parameters on calculated spectra through representative examples.

title: Deep Learning with Heterogeneous Graph Embeddings for Mortality Prediction from Electronic Health Records
text: Mortality prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is critical for early risk stratification and clinical decision support. However, EHR data are inherently heterogeneous, comprising diverse entities such as patients, diagnoses, medications, procedures, and laboratory tests, linked by complex clinical relationships. Conventional deep learning models often represent these data as homogeneous sequences or flat feature vectors, failing to capture the rich semantic and structural dependencies among clinical entities. To address this limitation, we propose a deep learning framework with heterogeneous graph embeddings for mortality prediction. The framework constructs a heterogeneous clinical graph from EHR data, learns node representations that preserve multi-type relations, and integrates them into a downstream prediction model. By explicitly modeling clinical heterogeneity, the proposed approach aims to improve predictive accuracy and interpretability. Experiments on a large real-world EHR dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of heterogeneous graph embeddings for mortality risk prediction.

title: TA-Dash: An Interactive Dashboard for Spatial-Temporal Traffic Analytics -- Demo Paper
text: Urban traffic analysis increasingly relies on large-scale spatial-temporal data, yet domain experts often lack accessible tools to explore such data interactively. We present TA-Dash, an interactive dashboard for visual analytics of spatial-temporal traffic data. TA-Dash integrates multiple coordinated views, including a map-based visualization, temporal charts, and flow views, enabling analysts to examine traffic patterns across both space and time. The system supports flexible filtering and querying by region, time interval, and traffic metrics, allowing users to drill down from city-wide overviews to fine-grained local patterns. Linked brushing across views helps reveal correlations between congestion evolution, road segments, and travel demand. TA-Dash is designed with a modular architecture that connects to standard traffic data sources and can be adapted to different urban datasets. We demonstrate its capabilities through real-world usage scenarios, showing how traffic analysts and planners can quickly identify bottlenecks, compare temporal trends, and derive actionable insights. A demonstration of TA-Dash will illustrate its interactive workflows and practical utility for spatial-temporal traffic analytics.

title: Performance Analysis of Adaptive Dynamic Tube MPC
text:
Model Predictive Control (MPC) has become a cornerstone of constrained control due to its ability to optimize performance while explicitly handling state and input constraints. However, its guarantees are predicated on the availability of an accurate system model, and even small mismatches between the model and the plant can degrade performance or, worse, lead to constraint violation and instability. Robust MPC addresses this by designing policies that remain feasible for all admissible uncertainties, but the resulting conservatism often comes at a substantial performance cost. Tube MPC mitigates this by steering a nominal trajectory while a feedback ancillary controller keeps the true state within a robust positively invariant tube around it; nevertheless, the tube must be sized for the worst-case uncertainty, which again limits achievable performance when the true uncertainty is smaller or structured differently than assumed.

Adaptive MPC seeks to overcome this trade-off by learning or estimating the uncertain dynamics online and adapting the controller accordingly. While adaptation can significantly reduce conservatism, it also introduces a fundamental difficulty: the uncertainty description used for constraint tightening evolves with the estimated parameters, and learning errors or transient estimation bias can invalidate the very robustness arguments on which tube-based guarantees rest. Adaptive dynamic tube MPC has emerged as a promising response to this challenge, wherein the tube geometry itself is adjusted online in response to updated uncertainty estimates, allowing the controller to be less conservative when confidence in the model is high and more cautious when it is not. Despite growing interest, the performance implications of these adaptive tube mechanisms—how much performance is actually recovered, under which conditions, and at what computational cost—remain insufficiently characterized.

This paper presents a systematic performance analysis of adaptive dynamic tube MPC. We formalize a general class of adaptive tube schemes, derive bounds that relate online tube adaptation to closed-loop performance, and compare these bounds against both static robust tube MPC and non-adaptive alternatives. Through numerical studies on representative uncertain systems, we quantify the performance gains attributable to dynamic tube adaptation and identify the regimes in which such adaptation is most beneficial.

title: The Right Tools for the Job: The Case for Spatial Science Tool-Building
text:
We evaluated three tool-building approaches—bespoke scripts, generalized libraries, and integrated platforms—across 120 spatial analysis tasks drawn from 15 research projects. Bespoke scripts completed 92% of tasks but required a mean of 4.7 hours per task and produced reusable code in only 18% of cases. Generalized libraries (e.g., GeoPandas, sf) completed 78% of tasks with a mean of 2.1 hours and 61% reuse. Integrated platforms completed 64% of tasks, averaging 1.4 hours, with 43% reuse but the highest dependency burden: 27% of workflows broke after upstream updates.

Task complexity moderated these effects. For routine operations (n = 71), platforms were fastest (0.9 hours vs. 1.8 for libraries and 3.2 for scripts). For novel or composite operations (n = 49), libraries outperformed platforms (2.6 vs. 5.8 hours), and scripts remained competitive (5.1 hours). A regression predicting completion time explained 54% of variance (R² = 0.54, p < .001), with tool type (β = −0.38) and complexity (β = 0.44) as significant predictors.

Qualitative coding of 38 developer interviews revealed that tool-building was undervalued in promotion criteria: 71% reported that maintenance work counted "little or not at all." Yet projects with dedicated tool-building components showed 2.3× higher downstream reuse and 31% fewer duplicated efforts. These findings support the argument that spatial science must treat tool-building as first-class scholarship rather than incidental infrastructure.

title: Cumulant methods in the estimation of response functions in time-invariant linear systems
text: This paper has examined the use of cumulant-based methods for estimating response functions in time-invariant linear systems. Unlike conventional correlation-based approaches, which rely on second-order statistics and are therefore blind to non-Gaussian features and vulnerable to additive Gaussian noise, cumulant methods exploit higher-order statistics to recover system characteristics with greater robustness. We have shown that for a time-invariant linear system driven by a non-Gaussian input, the third- and fourth-order cumulants of the output retain phase information about the system's impulse response, allowing consistent estimation of both magnitude and phase without requiring prior knowledge of the input distribution beyond its cumulant structure. The proposed estimators were demonstrated to be asymptotically unbiased and consistent under mild regularity conditions, and their performance was compared with that of classical spectral estimators. Simulation results confirm that cumulant-based estimates remain reliable in the presence of colored Gaussian noise, where correlation methods degrade substantially. However, the approach is not without limitations: computational cost increases with cumulant order, and estimation variance grows when the input deviates only mildly from Gaussianity. Future work should address adaptive order selection, robustness to impulsive noise, and extension to time-varying and multivariate systems. Overall, cumulant methods provide a valuable complement to existing techniques for response function estimation in linear systems.

title: Uncovering the structure of clinical EEG signals with self-supervised learning
text: Objective. Supervised learning paradigms are often limited by the amount of labeled data that is available. This phenomenon is particularly problematic in clinical settings where the acquisition of electroencephalographic (EEG) data is cheap, but the labeling of such data is expensive. To address this issue, we propose to use self-supervision to learn representations from unlabeled EEG data, which can then be fine-tuned for a specific clinical task. Approach. We investigate two pretext tasks for self-supervised learning on EEG: relative positioning and temporal shuffling. We evaluate the learned representations on three clinical tasks: abnormal EEG detection, sleep staging, and pathology detection. Main results. We show that self-supervised learning can be used to learn representations that are useful for a variety of clinical tasks, and that the learned representations outperform supervised baselines when only a small amount of labeled data is available. We also show that the learned representations are robust to inter-subject variability and can be used to transfer knowledge across datasets. Significance. Our results suggest that self-supervised learning is a promising approach for learning representations from clinical EEG data, and that it can be used to improve the performance of clinical decision support systems.

title: Distributed Solver for Discrete-Time Lyapunov Equations Over Dynamic Networks with Linear Convergence Rate
text:
Discrete-time Lyapunov equations play a central role in stability analysis, optimal control, and model reduction for discrete-time linear systems. For large-scale systems, centralized solvers become computationally prohibitive because they require global knowledge of the system matrices and repeated dense matrix operations. Distributed algorithms over multi-agent networks offer a promising alternative, as agents can cooperatively solve the equation using only local information and neighbor communications. However, most existing distributed methods for Lyapunov equations are developed for static networks and achieve only asymptotic convergence, which limits their applicability to real-world scenarios where communication links are time-varying and fast convergence is essential.

This paper addresses the distributed solution of discrete-time Lyapunov equations over dynamic networks. We propose a novel distributed algorithm that enables each agent to estimate the unique positive definite solution by iteratively exchanging information with its neighbors. The network topology is allowed to be directed and time-varying, subject to a standard uniform joint strong connectivity condition. By reformulating the matrix equation as a coupled set of linear equations and employing a push-sum based consensus strategy, the proposed algorithm removes the need for doubly stochastic weight matrices and thus broadens the range of admissible networks. We establish that the algorithm converges linearly to the exact solution under mild assumptions on the system and the network. The convergence rate is explicitly characterized in terms of the system dynamics and network parameters. Numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness and superior convergence performance of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.

title: Minimum wave speeds in monostable reaction-diffusion equations: sharp bounds by polynomial optimization
text: Many important classes of reaction-diffusion equations admit travelling wave solutions whose speed is determined by the nonlinear reaction term. In the monostable case, the minimum wave speed is notoriously difficult to characterize exactly, and explicit formulas are known only for a handful of special nonlinearities. We address the problem of computing sharp bounds on the minimum wave speed for a broad class of monostable reaction-diffusion equations in one spatial dimension. Our approach is based on two ingredients. First, we formulate the variational characterization of the minimum speed as an optimization problem over nonnegative functions satisfying a suitable integral identity, so that any feasible candidate yields a rigorous lower bound. Second, we relax this infinite-dimensional problem to a hierarchy of finite-dimensional semidefinite programs via sum-of-squares polynomial optimization, exploiting the fact that the nonlinearities and test functions can be represented or approximated by polynomials on a compact interval. This produces a sequence of certified lower bounds that increases monotonically and, under mild regularity assumptions, converges to the true minimum speed. Upper bounds are obtained by constructing explicit polynomial subsolutions, or by solving a dual hierarchy, and in many cases the lower and upper bounds coincide numerically to high precision, thereby determining the speed exactly. We illustrate the method on several benchmark problems, including reaction terms for which no closed-form speed is available, and compare the results with known analytical bounds and numerical estimates. The approach is fully rigorous, requires no a priori knowledge of the wave profile, and extends naturally to reaction-diffusion equations with density-dependent diffusion and to systems. Our results demonstrate that polynomial optimization provides a systematic and computationally tractable framework for obtaining sharp, certified bounds on propagation speeds in monostable media.

title: Data Assimilation in the Latent Space of a Neural Network
text:
Numerical weather prediction and other geophysical forecasting tasks rely on data assimilation (DA) to combine sparse, noisy observations with a dynamical model and produce an optimal estimate of the system state. Classical variational and ensemble-based methods perform this fusion in the model's physical space, where the state dimension is enormous and the observation operator is often nonlinear and computationally expensive. At the same time, deep learning has provided powerful reduced-order representations: autoencoders and related architectures can compress high-dimensional physical fields into low-dimensional latent spaces that preserve the dominant structure of the dynamics. This raises a natural question: can data assimilation be performed more efficiently, and perhaps more accurately, in such a learned latent space rather than in physical space?

In this paper we investigate data assimilation in the latent space of a neural network. We train an autoencoder on model trajectories, then formulate the DA problem entirely in the latent variables, using the encoder to map observations into latent space and the decoder to reconstruct physical states when required. We study how the choice of latent dimension, the treatment of observation noise under the nonlinear encoder, and the coupling between latent dynamics and the background error covariance affect analysis quality. Both variational and ensemble formulations are considered, and we compare them against physical-space baselines of comparable cost.

Experiments on idealized dynamical systems and a high-dimensional geophysical test case show that latent-space assimilation can match or exceed the accuracy of conventional methods while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. We further find that the learned latent coordinates act as an implicit, flow-dependent regularization that mitigates sampling error in ensemble estimates, although care is needed to avoid biases introduced by the encoder. These results suggest that learned latent representations offer a promising and general foundation for scalable data assimilation, and they point to several directions for extending the approach to online, nonlinear, and partially observed settings.

title: The Right Tools for the Job: The Case for Spatial Science Tool-Building
text: We evaluated our tool-building framework across three case studies. In Study 1, a spatial statistics toolkit reduced mean analysis time from 42.3 to 11.7 minutes per dataset (n = 50; 72.3% reduction, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.84). Study 2 compared a custom geovisualization pipeline against three off-the-shelf alternatives; task completion accuracy rose from 68.4% to 91.2% (n = 120; χ²(1) = 18.62, p < .001), while error rates fell by 61.5%. Study 3 measured reproducibility: 94% of analyses built with our tools reproduced exactly on independent hardware, versus 57% for ad hoc scripts (n = 35 projects). Across all studies, tool-building overhead averaged 9.6 hours, recouped after roughly 14 uses. Qualitative coding of 28 interviews revealed three themes: fit to domain-specific problems, transparency of computation, and long-term maintainability. These results support the argument that investing in spatial science tool-building yields measurable gains in efficiency, accuracy, and reproducibility, though benefits scale with reuse. Limitations include small samples and reliance on self-reported workflow data.

title: Amperometric Measurements and Dynamic Models Reveal a Mechanism for How Zinc Alters Neurotransmitter Release
text: In conclusion, we combined amperometric measurements with kinetic modeling to elucidate how zinc modulates neurotransmitter release. Our amperometric recordings from single chromaffin cells revealed that Zn²⁺ markedly alters the kinetics of individual exocytotic events, reducing the initial spike and slowing the decay of the amperometric foot, consistent with a direct action on the fusion pore. To explain these observations, we developed a dynamic model of vesicle fusion and transmitter release in which Zn²⁺ binds to key sites on the secretory machinery, modulating both the expansion of the fusion pore and the dissociation of transmitter from the vesicular matrix. The model reproduced the experimental amperometric traces across a range of Zn²⁺ concentrations, yielding quantitative estimates of the underlying rate constants. Together, these results support a mechanism whereby zinc acts not simply by inhibiting calcium entry or vesicle fusion, but by stabilizing the initial fusion pore and slowing its expansion, thereby shaping the amount and time course of transmitter release. This work provides a quantitative framework for understanding how endogenous zinc, which is co-released with glutamate in many brain regions, can dynamically tune synaptic signaling under physiological and pathological conditions.

title: On the possibility of through passage of asteroid bodies across the Earth's atmosphere
text: We study the physical conditions under which an asteroid body can traverse the Earth's atmosphere and emerge with a substantial fraction of its initial mass and velocity, a phenomenon we term a "through passage." Using a combined model of atmospheric entry dynamics, ablation, and mechanical fragmentation, we examine the parameter space of entry velocity, entry angle, body diameter, density, and strength. The analysis accounts for the competing effects of drag deceleration, convective and radiative heating, and the growth of internal stresses that can lead to catastrophic disruption. We find that through passage is possible only within a narrow corridor of entry parameters: for typical stony bodies, survival requires shallow entry angles, relatively low entry velocities, and diameters above a threshold that depends on material strength. Iron-rich bodies, owing to their higher strength and density, exhibit a broader survival window, while weak, porous bodies are destroyed even under otherwise favorable conditions. We derive an approximate analytical criterion separating the regimes of complete ablation, airburst, and through passage, and validate it against numerical simulations. The results imply that a small but non-negligible fraction of Earth-crossing objects may deposit material directly onto the surface or re-enter space without a major explosive event, with implications for impact hazard assessment, atmospheric sampling of interplanetary material, and the interpretation of certain meteorite and crater records.

title: Critical pedagogy in the implementation of educational technologies
text:
The rapid proliferation of educational technologies has fundamentally reshaped teaching and learning across global higher education. From learning management systems and massive open online courses to adaptive learning platforms and generative artificial intelligence, these tools promise greater access, efficiency, and personalization. Yet a growing body of scholarship cautions that such technologies are rarely neutral. They embed particular assumptions about knowledge, learners, and the purposes of education, often reinforcing instrumentalist and market-oriented agendas that privilege efficiency over equity and compliance over critique.

Critical pedagogy, rooted in the work of Freire and extended by later scholars such as Giroux and McLaren, offers a powerful lens for interrogating these assumptions. It foregrounds dialogue, reflection, and the co-construction of knowledge, positioning education as a practice of freedom rather than a mechanism of social reproduction. While critical pedagogy has been extensively theorized in relation to curriculum, classroom discourse, and teacher education, its encounter with educational technologies remains comparatively underexplored. Where the two fields do intersect, the discussion frequently reduces technology to either a liberatory tool or a disciplinary apparatus, obscuring the situated, contradictory ways in which digital practices actually unfold.

This paper addresses that gap by examining how critical pedagogy can inform the implementation of educational technologies in higher education. Drawing on a qualitative study of instructors and students in Chinese universities, it asks three questions: How do educators enact critical pedagogical principles when integrating digital tools? What tensions arise between critical aims and institutional, technological, and cultural constraints? And what conditions enable technology-mediated teaching to function as a genuinely dialogic and emancipatory practice?

By bringing critical pedagogy into conversation with educational technology implementation, the paper contributes both to theoretical debates on digital education and to practical discussions of how technologies might be designed and used in ways that foster critical consciousness rather than merely transmit content. It argues that implementation is never a purely technical matter but always a pedagogical and political one, and that attending to this dimension is essential if educational technologies are to serve democratic rather than merely efficient ends.

title: Individual Heterogeneity and Cultural Attitudes in Credence Goods Provision
text: Credence goods—such as medical treatments, repair services, and financial advice—are characterized by pronounced information asymmetries between experts and consumers, creating well-documented incentives for over- and undertreatment. While a substantial experimental literature has examined market outcomes in credence goods settings, comparatively little attention has been paid to how individual heterogeneity and cultural attitudes shape both expert behavior and consumer responses. This paper addresses this gap by combining a series of incentivized credence goods experiments with individual-level survey measures of cultural attitudes, including trust, uncertainty avoidance, and attitudes toward fairness and reciprocity. Drawing on data from participants across multiple cultural contexts, we examine whether and how these attitudinal dimensions predict the prevalence of overtreatment, undertreatment, and efficient provision. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity in expert behavior that is systematically related to cultural attitudes: experts scoring higher on uncertainty avoidance are more likely to overtreat, whereas those exhibiting stronger reciprocity norms are more likely to provide appropriate treatment. On the demand side, consumer trust and skepticism differentially affect search behavior, willingness to accept expert recommendations, and market participation. We further show that the interaction between expert and consumer attitudes influences overall market efficiency and the distribution of surplus. These results suggest that cultural attitudes constitute an important, and to date underexplored, determinant of credence goods markets, with implications for regulatory design, consumer protection policy, and the external validity of laboratory findings across populations.

title: Clinical connectivity map for drug repurposing: using laboratory tests to bridge drugs and diseases
text:
Drug repurposing, the identification of new therapeutic indications for existing drugs, offers a faster and less costly alternative to de novo drug development, yet its success depends on the ability to detect meaningful relationships between drugs and diseases. Over the past decade, transcriptomic connectivity mapping has emerged as a powerful paradigm, in which drug-induced gene expression signatures are compared with disease-associated signatures to prioritize candidate compounds. Despite its conceptual appeal, this approach faces practical constraints: expression profiling is costly, tissue-specific, and rarely available in routine care, and the resulting signatures can be unstable across platforms and cell types. These limitations motivate the search for alternative, clinically accessible readouts that can serve as a bridge between drugs and diseases.

Laboratory tests represent an attractive candidate for this role. Routine blood and urine tests such as complete blood counts, liver and renal function panels, and lipid and glucose measurements are inexpensive, standardized, and ubiquitously collected in electronic health records. Because many diseases induce characteristic shifts in these measurements, and because drugs frequently perturb them as intended or adverse effects, laboratory profiles constitute a dense, longitudinal, and patient-level phenotypic space in which both drugs and diseases can be embedded. However, laboratory tests have rarely been treated as a systematic connectivity substrate for drug repurposing; existing work typically focuses on single tests or narrow disease contexts, leaving their full discriminative and translational potential underexplored.

Here we introduce the concept of a clinical connectivity map, in which laboratory test profiles serve as the common currency linking drugs and diseases. We hypothesize that drugs whose population-level effects on laboratory tests oppose the test abnormalities associated with a disease are promising repurposing candidates. To test this, we assemble large-scale, real-world cohorts to derive disease-associated and drug-associated laboratory signatures, quantify their connectivity, and evaluate the resulting predictions against known indications and clinical evidence. This framework aims to complement molecular connectivity mapping by providing a scalable, clinically grounded strategy for drug repurposing.

title: An Algorithm to find Superior Fitness on NK Landscapes under High Complexity: Muddling Through
text: We evaluated the algorithm on NK landscapes with N = 100 loci and K = 90 (high complexity, rugged terrain). Across 500 independent runs, our muddling-through algorithm achieved a mean best fitness of 0.782 (SD = 0.031), compared to 0.641 (SD = 0.044) for random mutation hill climbing and 0.713 (SD = 0.038) for a standard genetic algorithm (population 100, 1,000 generations). A one-way ANOVA confirmed these differences were significant, F(2, 1497) = 214.6, p < .001, with post-hoc Tukey tests showing our method outperformed both baselines (p < .001 for both). Notably, performance gains were largest when K exceeded 80: at K = 95, our algorithm reached 0.759 versus 0.602 for hill climbing. Runtime scaled linearly with N, averaging 2.3 seconds per run (N = 100). Analysis of search trajectories revealed that muddling through escaped local optima by accepting transient fitness decreases in 68% of successful runs, whereas hill climbing stagnated within 200 steps on average. These results suggest that deliberate, short-term suboptimal moves are critical for superior fitness under high complexity.

title: Towards a Sustainable Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme
text: This paper has examined the design and performance of agricultural credit guarantee schemes (ACGSs) through the lens of sustainability, arguing that long-term viability rests on a careful balance between developmental outreach and financial self-sufficiency. The analysis shows that many schemes fail not because of inherent flaws in the guarantee instrument itself, but because of misaligned incentives, inadequate risk-sharing arrangements, weak institutional capacity, and dependence on uncertain public funding. A sustainable ACGS must therefore rest on three pillars: sound actuarial pricing and risk management, strong governance and transparency, and effective linkages with financial institutions and complementary services such as extension, insurance, and digital infrastructure. Evidence from diverse country experiences further indicates that schemes tailored to local contexts—rather than transplanted wholesale—are more likely to endure. Importantly, sustainability should not be equated with profit maximization; a scheme may legitimately pursue social objectives while still covering its costs over time. This requires realistic mandates, periodic evaluation, and mechanisms for orderly exit or restructuring when schemes underperform. Future research should explore hybrid models that blend public and private capital, the role of climate-related risks in guarantee design, and the potential of digital technologies to lower transaction costs and improve targeting. Ultimately, a sustainable agricultural credit guarantee scheme is one that expands access to finance for underserved farmers without undermining the fiscal, institutional, or financial systems on which it depends—an achievable but demanding goal requiring sustained commitment from governments, lenders, and development partners alike.

title: National debts and government deficits within European Monetary Union: Statistical evidence of economic issues
text: This paper investigates the economic implications of national debt and government deficits within the European Monetary Union (EMU), with particular attention to the statistical evidence surrounding fiscal sustainability and macroeconomic stability. Using a panel dataset covering EMU member states over the period 1999–2022, the study employs descriptive statistics, panel unit root tests, and fixed-effects regression models to examine the relationship between public debt levels, deficit ratios, and key economic outcomes such as GDP growth, inflation, and sovereign bond spreads. The empirical results reveal significant heterogeneity across member states, with high-debt countries exhibiting persistent fiscal imbalances and greater vulnerability to external shocks. The analysis further indicates that exceeding the Maastricht reference values of 60% debt-to-GDP and 3% deficit-to-GDP is systematically associated with slower growth and higher borrowing costs, although the strength of this relationship varies considerably between core and peripheral economies. Statistical evidence also points to a notable asymmetry in fiscal adjustment mechanisms, whereby surplus countries tend to stabilize more rapidly than deficit countries, exacerbating divergence within the monetary union. These findings suggest that the current fiscal framework may be insufficient to ensure long-term convergence and resilience in the absence of deeper fiscal integration and coordinated risk-sharing arrangements. The paper concludes by discussing policy implications for EMU governance, emphasizing the need for credible fiscal rules, enhanced surveillance, and structural reforms to mitigate the adverse effects of excessive debt and deficits on monetary stability and economic cohesion.

title: Value of agreement in decision analysis: Concept, measures and application
text: Decision analysis increasingly relies on expert judgement, yet the reliability of aggregated judgements depends on the agreement among decision makers. Although consensus and conflict have been extensively studied, the concept of agreement itself remains ambiguously defined and inconsistently measured in multi-criteria decision making. This paper addresses that gap by conceptualising agreement as the degree of concordance among decision makers' preferences, independent of the level of preference itself. We propose a set of measures that capture both ordinal and cardinal agreement, and we examine their properties, including sensitivity, normalisation and robustness to outliers. A comparative analysis with existing consensus indices is provided, followed by an application to a real-world group decision problem. The results demonstrate that explicitly quantifying agreement improves the transparency and credibility of decision outcomes, and that the proposed measures offer a practical complement to conventional consensus indicators. The paper thus contributes a clearer conceptual foundation and a usable measurement framework for agreement in decision analysis.

title: Model selection for ecological community data using tree shrinkage priors
text: Model selection in ecological community data is challenging because species responses are governed by many potentially weak and correlated environmental drivers, while the number of sites is often limited. We propose a Bayesian tree shrinkage prior for generalized linear models of multispecies community composition that performs simultaneous variable selection and grouping of related predictors. The prior is defined by a dyadic tree over covariates, in which internal nodes carry shrinkage parameters that are shared by their descendants; this structure adaptively collapses redundant or uninformative predictor groups toward zero while retaining flexibility for strong, isolated effects. We embed the prior in a hierarchical occupancy and abundance modeling framework suitable for counts and presence–absence data, and develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler that updates tree nodes and regression coefficients in blocks. Through simulation studies we show that the tree shrinkage prior outperforms horseshoe, spike-and-slab, and ridge alternatives in recovering sparse signals and correlated predictor clusters, particularly when signal strength is low and collinearity is high. Applying the method to multiscale vegetation and bird survey data, we identify interpretable groups of environmental covariates associated with community structure and obtain improved predictive performance relative to standard shrinkage approaches. The approach provides a practical, scalable tool for ecological variable selection.

title: A hierarchical distributed predictive control approach for microgrids energy management
text:
The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources and the growing complexity of modern power systems have accelerated the development of microgrids as a promising solution for integrating distributed generation, energy storage, and controllable loads. However, the inherent intermittency of renewable generation, together with fluctuating load demands and dynamic electricity prices, poses significant challenges for optimal energy management. Effective coordination of distributed energy resources is therefore essential to ensure economic efficiency, operational reliability, and secure real-time performance.

Centralized model predictive control has been widely adopted for microgrid energy management due to its ability to handle constraints and predict future system behavior. Nevertheless, as microgrids expand in scale and incorporate numerous heterogeneous components, centralized schemes suffer from high computational burden, single-point failure risk, and limited scalability. These limitations motivate the development of distributed control architectures, in which local controllers cooperate to achieve global objectives while preserving privacy and reducing communication requirements. Despite recent progress, many existing distributed approaches neglect the inherent hierarchical structure of microgrid operations, where slow-timescale economic scheduling and fast-timescale power balancing must be coordinated consistently.

This paper proposes a hierarchical distributed predictive control approach for microgrid energy management that bridges these temporal and spatial scales. The proposed framework decomposes the management problem into an upper layer performing economic dispatch over a long prediction horizon and a lower layer executing distributed predictive control for real-time power allocation among subsystems. Coordination between layers is achieved through a price-based interaction mechanism, while inter-subsystem coupling is handled by a distributed optimization algorithm. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed approach improves economic performance, reduces computational cost, and enhances robustness compared with centralized and flat distributed benchmarks.

title: MDE-ITMF and DEwI: Two New Multiple Solution Algorithms for Multimodal Optimization
text: Table 2 reports the results. MDE-ITMF achieved a peak ratio (PR) of 0.987 on the 2-D Six-Hump Camel Back function and 0.962 on the 10-D Rastrigin function, outperforming DEwI (0.941 and 0.903, respectively) and the niching CMA-ES baseline (0.918 and 0.877). On the 20-D Schwefel function, MDE-ITMF attained PR = 0.914 versus 0.856 for DEwI. DEwI was faster, requiring 18,400 evaluations on average versus 24,700 for MDE-ITMF, but converged to 4.2 fewer peaks per run on the 5-D Shubert function. Both algorithms significantly outperformed the baseline (Wilcoxon rank-sum, p < 0.01). These results indicate that MDE-ITMF's island-model transfer mechanism improves peak coverage at moderate computational cost, while DEwI offers a favorable speed-accuracy trade-off.

title: Biophysically grounded mean-field models of neural populations under electrical stimulation
text: We have developed and analyzed biophysically grounded mean-field models of neural populations subject to electrical stimulation. By deriving the mean-field dynamics from networks of conductance-based spiking neurons with spatial and temporal averaging, we obtained low-dimensional descriptions that retain essential biophysical features—such as synaptic conductances, reversal potentials, and nonlinear firing-rate dynamics—while remaining amenable to analytical treatment. Applying external electrical stimulation as an additive current to the mean-field equations, we systematically explored how stimulation amplitude, frequency, and waveform shape modulate population activity across regimes of asynchronous, oscillatory, and bistable dynamics. Our results reveal that stimulation can induce transitions between dynamical states through mechanisms that depend critically on the underlying bifurcation structure, including stimulation-induced switching, entrainment, and suppression of pathological oscillations. We further showed that the mean-field responses to stimulation are consistent with those of the corresponding finite-size spiking networks, validating the reduction and highlighting the role of finite-size fluctuations near bifurcation points. Importantly, the models predict that the efficacy of stimulation depends non-monotonically on stimulus intensity and frequency, with optimal parameters determined by the proximity of the unstimulated system to a bifurcation. These findings provide a theoretical bridge between detailed biophysical models and phenomenological descriptions of stimulation effects, and they offer testable predictions for experiments using deep brain stimulation, transcranial electrical stimulation, and related techniques. Future work should incorporate plasticity, heterogeneity across cell types, and spatially structured stimulation to further close the gap between mean-field theory and clinical applications. Overall, our framework demonstrates that biophysically grounded mean-field models are a powerful tool for understanding and predicting the response of neural populations to electrical stimulation.

title: Collaborative residual learners for automatic icd10 prediction using prescribed medications
text: Automatic ICD-10 prediction from prescribed medications is challenging because medication records are sparse, heterogeneous, and only indirectly reflect underlying diagnoses. Existing approaches often rely on a single monolithic model and treat medication codes as independent features, overlooking the complementary information encoded in different therapeutic subgroups. We propose Collaborative Residual Learners (CRL), a framework that decomposes ICD-10 prediction into a set of lightweight residual learners, each specializing in a clinically coherent medication subset and correcting the errors of a shared base predictor. A gating mechanism adaptively aggregates learner outputs according to each patient's medication profile, while a collaborative training objective encourages learners to capture complementary rather than redundant signals. We evaluate CRL on a large real-world prescription dataset spanning thousands of ICD-10 codes.
