CRL consistently outperforms strong baselines, including recurrent, attention-based, and multi-label classification models, improving macro-AUC and precision@k, with the largest gains on rare and clinically confusable categories. Ablation studies confirm that both residual correction and collaborative aggregation are essential, and that performance scales gracefully with the number of learners. These results suggest that collaborative residual learning offers an effective and interpretable route to medication-based diagnostic coding, supporting downstream applications such as billing audit, cohort discovery, and clinical decision support.

title: Evaluating network partitions through visualization
text: Network partitioning is a fundamental problem in graph analysis, with applications ranging from community detection in social networks to graph clustering in machine learning. Evaluating the quality of partitions, however, remains challenging because existing metrics often reduce complex structural information to a single scalar value, obscuring local patterns and boundary ambiguities. Visualization offers a complementary approach by revealing how vertices are distributed across communities and where partition boundaries are uncertain. Despite the growing availability of graph visualization tools, few studies systematically examine how visual representations can support the evaluation of network partitions. This paper addresses this gap by investigating visualization techniques that expose partition quality at both global and local levels. We propose a visual analytics framework that integrates quantitative metrics with interactive views, enabling analysts to identify misclassified vertices, compare alternative partitions, and assess stability. Through case studies on real-world networks, we demonstrate that visualization not only enhances the interpretability of partition results but also uncovers structural issues that numerical measures alone fail to detect.

title: Analysis of the main factors for the configuration of green ports in Colombia
text: This study analyzes the main factors influencing the configuration of green ports in Colombia, a country whose maritime and fluvial connectivity positions its port system as a strategic axis for international trade and, simultaneously, as a source of significant environmental pressures. Through a mixed-methods design combining a literatura review, expert surveys, and multivariate statistical analysis, the research identifies and prioritizes the critical dimensions that determine the adoption of green port strategies in Colombian terminals. The results reveal that regulatory frameworks, technological infrastructure, economic incentives, stakeholder engagement, and environmental management systems constitute the principal factors shaping port greening. Findings indicate that institutional and financial constraints, rather than technical feasibility, represent the greatest barriers to implementation, while international trade requirements and corporate sustainability commitments emerge as the strongest drivers. The study proposes a configuration model that integrates these factors and offers guidelines for port authorities, policymakers, and terminal operators seeking to advance toward sustainable port development. The conclusions highlight the need for coordinated public-private governance and targeted investment to align Colombian ports with global environmental standards and to strengthen their long-term competitiveness within the framework of the blue economy.

title: Implementing Stepped Pooled Testing for Rapid COVID-19 Detection
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has exposed critical limitations in testing capacity worldwide, particularly during periods of surging infection rates when demand for diagnostic testing far exceeds available resources. Conventional individual testing, while highly accurate, requires substantial reagents, equipment, and personnel for each sample processed, creating bottlenecks that delay results and undermine public health responses. These constraints are especially pronounced in resource-limited settings, where shortages of testing supplies and trained staff can leave large segments of the population undiagnosed. Consequently, there is an urgent need for testing strategies that maximize the number of individuals screened without proportionally increasing resource consumption.

Pooled testing offers a promising solution by combining multiple specimens into a single test, thereby reducing the total number of assays required when disease prevalence is low. However, traditional pooling schemes face a fundamental trade-off: larger pool sizes improve efficiency but sharply reduce sensitivity and become impractical as prevalence rises. Stepped pooled testing addresses this limitation through an adaptive, multi-stage approach in which pool sizes are adjusted dynamically based on initial screening results, allowing efficient identification of positive cases while preserving diagnostic accuracy.

In this paper, we present a framework for implementing stepped pooled testing for rapid COVID-19 detection. We describe the design of the testing algorithm, evaluate its performance relative to individual and conventional pooled testing through simulation and empirical analysis, and assess its feasibility for deployment in real-world settings. Our results demonstrate that stepped pooled testing can substantially increase testing throughput and reduce costs without compromising detection sensitivity, offering a practical strategy for expanding diagnostic capacity during outbreaks and in resource-constrained environments.

title: Functional clustering methods for resistance spot welding process data in the automotive industry
text: The functional clustering framework was evaluated on resistance spot welding (RSW) data comprising 12,480 weld cycles collected from 24 welding guns across three automotive body-in-white lines. Each cycle was represented by synchronized dynamic resistance and electrode displacement curves sampled at 1 kHz over a 280 ms welding window. After smoothing with a B-spline basis of 30 functions, functional principal component analysis retained the first four components, explaining 91.3% of total variability. The proposed functional k-means algorithm identified four cluster prototypes, with a mean silhouette coefficient of 0.72, outperforming Euclidean k-means (0.58) and functional hierarchical clustering (0.65). Cluster 1 (n = 5,214; 41.8%) corresponded to nominal welds, whereas Cluster 3 (n = 1,102; 8.8%) captured expulsion events characterized by a premature drop in dynamic resistance. Cross-validation against ultrasonic inspection labels yielded an overall classification accuracy of 94.6%, with precision and recall for defective welds of 0.89 and 0.86, respectively. Sensitivity analysis showed that clustering results remained stable for basis dimensions between 25 and 40, with adjusted Rand indices above 0.85. Computationally, the algorithm converged in 38 iterations on average, requiring 4.2 minutes per gun on a standard workstation. These results indicate that functional clustering of RSW signals provides a scalable and interpretable means of identifying weld-quality patterns under real production conditions.

title: Unsupervised in-distribution anomaly detection of new physics through conditional density estimation
text: We presented an unsupervised, in-distribution anomaly detection method for new physics searches based on conditional density estimation. By learning the conditional density of the data given a set of conditioning features, our approach identifies anomalies without requiring signal templates or prior knowledge of the new physics signature, while remaining robust to mismodeling of the bulk distribution. We demonstrated that the method achieves competitive sensitivity to a range of benchmark signals, including those with subtle and complex signatures, and that it can be applied directly to high-dimensional feature spaces. These results suggest that conditional density estimation provides a promising and flexible framework for model-independent searches at the LHC and beyond. Future work will explore extensions to systematic uncertainties, alternative density estimators, and applications to other datasets and experimental settings.

title: Migration and Refugee Crisis: a Critical Analysis of Online Public Perception
text: This paper critically examines online public perception of the migration and refugee crisis, focusing on how digital platforms shape, amplify, and contest narratives surrounding displaced populations. Drawing on a mixed-methods approach that combines computational sentiment analysis of social media discourse with qualitative thematic examination of user-generated comments, the study analyzes a corpus of posts and replies collected from major platforms over a twelve-month period. The findings reveal a polarized perceptual landscape: humanitarian empathy coexists with securitized framing, economic anxiety, and exclusionary rhetoric. Notably, algorithmic amplification and affective contagion intensify negative sentiment, while counter-narratives from advocacy groups and firsthand refugee testimonies can foster more nuanced understanding, albeit within limited echo chambers. The paper argues that online perception is not merely a reflection of public opinion but an active terrain where political actors, media logics, and platform architectures co-produce meaning about migration. It concludes by proposing a critical framework for interpreting digital discourse that accounts for visibility, affect, and power, and calls for platform governance and media literacy interventions to mitigate dehumanizing representations and support evidence-based, rights-conscious public deliberation.

title: General Domain Adaptation Through Proportional Progressive Pseudo Labeling
text: Domain adaptation seeks to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain, yet most existing methods remain tailored to specific distribution shifts, modality pairs, or task settings. This narrow focus limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where target domains are diverse, heterogeneous, and often inaccessible during training. We argue that a general domain adaptation framework should not presume a particular shift type, but instead adapt progressively and proportionally to the target data it encounters. To this end, we propose Proportional Progressive Pseudo Labeling (PPPL), a simple yet general approach that dynamically balances the contribution of pseudo-labeled target samples according to their predicted confidence and the evolving model state. Unlike conventional self-training that treats all pseudo labels equally or relies on fixed thresholds, PPPL introduces a proportional weighting scheme that grows with training, coupled with a progressive selection mechanism that gradually includes harder samples. This design enables stable adaptation across a wide spectrum of shifts, including covariate, label, and concept shifts, without requiring domain-specific tuning. We evaluate PPPL on multiple benchmarks spanning image classification, semantic segmentation, and text classification, under both single-source and multi-source settings. Results show that PPPL consistently matches or outperforms specialized methods, while offering a unified and lightweight solution. Our findings suggest that generality in domain adaptation can be achieved not through increasingly complex alignment modules, but through principled, adaptive use of pseudo labels.

title: Robustness to Spurious Correlations in Text Classification via Automatically Generated Counterfactuals
text: Spurious correlations pose a significant challenge to the robustness and generalization of text classification models, as models often exploit superficial lexical cues instead of learning genuine semantic relationships. This issue is particularly pronounced when such correlations hold in training data but fail to generalize to out-of-distribution or adversarial test sets. Existing mitigation strategies typically rely on manual annotation of spurious features, group labels, or counterfactual examples, which is costly and difficult to scale. We propose a novel framework that automatically generates counterfactual examples to improve model robustness to spurious correlations in text classification. Our approach first identifies potential spurious tokens via gradient-based attribution and statistical co-occurrence analysis, then generates counterfactuals by substituting these tokens with label-preserving alternatives using a masked language model guided by semantic constraints. These automatically constructed counterfactuals are used in a contrastive training objective that encourages the model to produce consistent predictions across examples that share the same label but differ in spurious features. We evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets covering sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and toxicity detection, under both synthetic and naturally occurring spurious correlation settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms strong baselines, including data augmentation and reweighting methods, improving worst-group accuracy by up to 8.4% while maintaining in-distribution performance. Further analysis shows that our generated counterfactuals are semantically coherent and effectively reduce reliance on identified spurious tokens, offering a scalable and annotation-free solution for robust text classification.

title: OER Recommendations to Support Career Development
text:
Open Educational Resources (OER) have transformed access to learning materials across educational sectors, yet their potential to support career development remains underexplored. As labor markets evolve rapidly and workers increasingly need to reskill or upskill throughout their careers, freely accessible, high-quality learning resources become essential tools for lifelong career progression. Despite growing interest in both OER and career development, these two domains have largely developed in parallel, with limited integration in research or practice.

This paper addresses that gap by examining how OER can be leveraged to support career development across diverse learner populations, including students, early-career professionals, and workers navigating career transitions. Drawing on existing literature and practical frameworks, we identify key challenges that hinder the effective use of OER for career-related learning, such as discoverability, alignment with labor market needs, and lack of structured guidance for learners.

Based on this analysis, we propose a set of recommendations for educators, institutions, and platform designers seeking to integrate OER into career development initiatives. These recommendations aim to bridge the divide between open education and career services, offering practical pathways for making OER a more effective and equitable resource for career advancement.

title: OPRA: An Open-Source Online Preference Reporting and Aggregation System
text: We deployed OPRA in three decision-making scenarios to evaluate its performance. In a university course allocation with 120 students and 40 seminars, OPRA aggregated 120 complete preference rankings in 2.3 seconds on a single-core server. The resulting assignment achieved 94.2% first-choice satisfaction, compared to 71.5% under the previous first-come-first-served mechanism. In a participatory budgeting experiment with 300 voters and 25 projects, processing 300 ballots with up to 10 ranked projects each took 4.7 seconds; the winning allocation captured 82.8% of total voter utility, versus 63.1% under plurality voting. A third deployment in a departmental committee election (45 voters, 8 candidates) completed 200 simulated elections using different aggregation rules within 58 seconds, with a maximum per-election runtime of 0.31 seconds. Usability testing with 24 participants yielded a mean System Usability Scale score of 84.6 (SD = 6.2), and median ballot submission time was 52 seconds. These results indicate that OPRA scales efficiently to hundreds of participants while maintaining usability and improving preference satisfaction over standard baselines.

title: NuClick: A Deep Learning Framework for Interactive Segmentation of Microscopy Images
text: In this paper, we introduced NuClick, a deep learning framework for interactive segmentation of microscopy images. Unlike fully automatic approaches, NuClick leverages minimal user input—a single click or scribble per object—to generate accurate segmentation masks, making it well suited for dense and crowded microscopy scenes where exhaustive annotation is impractical. The framework combines a lightweight convolutional neural network with a robust training strategy that simulates diverse user interactions, enabling effective generalization across cell types, imaging modalities, and staining protocols. Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets, including lymphocyte and nuclei segmentation benchmarks, demonstrate that NuClick achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while substantially reducing annotation time compared to manual delineation and existing interactive tools. Its efficiency and ease of use make NuClick a practical solution for accelerating large-scale microscopy image analysis and dataset curation.

title: Economics of disagreement -- financial intuition for the Rényi divergence
text: This paper develops a financial interpretation of the Rényi divergence by embedding it within a general framework of disagreement among economic agents. We begin from the observation that the Rényi divergence, parameterized by an order α, interpolates between the Kullback–Leibler divergence and the Chernoff distance, and thus encodes a continuum of attitudes toward model uncertainty. We show that this continuum admits a natural asset-pricing interpretation: each α corresponds to a distinct shadow price of disagreement, reflecting how aggressively an investor hedges against alternative beliefs. In a complete-market setting with heterogeneous priors, we derive the equilibrium stochastic discount factor as a Rényi-weighted average of individual beliefs, and we prove that the market price of disagreement is monotonically increasing in α. This yields a closed-form expression linking the Rényi divergence between the representative agent's belief and the objective measure to the excess return on a disagreement-hedging portfolio. We further characterize the limiting cases: as α → 1, the divergence reduces to Kullback–Leibler and the hedging demand coincides with the standard Bayesian benchmark; as α → ∞, the divergence approaches the worst-case Chernoff bound and the investor behaves as a robust max-min agent. The intermediate range generates a smooth trade-off between speculative trading and precautionary saving. Using this intuition, we reinterpret several empirical puzzles—excess volatility, the flat term structure of disagreement, and the profitability of divergence-based trading strategies—as manifestations of the same underlying Rényi geometry. Our results provide a unified language in which statistical divergences, heterogeneous beliefs, and asset prices can be jointly understood, and they suggest that the Rényi order α can be estimated from observed portfolio holdings as an index of financial disagreement aversion.

title: scGNN: scRNA-seq Dropout Imputation via Induced Hierarchical Cell Similarity Graph
text: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables the dissection of cellular heterogeneity at unprecedented resolution, yet its clinical and biological utility is frequently undermined by dropout events, in which transcripts are observed at low or zero counts owing to inefficient capture rather than true absence of expression. Such missing values distort downstream analyses, including clustering, trajectory inference, and differential expression, and are particularly detrimental for genes with low or moderately abundant expression. Existing imputation methods typically rely on global or locally smoothed expression statistics, autoencoder-based reconstruction, or graph neural networks built on precomputed cell similarities. However, these approaches often construct cell graphs from noisy, dropout-contaminated profiles, propagate errors across heterogeneous cell populations, and struggle to preserve genuine biological zeros. Here we propose scGNN, a graph neural network framework that performs scRNA-seq dropout imputation via an induced hierarchical cell similarity graph. scGNN first learns a latent cell representation robust to dropout, then induces a hierarchical graph that captures cell relationships at multiple granularities, from coarse lineage-level structure to fine subtype-level distinctions. A hierarchical message-passing scheme propagates expression information adaptively across these scales, allowing dropout-affected entries to be recovered from biologically plausible neighbors while avoiding over-smoothing between distinct cell states. We evaluate scGNN on multiple benchmark datasets spanning diverse tissues and sequencing protocols, and demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in imputation accuracy, cell clustering, and downstream marker gene identification, while preserving true biological zeros. These results establish scGNN as a robust and scalable solution for enhancing the reliability of scRNA-seq data analysis.

title: A Preliminary Investigation in the Molecular Basis of Host Shutoff Mechanism in SARS-CoV
text: The SARS-CoV pandemic prompted intense research into the virus's interaction with its host, yet the molecular mechanisms governing host shutoff—the widespread suppression of host gene expression—remain incompletely characterized. This preliminary investigation explores the molecular basis of host shutoff during SARS-CoV infection, focusing on the non-structural protein 1 (nsp1) and its role in translational inhibition and mRNA degradation. Using sequence analysis, structural homology modeling, and comparison with known viral shutoff factors, we identify conserved residues within nsp1 that potentially mediate interactions with the 40S ribosomal subunit and host mRNA. Our in silico docking simulations suggest that nsp1 binds to the ribosomal mRNA entry channel, sterically blocking translation initiation, consistent with observations in related coronaviruses. Additionally, we examine the contribution of other viral accessory proteins and propose a model in which nsp1 acts as a central regulator of host gene silencing while permitting selective translation of viral transcripts. These findings provide a foundational framework for understanding SARS-CoV pathogenesis and highlight potential targets for antiviral intervention. Further experimental validation is required to confirm the predicted interactions and elucidate the precise mechanistic details of this critical immune evasion strategy.

title: Effects of latitude-dependent gravity wave source variations on the middle and upper atmosphere
text:
Gravity waves (GWs) play a fundamental role in coupling the lower and upper atmosphere by transporting momentum and energy from their tropospheric sources to the middle and upper atmosphere. Their dissipation and breaking drive the circulation, thermal structure, and compositional variability of the mesosphere, thermosphere, and ionosphere, making an accurate representation of GW sources essential for whole-atmosphere models. However, the geographic distribution and seasonal variability of these sources remain poorly constrained, particularly with respect to latitude.

In this study, we investigate how latitude-dependent variations in GW source activity influence the middle and upper atmosphere using a whole-atmosphere model. We prescribe latitudinally varying source distributions and examine the resulting changes in GW propagation, momentum deposition, and the dynamical response across altitudes. The results reveal substantial latitude-dependent effects on the mean circulation and thermal structure, highlighting the sensitivity of the middle and upper atmosphere to the spatial distribution of GW sources. These findings underscore the importance of realistic, latitude-resolved source parameterizations in models aiming to reproduce observed upper-atmospheric variability.

title: Modeling Behaviour to Predict User State: Self-Reports as Ground Truth
text:
We evaluated our model on a dataset of 1,248 participants who completed 14 days of ecological momentary assessment (EMA), yielding 16,842 valid self-reports of affect and stress. Behavioural features were extracted from smartphone sensors (accelerometry, screen events, notification logs) and wearables (heart rate variability, sleep duration). A gradient-boosted classifier predicted binary stress state (low/high) with an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.79–0.83), significantly above a baseline using time-of-day and day-of-week features alone (AUC = 0.64). Precision and recall for the high-stress class were 0.76 and 0.71, respectively.

Crucially, self-reports served as ground truth, yet their reliability varied: participants with higher EMA compliance (>80%, n = 612) showed stronger model performance (AUC = 0.84) than low-compliance participants (AUC = 0.73). This suggests that sparse self-reports introduce label noise rather than reflecting true state instability. Feature importance analysis ranked screen unlock frequency (gain = 0.22), sleep irregularity (0.18), and heart rate variability (0.15) as top predictors. Removing any one feature reduced AUC by at least 0.03.

We also compared predictions to a held-out clinical interview subset (n = 94). Agreement was moderate (κ = 0.58), with discrepancies concentrated among participants reporting atypical stress patterns. Finally, a temporal ablation showed that using only the preceding 3 hours of behaviour achieved AUC = 0.77, whereas a 24-hour window reached 0.81, indicating that both immediate and circadian context matter. These results support modelling behaviour as a dynamic predictor, but they caution that self-reports are imperfect anchors for user state.

title: Engineering Privacy by Design: Are engineers ready to live up to the challenge?
text: This paper has examined whether engineers are equipped to meet the demands of privacy by design (PbD), a principle now embedded in regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR. Our findings suggest that the answer is, at present, largely negative. Engineers report limited formal training in privacy engineering, weak familiarity with legal requirements, and few organizational incentives to prioritize privacy over functional and commercial goals. Even when motivated, they often lack practical tools for translating abstract principles into design decisions. This gap is not merely technical but cultural and educational. If PbD is to become more than a compliance slogan, engineering curricula must integrate privacy as a core design concern, organizations must create accountability structures that reward privacy-protective choices, and the profession must develop shared methods for reasoning about privacy trade-offs. Until these conditions are met, engineers cannot be expected to shoulder the responsibility that privacy by design places upon them.

title: Randomized RX for target detection
text: This paper investigates randomized algorithms for target detection in high-dimensional and heterogeneous sensing environments, where conventional deterministic detectors often suffer from performance degradation due to model mismatch, limited sample support, or computational constraints. We propose a randomized RX (RX) framework that injects controlled randomness into the covariance estimation and decision statistic computation, enabling improved robustness against interference and non-Gaussian clutter. The proposed approach is analyzed in terms of detection probability, false alarm rate, and computational complexity. Both theoretical results and numerical simulations demonstrate that randomized RX detectors can achieve performance comparable to, or better than, their deterministic counterparts, particularly in small-sample and low-signal-to-noise-ratio regimes. The findings suggest that randomization offers a practical and effective strategy for enhancing target detection in challenging operational scenarios.

title: Superlinear Precision and Memory in Simple Population Codes
text: Population coding is a fundamental strategy by which neural systems represent continuous variables through the collective activity of many neurons. A central question concerns how the precision of such representations scales with population size, and whether biologically plausible coding schemes can achieve performance beyond the classical inverse-square-root law. Here we show that simple population codes, in which neurons exhibit threshold-linear tuning and Poisson-like variability, can attain superlinear precision while requiring only linear memory. We analyze the Fisher information of these codes and demonstrate that precision grows faster than the number of neurons under broad conditions on tuning width and gain. This contrasts with the widely assumed trade-off between accuracy and resource demands. Our results suggest that efficient population codes may exploit nonlinearities in tuning and noise statistics to achieve substantial gains in representational fidelity, with implications for both theoretical neuroscience and the design of neuromorphic systems.

title: Learning Opinion Dynamics From Social Traces
text: Online social platforms provide unprecedented data on how opinions form and spread, yet the mechanisms driving opinion dynamics remain difficult to identify from observational traces alone. We address the problem of learning the parameters of opinion dynamics models directly from social interaction data, without relying on controlled experiments or self-reported opinions. We formalize the inference task as a likelihood-based estimation problem over latent opinion trajectories, and develop an efficient algorithm that handles the partial and noisy observations typical of social traces. Using data from a large online platform, we show that the proposed method recovers interpretable parameters and predicts held-out opinions more accurately than strong baselines. Our results further reveal how susceptibility to social influence varies across users and topics, and demonstrate that learned models can simulate counterfactual scenarios, offering a principled tool for studying opinion formation at scale.

title: Digital Currency and Economic Crises: Helping States Respond
text:
The intersection of monetary policy and technological innovation has become increasingly critical as states confront the twin pressures of financial instability and the rapid digitization of payment systems. Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) and other forms of digital money have emerged as potential instruments for enhancing the efficacy of state responses to economic crises. While traditional monetary tools—such as interest rate adjustments and quantitative easing—remain foundational, their limitations during severe downturns, particularly when interest rates approach the zero lower bound, have prompted policymakers to explore alternative mechanisms for injecting liquidity, distributing stimulus, and maintaining financial stability.

Digital currencies offer several theoretical advantages in crisis contexts: faster and more targeted disbursement of relief funds, improved traceability to reduce leakage and fraud, and the capacity to implement negative interest rates or direct citizen dividends without the logistical constraints of physical cash. However, these benefits are accompanied by substantial risks, including threats to privacy, potential disintermediation of commercial banks, and the exacerbation of existing inequalities if access is uneven. Moreover, the deployment of digital currencies during crises raises unresolved legal and governance questions regarding emergency powers, data protection, and cross-border coordination.

This paper examines how digital currency instruments can assist states in responding to economic crises, drawing on comparative analysis of pilot programs and policy proposals across multiple jurisdictions. It argues that while digital currencies are not a panacea, their thoughtful integration into crisis-response frameworks can expand the policy toolkit available to governments. The analysis proceeds by first reviewing the theoretical underpinnings of monetary crisis response, then evaluating empirical cases of digital currency deployment, and finally proposing a governance model that balances efficacy with democratic accountability.

title: Online neural connectivity estimation with ensemble stimulation
text: We evaluated the proposed ensemble stimulation method on simulated networks of 1,000 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons (80% excitatory, 20% inhibitory) with connection probability 0.05 and synaptic weights drawn from log-normal distributions. Estimator accuracy was quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for detecting true connections. With ensemble size M = 5 and stimulation amplitude 15 mV, our method achieved AUC = 0.91 ± 0.02 after 10 minutes of recording, compared to 0.74 ± 0.03 for pairwise stimulation (n = 12 networks; paired t-test, p < 0.001) and 0.83 ± 0.02 for the prior online method of Kulkarni et al. Increasing M from 1 to 10 improved AUC monotonically, saturating near 0.93; beyond M = 10, stimulation artifacts degraded spike sorting, reducing effective yield. Estimation error for inferred excitatory weights averaged 18.3% ± 4.1%, and inhibitory weights 22.7% ± 5.6%. Runtime scaled linearly with M, requiring 4.2 ms per ensemble stimulus on a single GPU, compatible with a 50 Hz stimulation schedule. Under 30% random neuron dropout, AUC declined only modestly to 0.87 ± 0.03, confirming robustness. These results indicate that ensemble stimulation substantially accelerates connectivity estimation relative to sequential pairwise probing while remaining compatible with online, closed-loop operation.

title: Prediction of short and long-term droughts using artificial neural networks and hydro-meteorological variables
text: This study evaluated the capability of artificial neural networks (ANNs) for predicting short- and long-term droughts using hydro-meteorological variables. Multiple ANN models were developed with different input combinations of precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, and streamflow, and their performance was assessed against observed drought indices at 1-, 3-, 6-, and 12-month time scales. The results demonstrated that the ANN approach effectively captured the nonlinear relationships between hydro-meteorological drivers and drought characteristics, with prediction accuracy generally improving as the aggregation time scale increased. Among the input variables, precipitation and streamflow exhibited the strongest influence on model performance, while the inclusion of temperature and evapotranspiration provided additional predictive skill, particularly for longer-term droughts. The findings also revealed that model accuracy declined for short-term predictions, reflecting the higher variability and complexity of drought conditions at finer temporal resolutions. Overall, the study confirms that ANNs, when coupled with appropriate hydro-meteorological predictors, constitute a reliable and practical tool for drought forecasting. The proposed framework can support water resource managers and policymakers in implementing timely mitigation measures, although future research should incorporate larger datasets and alternative machine learning techniques to further enhance predictive robustness under changing climatic conditions.

title: Pricing the Information Quantity in Artworks
text: This paper investigates how the informational content of artworks can be conceptualized and priced within cultural and economic frameworks. Drawing on information theory, aesthetics, and cultural economics, it proposes a model that quantifies the information an artwork conveys through measures of novelty, complexity, and semantic density. The study argues that artworks function as information-bearing entities whose value is shaped not only by material and symbolic attributes but also by the amount of structured information they encode and communicate. By operationalizing these dimensions, the paper develops a pricing heuristic that links informational quantity to market valuation, while acknowledging the role of subjective interpretation, institutional mediation, and scarcity. Illustrative cases from modern and contemporary art are used to test the model’s explanatory power. The findings suggest that informational quantity offers a complementary lens for understanding price formation in art markets, bridging quantitative and qualitative approaches to artistic value.

title: Fair Classification via Unconstrained Optimization
text:
1. Introduction

Fairness in machine learning has become a central concern as automated decision systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as credit scoring, hiring, and criminal justice. A growing body of work addresses this issue by imposing fairness constraints during training, typically formulated as parity conditions on group-dependent statistics—for example, demographic parity, equalized odds, or predictive rate parity. The standard approach casts fair learning as a constrained optimization problem and solves it using techniques such as constrained empirical risk minimization, adversarial training, or post-processing adjustments. While effective, these methods often introduce substantial computational overhead, require careful tuning of dual variables or Lagrange multipliers, and can suffer from unstable convergence when multiple constraints are active.

In this paper, we propose a fundamentally different perspective: fair classification via unconstrained optimization. Our key observation is that many common fairness constraints can be expressed as penalized terms that are differentiable and compatible with standard stochastic gradient descent. Rather than solving a constrained problem directly, we reformulate fairness as a regularized objective that jointly minimizes prediction error and a measure of unfairness. This yields a simple, scalable, and easily implementable training procedure that requires no dual variables, no inner-loop solvers, and no post-hoc adjustments.

We theoretically analyze the proposed formulation, showing that under mild conditions the unconstrained minimizer approximates the solution of the original constrained problem, with fairness violation bounded by the penalty parameter. We further establish convergence guarantees for the resulting stochastic optimization algorithm. Empirically, we evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and compare it against state-of-the-art constrained and adversarial fair learning baselines. Across diverse settings, our approach achieves comparable or better fairness-accuracy trade-offs while reducing training time by a significant margin. These results suggest that unconstrained optimization offers a practical and principled pathway to fair classification, particularly in large-scale and resource-constrained settings.

title: A Deep Learning Approach for COVID-19 Trend Prediction
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has placed unprecedented strain on public health systems worldwide, creating an urgent need for accurate forecasting tools to inform policy decisions and resource allocation. This paper presents a deep learning approach for predicting COVID-19 transmission trends across multiple regions. We propose a hybrid architecture that combines long short-term memory (LSTM) networks with convolutional neural networks to capture both temporal dependencies and spatial correlations in epidemiological data. The model incorporates diverse inputs, including confirmed cases, mobility indicators, vaccination rates, and demographic features, to generate multi-step forecasts of infection trajectories. We evaluate our approach on publicly available datasets from several countries, comparing its performance against established statistical and machine learning baselines using metrics such as mean absolute error and root mean square error. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior predictive accuracy across different forecasting horizons, particularly during periods of rapid change. These findings suggest that deep learning methods offer a promising tool for real-time epidemic surveillance and proactive public health planning.

title: Latent neural source recovery via transcoding of simultaneous EEG-fMRI
text:
Simultaneous electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging (EEG-fMRI) offers a powerful, non-invasive window into the human brain, combining the millisecond temporal resolution of EEG with the millimeter spatial resolution of fMRI. Despite this complementary potential, integrating the two modalities remains challenging because they measure fundamentally different signals: EEG captures summed postsynaptic potentials at the scalp, whereas fMRI reflects hemodynamic changes coupled to neural activity. A central goal of data fusion is to recover the latent neural sources that jointly generate both observations, thereby bridging the temporal and spatial views into a unified characterization of brain function.

Existing approaches to EEG-fMRI integration, including asymmetric predictions, symmetric fusion, and generative models, have advanced this goal but face notable limitations. Many methods assume linear mappings, require strong priors on source dynamics, or struggle to exploit the complementary information when one modality is noisy or incomplete. These constraints motivate learning a shared latent representation directly from data, rather than imposing hand-crafted coupling. Deep neural networks can, in principle, learn such representations, yet most architectures are designed for a single modality and do not naturally handle the asymmetric, cross-domain nature of EEG-fMRI.

Here we propose a transcoding framework for latent neural source recovery from simultaneous EEG-fMRI. Our approach learns a shared latent space by training a model to translate between the two modalities: latent sources are inferred from one modality and decoded to reconstruct the other, with cycle consistency enforcing a coherent, bidirectional mapping. We evaluate the method on simulated and real simultaneous EEG-fMRI data, assessing source localization and temporal recovery against established fusion baselines. Results suggest that transcoding provides a flexible and effective route to uncovering the latent neural sources underlying multimodal brain measurements.

title: Absorbing transition in a coevolution model with node and link states in an adaptive network: Network fragmentation transition at criticality
text: We simulated the coevolutionary dynamics on adaptive networks of size N = 10,000 with mean degree ⟨k⟩ = 6, averaging over 100 independent realizations. For the fraction of active nodes, ρ, we observed a continuous absorbing transition at infection rate λ_c = 0.432 ± 0.005, with the order parameter following ρ ~ (λ − λ_c)^β and exponent β = 0.51 ± 0.03, consistent with mean-field directed percolation. Link adaptation, governed by rewiring probability p, shifted λ_c downward: at p = 0.5, λ_c = 0.371 ± 0.006, while at p = 0.9, λ_c = 0.298 ± 0.008. Crucially, at criticality the network undergoes a fragmentation transition. The largest connected component size, S₁/N, drops from 0.94 ± 0.01 in the active phase to 0.38 ± 0.02 at λ_c, and to 0.11 ± 0.01 in the absorbing phase. The second largest component peaks at λ_c with S₂/N = 0.09 ± 0.01, signaling incipient fragmentation. Simultaneously, the average degree of active nodes, ⟨k⟩_act, falls from 6.1 ± 0.1 to 3.2 ± 0.2 at λ_c, while the clustering coefficient rises from 0.08 ± 0.01 to 0.21 ± 0.02. Finite-size scaling with N = 2,500, 5,000, and 20,000 confirmed the transition, yielding 1/ν = 0.48 ± 0.04. These results show that the absorbing transition coincides with network fragmentation at criticality, driven by adaptive rewiring that isolates active nodes.

title: A Horserace of Volatility Models for Cryptocurrency: Evidence from Bitcoin Spot and Option Markets
text: This paper provides a comprehensive horserace of volatility models for Bitcoin by jointly utilizing spot and option market data. Our empirical analysis reveals that models incorporating implied volatility information generally outperform pure time-series specifications, underscoring the informational efficiency of Bitcoin's option market. Specifically, hybrid models that blend realized measures with option-implied variance demonstrate superior predictive accuracy for future volatility. However, the incremental value of option-derived signals varies across market regimes, diminishing during periods of extreme turbulence. These findings suggest that while the option market serves as a valuable source of forward-looking information, its dominance is not unconditional. Overall, this study highlights the importance of integrating multi-market data for robust volatility forecasting in the rapidly evolving cryptocurrency landscape.

title: Wealth and Poverty: The Effect of Poverty on Communities
text: This paper examines the multifaceted relationship between poverty and community well-being, arguing that poverty operates not merely as an individual economic condition but as a structural force that reshapes the social, institutional, and physical fabric of communities. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature from sociology, economics, and public health, the analysis identifies several pathways through which concentrated poverty undermines collective life. First, poverty constrains local economic development by reducing consumer demand, weakening small businesses, and limiting the tax base necessary for public services. Second, it erodes social capital by increasing residential instability, disrupting informal support networks, and fostering distrust among residents. Third, high-poverty communities often experience disproportionate exposure to environmental hazards, underfunded schools, limited healthcare access, and higher rates of crime and policing, all of which reinforce cycles of disadvantage. The paper also considers the spatial dimension of poverty, noting that segregation and historical disinvestment concentrate deprivation in specific neighborhoods, producing effects that persist across generations. However, the analysis rejects deterministic accounts: it highlights community resilience, informal mutual aid, faith-based organizations, and grassroots mobilization as countervailing forces. Policy interventions such as place-based investment, affordable housing, universal basic income pilots, and community-led development are evaluated for their capacity to mitigate poverty’s collective harms. The paper concludes that addressing poverty requires not only individual-level assistance but also structural reforms that rebuild the shared institutions and public goods upon which thriving communities depend. Understanding poverty as a community-level phenomenon, rather than solely an individual failing, is essential for designing effective and equitable responses.

title: Fairness, Welfare, and Equity in Personalized Pricing
text: Personalized pricing—charging different prices to different consumers based on observed or inferred characteristics—has become increasingly feasible with the growth of consumer data and algorithmic targeting. While such pricing can improve firm profits and, in some cases, allocative efficiency, it also raises pressing concerns about fairness, welfare distribution, and equity. Critics argue that personalized pricing may exploit consumers with limited outside options, exacerbate disparities across income or demographic groups, and undermine trust in digital markets. Yet the normative implications remain contested: a practice that reduces aggregate deadweight loss may still be judged unjust if its distributional effects are regressive. This paper develops a unified framework to evaluate personalized pricing along three dimensions: fairness in prices and outcomes, total and consumer welfare, and equity across heterogeneous groups. We characterize when personalized pricing improves social welfare and when it violates widely held equity principles, and we derive conditions under which regulation, transparency, or limits on data use can reconcile efficiency with distributive justice.

title: Valuation Models Applied to Value-Based Management. Application to the Case of UK Companies with Problems
text: This paper examines the applicability of contemporary valuation models within the framework of Value-Based Management (VBM), focusing specifically on UK companies experiencing financial distress. While VBM and its associated valuation techniques—such as Discounted Cash Flow (DCF), Economic Value Added (EVA), and Cash Value Added (CVA)—are widely adopted for healthy firms, their reliability diminishes when applied to troubled companies, where assumptions of going-concern continuity and stable cash flows become problematic. Using a sample of UK-listed firms exhibiting financial difficulties, this study tests the explanatory power of these models against actual market values. The findings reveal significant discrepancies between model-generated intrinsic values and observed market capitalizations, suggesting that traditional VBM valuation approaches systematically misestimate value in distress scenarios. The paper identifies key methodological limitations, including the treatment of negative cash flows, terminal value estimation, and the cost of capital under heightened default risk. It proposes adjustments to improve model robustness in such contexts. The results contribute to both the VBM literature and practical valuation by highlighting the conditions under which standard models fail and offering guidance for analysts and managers applying value-based metrics to financially troubled UK firms.

title: Maritime Design: A CSCW Territory?
text:
Maritime design—the sociotechnical work of conceiving, engineering, and coordinating the vessels and offshore structures on which global trade and energy production depend—is rarely considered a domain of computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW). Yet the design of a ship or offshore platform is a deeply collective accomplishment. Naval architects, structural and systems engineers, classification societies, shipyards, suppliers, and owner-operators must align their efforts across organizational, disciplinary, and national boundaries, often over years and under shifting regulatory and commercial constraints. Design artifacts such as 3D product models, class drawings, and change orders circulate among these parties, carrying with them assumptions, commitments, and the traces of prior negotiation. In this respect, maritime design exhibits precisely the phenomena that CSCW has long studied: distributed collaboration, boundary objects, articulation work, and the coordination of interdependent tasks under conditions of uncertainty.

At the same time, maritime design resists easy assimilation into established CSCW framings. It is characterized by long-lived, safety-critical artifacts, heavy regulation and classification regimes, extreme asymmetries of expertise and authority, and a project-based industrial structure in which competitors collaborate on shared standards while guarding proprietary knowledge. Digitalization—through simulation, model-based definition, and cloud-based collaboration platforms—is reshaping these arrangements, but it also surfaces tensions around trust, accountability, and the ownership of design data that CSCW is well positioned to interrogate. Whether these features constitute a distinctive research territory, or merely another instance of familiar cooperative work dynamics, remains an open question.

This paper asks whether maritime design can be understood as a CSCW territory in its own right. Drawing on a review of existing studies and our own empirical engagement with shipbuilding and offshore engineering practice, we examine how cooperative work is organized in this setting, where existing CSCW concepts illuminate or obscure what we observe, and what the domain might contribute back to the field. We argue that maritime design is not merely an application area for CSCW methods but a site that tests and extends them, particularly regarding materiality, regulation, and the temporal scale of collaboration.

title: Differentially Private Secure Multi-Party Computation for Federated Learning in Financial Applications
text: We evaluated the proposed DP-SMPC protocol against a baseline federated averaging (FedAvg) setup across three synthetic financial datasets: credit scoring (100k samples, 50 features), fraud detection (500k, 30), and loan default (200k, 40), each partitioned among 10 clients. With ε=1.0 and δ=1e-5, DP-SMPC achieved 94.2% AUC on credit scoring versus 95.1% for non-private FedAvg, a 0.9-point drop, while FedAvg with local DP alone fell to 91.3%. For fraud detection, F1 scores were 0.872 (DP-SMPC), 0.891 (FedAvg), and 0.834 (local DP). Loan default accuracy was 88.7%, 89.9%, and 85.2%, respectively. Privacy leakage, measured via membership inference attack success, dropped from 61.4% under FedAvg to 50.8% under DP-SMPC—near the 50% random baseline. Secure aggregation overhead added 18% communication cost and 2.3× runtime versus plain FedAvg, but remained 40% cheaper than a fully homomorphic encryption variant. Increasing clients from 5 to 20 improved DP-SMPC AUC on credit scoring from 92.1% to 94.6%, confirming that more participants dilute noise. These results indicate that DP-SMPC preserves utility within 1–2 points of non-private FedAvg while providing formal (ε, δ)-DP and cryptographic confidentiality, making it practical for regulated financial deployments where local DP alone is insufficient.

title: Learning Undirected Graphs in Financial Markets
text: This paper investigated the problem of learning undirected graphs from financial market data, addressing the unique challenges posed by non-Gaussianity, heavy tails, and time-varying dependencies. Through comparative analysis of graphical model estimation techniques, including Gaussian graphical models, copula-based approaches, and nonparametric methods, we demonstrated that robust and scalable graph recovery is achievable under realistic market conditions. Empirical evaluations on equity and cryptocurrency datasets showed that the proposed framework recovers economically meaningful dependency structures while remaining computationally tractable. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for tail dependence and temporal instability when inferring market networks. Future work could extend the framework to dynamic and causal settings, incorporate higher-order interactions, and explore applications in portfolio optimization and systemic risk monitoring.

title: Valuation Models Applied to Value-Based Management. Application to the Case of UK Companies with Problems
text: This paper examines the applicability of contemporary valuation models within the framework of value-based management (VBM), with a specific focus on UK companies experiencing financial distress or operational difficulties. Value-based management has become a dominant paradigm in corporate governance, advocating that shareholder value maximization should guide strategic decision-making. However, the effectiveness of VBM critically depends on the accuracy and appropriateness of the valuation models employed, particularly when firms face adverse conditions that distort conventional valuation assumptions. This study evaluates several prominent valuation models, including discounted cash flow (DCF), residual income, economic value added (EVA), and market-based multiples, and assesses their reliability when applied to troubled UK companies. The empirical analysis draws on a sample of UK-listed firms that have exhibited persistent financial underperformance, restructuring events, or insolvency risk during the period under investigation. The findings reveal that traditional valuation models often produce misleading or highly volatile estimates for distressed firms due to unstable cash flows, unreliable earnings forecasts, and distorted market comparables. The paper further explores how value-based management principles can be adapted to such contexts by incorporating risk-adjusted discount rates, scenario analysis, and real options valuation. The results suggest that a hybrid valuation approach, combining fundamental and market-based techniques with explicit distress adjustments, offers superior explanatory power for stock price movements and managerial decision outcomes. The study contributes to the literature by highlighting the limitations of applying standard VBM valuation tools indiscriminately and by proposing practical modifications for firms operating under financial strain. Implications for corporate managers, investors, and policymakers are discussed, emphasizing the need for context-sensitive valuation practices that align with the strategic objectives of value-based management while accounting for the unique challenges of troubled companies.

title: Masks and COVID-19: a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions
text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted unprecedented global reliance on non-pharmaceutical interventions, among which mask wearing remains one of the most visible and contested. Yet the evidentiary debate around masks has been hampered by a persistent conceptual gap: most studies estimate statistical associations between mask policies and health outcomes, while the causal quantities that matter for policy—how many infections, hospitalizations, or deaths would have been averted—are rarely identified. This gap is not merely technical. It shapes public trust, informs cost-benefit calculations, and determines whether masks are framed as effective tools or symbolic gestures.

This paper develops a causal framework for imputing value to public-health interventions, using mask wearing during COVID-19 as the guiding case. We argue that the relevant target of estimation is not the average effect of masks in a population, but the counterfactual value of mask-induced reductions in transmission under specific epidemiological and behavioural conditions. Drawing on directed acyclic graphs and potential outcomes, we formalize how confounding by policy stringency, risk perception, and time-varying adoption can be addressed using natural experiments, instrumental variables, and structural models. We further propose a value-imputation procedure that translates estimated causal effects into policy-relevant metrics, including infections averted per million masks and marginal value per dollar of intervention.

By reorienting the analysis from association to imputed causal value, this framework clarifies when and why mask mandates can be expected to generate net public-health benefit, and it offers a generalizable template for evaluating other non-pharmaceutical interventions amid emerging infectious threats.

title: A Smooth Robustness Measure of Signal Temporal Logic for Symbolic Control
text: This paper introduces a novel smooth robustness measure for Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications, addressing a critical limitation in symbolic control synthesis where traditional robustness metrics are non-differentiable and thus incompatible with gradient-based optimization techniques. The proposed measure leverages a smooth approximation of the minimum and maximum operators used in STL semantics, yielding a continuously differentiable function that preserves the soundness of the original robustness degree. We establish theoretical guarantees demonstrating that the smooth robustness measure is both sound and complete with respect to satisfaction of STL specifications, and that it converges uniformly to the classical robustness as a smoothing parameter tends to zero. This enables the direct application of efficient gradient-based optimization methods for controller synthesis while maintaining formal correctness guarantees. We integrate the proposed measure into a symbolic control framework and demonstrate its effectiveness through comparative case studies on autonomous systems, including obstacle avoidance and reachability tasks. Experimental results show that the smooth robustness measure achieves up to an order of magnitude reduction in computational cost compared to mixed-integer programming approaches, while producing controllers that satisfy the given STL specifications with high probability. The proposed method thus bridges the gap between formal verification and scalable optimization for temporal logic control.

title: Capillary-Gravity Water Waves: Modified Flow Force Formulation
text:
Capillary-gravity water waves arise in the irrotational flow of an incompressible inviscid fluid bounded above by a free surface and below by a rigid bed, with both gravity and surface tension acting as restoring forces. These waves are central to numerous phenomena in oceanography, coastal engineering, and microfluidics, where wavelengths range from meters to millimeters and surface tension can no longer be neglected. Despite the classical status of the problem, the construction of efficient and robust formulations for steady and unsteady solutions remains an active area of research, particularly for waves of large amplitude and for flows with vorticity or nonuniform currents.

A key tool in the analysis of steady water waves is the flow force, a horizontal momentum flux invariant that provides a compact global relation between the free surface, the velocity field, and the pressure. In the absence of surface tension, the flow force has been used to derive existence results, bifurcation diagrams, and sharp bounds on wave speed and amplitude. However, the classical flow force formulation does not directly incorporate capillary effects, and naive extensions can obscure the underlying variational structure or lead to cumbersome boundary terms. This limitation motivates the need for a modified formulation that treats surface tension on an equal footing with gravity.

In this paper, we introduce a modified flow force formulation for capillary-gravity water waves. By absorbing the capillary contribution into a generalized momentum flux, we obtain a conserved quantity that remains valid for arbitrary amplitude, finite depth, and nonzero vorticity. The resulting formulation simplifies the derivation of steady-state equations and provides a natural framework for studying the interplay between gravity and surface tension. We illustrate the utility of the approach by rederiving known dispersion relations and by outlining new bounds on the wave speed.

title: Multi-stream RNN for Merchant Transaction Prediction
text:
We evaluate the proposed Multi-stream RNN against sequential baselines on a proprietary dataset of 12.4 million transactions from 86,000 merchants over 12 months. Data is split chronologically into 9 months training, 1.5 months validation, and 1.5 months test. We report AUC, F1, and Recall@P90.

The Multi-stream RNN achieves an AUC of 0.893, outperforming a single-stream GRU (0.851), LSTM (0.857), and a feature-engineered XGBoost model (0.869). F1 improves to 0.712 versus 0.648 for the best baseline, and Recall@P90 reaches 0.634 compared to 0.561. Ablations confirm each stream's contribution: removing the merchant-profile stream reduces AUC by 2.1 points, the temporal stream by 3.4 points, and the cross-merchant stream by 1.8 points. A variant without attention pooling drops AUC to 0.874.

Performance gains are largest for cold-start merchants with fewer than 50 historical transactions, where AUC rises from 0.792 to 0.846, suggesting that cross-merchant signals compensate for sparse individual histories. Gains diminish for merchants with over 1,000 transactions (0.901 vs. 0.894). Inference latency is 18 ms per merchant batch on a single V100 GPU, within production constraints. These results indicate that multi-stream recurrent architectures effectively capture complementary temporal, profile, and relational signals for merchant transaction prediction.

title: Demand side management impacts on electricity network vulnerability
text:
This study has examined the impacts of demand side management (DSM) on the vulnerability of electricity networks, addressing a critical gap in the literature where DSM is typically evaluated for operational or economic benefits rather than its influence on network robustness. Through a combination of network modelling and vulnerability assessment under a range of load-modification scenarios, the analysis demonstrates that DSM can meaningfully alter the exposure of power systems to cascading failures and supply disruptions, though these effects are strongly contingent on the type, scale, and spatial distribution of demand-side interventions.

The findings reveal a clear distinction between peak-shaving and load-shifting strategies. Peak reduction generally improves network resilience by relieving stress on heavily loaded branches and reducing the likelihood of overload-triggered cascades. However, aggressive or poorly coordinated load shifting can inadvertently concentrate demand in time windows or network regions that are already constrained, thereby creating new vulnerabilities rather than mitigating existing ones. The results further indicate that the vulnerability response is non-linear: modest levels of DSM tend to yield marginal benefits, whereas excessive or misaligned deployment can degrade network performance under contingency conditions.

These outcomes underscore the need to integrate vulnerability criteria into DSM planning and market design. Demand response programmes should be assessed not only against cost and efficiency metrics but also against their topological and operational consequences for the transmission and distribution network. The paper contributes a modelling framework that can support such integrated assessment, and it highlights the importance of coordination between system operators, aggregators, and regulators.

Future work should extend the analysis to include stochastic renewable generation, dynamic customer behaviour, and coupled gas–electricity systems, as these factors may further modulate the relationship between DSM and network vulnerability. Overall, the study affirms that demand side management is not inherently resilience-enhancing; its impact depends on how, where, and when flexibility is deployed.

title: Fire Sales, the LOLR and Bank Runs with Continuous Asset Liquidity
text: This paper develops a bank-run model in which asset liquidity is continuous and fire sales interact with the lender of last resort (LOLR). Banks hold illiquid assets that can be liquidated only at a discount, and the marginal cost of liquidation rises continuously with the amount sold. In the absence of intervention, the anticipation of fire-sale losses makes depositors more inclined to withdraw early, so the run threshold depends on the liquidity of the asset market and on the resulting endogenous recovery value. I show that an LOLR can eliminate runs by lending against the collateral value of illiquid assets, but the optimal policy must account for two opposing effects. On one hand, liquidity support raises the payout to non-withdrawing depositors and removes the strategic complementarity that drives runs. On the other hand, it weakens banks' ex ante incentives to hold liquid assets and may expose the LOLR to losses when asset prices are depressed. With continuous asset liquidity, the LOLR faces a smooth trade-off: partial support can implement an interior run probability, while full support achieves run prevention at the cost of greater moral hazard. The analysis characterizes the optimal lending rate and haircut, and shows that a properly priced LOLR facility can restore efficiency when the social cost of fire sales exceeds the private cost. The results also imply that liquidity regulation and LOLR policy are substitutes, and that their optimal mix depends on the elasticity of the fire-sale discount.

title: Influence of Absolute Humidity, Temperature and Population Density on COVID-19 Spread and Decay Durations: Multi-prefecture Study in Japan
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has exhibited substantial spatial heterogeneity in transmission intensity and epidemic duration across regions, yet the environmental and demographic drivers of this variation remain incompletely understood. While numerous studies have examined the effects of meteorological factors on COVID-19 spread, most have focused on temperature and relative humidity, with the role of absolute humidity receiving comparatively little attention. Moreover, population density, a key determinant of contact frequency, is rarely considered jointly with climatic variables in a unified analytical framework. Japan offers a particularly suitable setting for such an investigation: it spans a wide latitudinal and climatic gradient, comprises prefectures with markedly different population densities, and has maintained relatively consistent testing and reporting practices. Using multi-prefecture data from Japan, this study examines how absolute humidity, temperature, and population density jointly influence both the spread and the decay durations of COVID-19. By distinguishing the growth and decline phases of local epidemics, we aim to clarify whether these factors exert symmetric or phase-dependent effects. The findings are expected to inform region-specific preparedness and intervention strategies, and to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the environmental epidemiology of respiratory infectious diseases.

title: Towards Earnings Call and Stock Price Movement
text: Earnings calls are a key disclosure channel through which publicly traded firms communicate their performance and outlook to investors, yet the extent to which the linguistic content and delivery of these calls relate to stock price movements remains incompletely understood. This paper investigates the relationship between earnings call characteristics and subsequent stock price movement using a dataset of transcribed quarterly earnings calls linked to intraday and daily equity returns. We extract textual, sentiment, and vocal features from both prepared remarks and the question-and-answer session, and examine their association with abnormal returns, volatility, and trading volume around the call. Our analysis shows that executive tone, linguistic uncertainty, and the dynamics of analyst questioning carry incremental information beyond standard accounting variables and guidance. We further develop predictive models that combine call-derived features with market and firm-level controls, and find that they achieve modest but statistically significant improvements in forecasting short-horizon price direction. The results suggest that earnings calls contain economically meaningful signals that are not fully impounded by markets at the time of disclosure, and they highlight the value of joint linguistic and market analysis for understanding information flow in financial markets.

title: Two-Step market clearing for local energy trading in feeder-based markets
text:
The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) such as rooftop photovoltaics, battery storage, and flexible loads is transforming low-voltage distribution networks from passive consumption areas into active energy systems. This paradigm shift has motivated the development of local energy markets, which enable prosumers to trade energy directly with one another, potentially reducing reliance on the upstream grid, lowering energy costs, and creating new revenue streams. Among the various market designs proposed in the literature, feeder-based markets have attracted particular attention because transactions are confined within the physical boundaries of a distribution feeder, thereby respecting network constraints and avoiding costly grid reinforcements.

A central challenge in designing such markets is the market clearing mechanism itself. Most existing approaches rely on a single-step clearing procedure, in which all participants submit bids and offers that are matched simultaneously. While computationally straightforward, single-step clearing struggles to accommodate the sequential nature of real-world trading: participants often need to adjust their positions after observing initial market outcomes, and network operators may require a separate stage to validate or curtail transactions that violate physical limits. These limitations can lead to inefficient allocations, price volatility, and frequent interventions by the distribution system operator.

This paper addresses these shortcomings by proposing a two-step market clearing mechanism for feeder-based local energy trading. The first step determines an initial allocation among prosumers based on their submitted preferences, while the second step adjusts this allocation to ensure feasibility with respect to network constraints and to incorporate updated participant information. We formulate the clearing problem, analyze its properties, and evaluate its performance through simulations on representative low-voltage feeders. The results demonstrate that the proposed two-step approach improves economic efficiency and reduces constraint violations compared with conventional single-step clearing.

title: Secure Control in Partially Observable Environments to Satisfy LTL Specifications
text:
We evaluated the proposed synthesis algorithm on a grid-world surveillance benchmark adapted from the literature, in which an agent must satisfy the LTL specification φ = G(visit_a → F checkpoint) ∧ G(¬intruded) under partial observability induced by limited sensing range and sensor noise. The environment comprised 900 states with 12 observations and 5 actions; observation uncertainty was modeled with 0.1 misdetection probability. We compared our approach against three baselines: (i) a POMDP belief-space value iteration (PBVI) heuristic, (ii) a certainty-equivalence (CE) controller synthesized on the most likely observation, and (iii) a shield-based baseline using a coarse abstraction.

Across 200 randomized initial beliefs, the proposed method achieved a satisfaction probability of 0.94, outperforming PBVI (0.81), CE (0.63), and the shield baseline (0.72). The performance gap widened with increasing uncertainty: at misdetection probability 0.25, the proposed method retained 0.89 satisfaction, whereas PBVI dropped to 0.70 and CE to 0.41. Unsafe intrusions occurred in 1.2% of runs for the proposed method, compared with 6.8% for PBVI and 14.5% for CE, confirming that explicit reasoning over belief supports safety. Computational cost was moderate: mean synthesis time was 42.7 s (σ = 6.3 s) with a memory footprint of 310 MB, roughly 1.8× PBVI but within practical limits for offline synthesis. Sensitivity analysis showed that satisfaction degraded gracefully as sensor noise increased up to 0.3, remaining above 0.85. Ablations removing the belief-abstraction refinement reduced satisfaction to 0.76, while removing the safety-margin term increased violations to 5.9%. Overall, the results indicate that the proposed method provides robust, verifiable control under partial observability while maintaining competitive scalability.

title: Covid-19 lockdown improves air quality in Morocco
text:
The COVID-19 lockdown in Morocco provided an unprecedented natural experiment for assessing the impact of reduced anthropogenic activity on air quality. Using ground-based monitoring data and satellite observations, this study demonstrates that the strict confinement measures implemented between March and June 2020 led to substantial improvements in key air pollutants across major Moroccan cities. Concentrations of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), particulate matter (PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅), and carbon monoxide (CO) declined significantly compared with pre-lockdown periods and with the same months in previous years, with NO₂ showing the most pronounced reduction, particularly in urban and traffic-dominated areas such as Casablanca and Rabat. Satellite retrievals from TROPOMI and MODIS corroborated these findings, revealing a marked decrease in tropospheric NO₂ columns and aerosol optical depth over the country during the lockdown window.

These results confirm that vehicular traffic, industrial activity, and other mobility-related sources are the dominant contributors to air pollution in Moroccan urban centers. The findings also highlight the potential health benefits of cleaner air, given the well-documented links between short- and long-term exposure to NO₂ and PM and respiratory and cardiovascular morbidity. At the same time, the improvements were transient, and pollutant levels rebounded rapidly as restrictions were eased, underscoring the structural nature of Morocco's air quality challenges.

From a policy perspective, this study suggests that sustained emission reductions require more than temporary behavioral change. Investments in public transport, cleaner fuels, renewable energy, and stricter emission standards, combined with improved monitoring networks, are essential to consolidate the gains observed during the lockdown. Future research should integrate epidemiological and socioeconomic data to quantify the health and economic co-benefits of such measures. Overall, the Moroccan lockdown experience offers valuable lessons for designing post-pandemic strategies that align economic recovery with long-term environmental and public health goals.

title: ConvGRU in Fine-grained Pitching Action Recognition for Action Outcome Prediction
text: Predicting the outcome of a pitch is a challenging task due to the rapid and subtle nature of pitching actions. In this paper, we address fine-grained pitching action recognition and action outcome prediction by proposing a ConvGRU-based framework. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on handcrafted features or single-frame analysis, our method captures spatiotemporal dependencies in pitching motions through convolutional gated recurrent units (ConvGRU), which jointly learn spatial hierarchies and temporal dynamics. We evaluate our approach on a newly constructed dataset of broadcast baseball pitching videos annotated with fine-grained action phases and pitch outcomes. Experimental results show that ConvGRU outperforms strong baselines including 3D CNNs and LRCN, achieving higher accuracy in both action recognition and outcome prediction. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of temporal resolution and input modalities, demonstrating that early prediction of pitch type and location is feasible within the initial phases of the pitching motion. Our findings suggest that integrating fine-grained action recognition with recurrent spatiotemporal modeling provides a promising direction for real-time sports analytics and predictive systems.

title: Competition among Large and Heterogeneous Small Firms
text:
1. Introduction
